c.t: The end of the long walk back. Park a station at your base, keep the remote in your pocket, and the mine is never far from home again. The station banks the power and pays for the jump itself; the remote only picks where. A trip is exactly as reliable as your base is charged: a full station is good for 25–50 trips home.

Place the station at your base and wire it up — it quietly banks up to 500,000 EU. Shift-right-click it with the remote — point saved. Name it, or leave it as "Teleporter 1". Right-click the remote anywhere — the list opens with the first point already selected. Hit Teleport — you're home. The remote works from either hand, and needs no clear sky to point at. Clicking stone, dirt or any block without its own action opens the list too — a mine has no sky, and a mine is exactly where you need it. Chests, crafting tables and machines still open as normal. One remote remembers up to 16 stations. Binding the same one twice does nothing — no duplicates.

Five seconds of wind-up: a purple vortex tightens around you — bystanders see it, and so do you in third person — a hum rises, and in the last second the screen fades almost to black. Then it snaps clear: you're there. What cancels it: stepping more than 2 blocks, taking damage, dying, logging out. A cancelled jump costs nothing — energy is only spent once you land. You cannot teleport out of a fight; you can absolutely finish mining and leave. After a jump, one minute of cooldown. You cannot jump while riding a horse, boat or minecart — dismount first. The teleporter moves the player and nobody else — it never drags anything along. What happens to a pet after that is vanilla's business, not the mod's. A tamed pet that is sitting, leashed or riding something stays where it is. A free-standing wolf or cat, on the other hand, will catch up on its own: a vanilla pet teleports to its owner once it is more than 12 blocks away. That only works while the pet is in a loaded chunk — after a jump halfway across the map it simply stays home.

The target station pays, not the remote. The price grows with distance and with how much you are hauling: a full inventory doubles the bill. Jump Cost Trips on a full station 100 blocks, travelling light 5,500 EU ~90 1,000 blocks, light 10,000 EU 50 1,000 blocks, full inventory 20,000 EU 25 10,000 blocks, full inventory 110,000 EU 4 It is the hungriest block in the mod — for comparison, the pump spends 1,000 EU per bucket. An everyday trip home, though, barely dents the buffer. 64 dirt and 64 diamonds weigh the same. What counts is how full your inventory is, not what is in it — simpler to grasp than a weight table for every item.

A station can be upgraded — and then it can throw you at a random point in the world, with no second station at the far end at all. Fitting the upgrade. Craft a Random Jump Chip and shift-right-click a placed station. The chip is consumed and the station keeps the module for good. A plain right-click will not do — that opens the station's screen; the sneak is the same one the remote uses to bind it. The module survives the block being broken (it rides the item along with the stored EU and the privacy flag), but the chip cannot be taken back out: one chip, one station. An upgraded station can be told apart at a glance. Teal brackets light up in the corners of its faces — the only teal on a violet-and-slate block, so there is nothing to confuse it with. The mark appears the moment the chip goes in and travels with the block. You never need to open a screen to find out whether a station is upgraded. Making the jump. Select a station in the remote's list and press Random. The station you selected is the one that pays — and the one that must carry the chip. Price 50 000 EU, flat — shown in the tooltip before you press Where to a random point in a ring 500…5000 blocks out Where it works the Overworld only Warmup / cooldown the same 5 s and 60 s as an ordinary jump Why the price is flat. An ordinary jump is priced by distance — but here the distance is unknown until the dice have been thrown. A flat price is the only one that can be shown to the player before they commit. Inventory weight is left out for the same reason. Why the Overworld only. The search leans on surface height. In the Nether that runs into the bedrock ceiling, and in the End there is void between the islands — "surface" means nothing there, and refusing honestly beats guessing and dropping someone into rock or into nothing. The landing is safe or the jump does not happen. The mod tries up to 8 spots: no lava, no water, no cactus, not inside a block, two clear blocks overhead. Nothing found means the jump is cancelled for free and you can simply press again. The spot is picked the moment you press (so a refusal is immediate rather than five seconds late) and measured again at the end of the warmup — if it went bad in those five seconds the jump is cancelled rather than carried out blind. Random is dearer than a targeted jump of the same length (5000 blocks would cost ~30 000 with an empty pack). That is what you pay for needing nothing built at the far end.

A stolen remote is useless — it binds to whoever first uses it, so a thief cannot follow it to your base. Stations are private by default: only the owner may jump to one. You can open it to everyone with the switch on its screen, but only after opening the padlock beside it — two deliberate clicks instead of one stray one. The lock closes itself again after each change. The same padlock guards the remote's Delete button: removing a point erases the only record of where home was.

Station screen: charge bar, owner name, and a Private/Public switch behind a padlock. A public station reads "Teleporter — <owner> (public)" in its title. Remote screen: your points with names and coordinates, a rename field, Delete (behind the padlock) and Teleport. If a jump will not start — station flat, still cooling down, station gone — the reason appears as a red band inside the screen and clears itself.

Field Value Role consumer with a buffer (accepts EU only) Buffer (EU) 500,000 — 25× the battery box Max input (EU/tick) 512 (HV) Max output (EU/tick) n/a (never gives EU back) EU/tick 0 while idle; one lump sum per jump The station is an ordinary HV consumer — the network finds it by itself. Idle, it costs nothing. It charges in minutes, not seconds. There is no HV infrastructure in the mod yet: a copper cable only carries 12 EU/tick (its ceiling is the segment buffer, not the tier voltage), so a full buffer is ~35 minutes over copper cable, or ~26 minutes from a single geothermal generator. That is the intent — the teleporter is slow-charging endgame gear.

A full 16³ cube, broken with a pickaxe. It keeps its privacy flag and stored EU when broken, but forgets its owner — replace the block and it is yours. The front face is inert; the other five accept EU.

The station is a real endgame recipe: electronic circuit eye of ender electronic circuit copper coil block of diamond copper coil uranium ingot uranium ingot uranium ingot The remote is cheaper: an ender pearl, an electronic circuit and 3 tempered iron. A station is useless without one, and a remote leads nowhere without a station.

Tier: HV, part of the "Beyond MV" cluster (ROADMAP). The gate is uranium and an eye of ender rather than an HV transformer: no such item exists in the mod, and a recipe cannot point at something that is not there. Grows into: cross-dimension jumps, whitelist privacy, a chunk-loading station mode.

The station is a fund, not a machine: the network feeds working machines first and tops the fund up from what is left. That gives three ways to charge it, at three different speeds. How Speed Stops when Generator over cable whatever the generator makes never, while the generator runs Storage over cable 12 EU/tick the donor is down to half its capacity Storage placed flush (no cable) up to 32 EU/tick the donor is empty Over a cable a store only gives away its surplus — whatever it holds above half. That is deliberate: the station's buffer is 500 000 EU against a Battery Box's 20 000, and without the floor a single station would drain the whole base bank and leave the machines dark. To fill it outright, put a store flush against it: the direct path has neither a rate limit nor a reserve, and it is the player's explicit way of saying "take everything". Machines always come first: while anything is working on the same network, the station charges only from the remainder.
Battery box — what charges the station. Electronic circuit — a crafting component. Pump — for comparison on EU appetite.

The Garden Drone Station is a 1×1 dock block (like a robot-vacuum base) from which a drone lifts off and patrols the area around the station within a 4-block radius. The drone is not an Entity — it's an object drawn by the station's own. Visually it looks and moves like a flying craft, but physically it always "belongs" to the station block and can never leave its zone. The player puts seeds and bone meal into the station and hooks up EU — from there the drone tends the farm on its own: tilling free dirt, planting seeds into empty tilled tiles, speeding up immature crops with bone meal, and hauling ripe harvest straight into its own output slots (no ever spawns in the world). It supersedes the planned-but-unbuilt "Crop Matron" and "Crop Harvester" — one block instead of two, no duplicated mechanics.

Field Value Role consumer with buffer Buffer (EU) 4000 Max input (EU/tick) 32 (LV) Max output (EU/tick) n/a (does not emit) EU per action 8 The station connects to the energy network like any consumer, on all its working faces. EU is spent only for a completed action — tilling, planting, fertilizing, or harvesting one tile — following the Electric Heater pattern: idling (nothing to do in the zone — out of seeds/fertilizer, or every tile already tended) costs 0 EU, and the station goes into idle sleep instead of wasting energy or becoming a parasitic sink on the network.

The station doesn't use the crafting-recipe system — instead, on every drone flight (when a target is found) it performs one of four actions on a single zone tile. Field Value Recipe type none (not a recipe machine) Actions per flight 1 (one action — one tile) Auto-unload yes (harvest lands directly in the station's output slots) The hoe powers two actions. Tilling and harvesting each spend one point of the hoe's durability and will not run without one: a tool that an action consumes but does not require makes no sense to the player. Planting and fertilizing need no hoe. Action priority (checked in this order, the first match runs): Harvest — a tile with a ripe crop in the zone (needs a hoe). Plant — an empty tilled tile, provided matching seeds sit in the seed slot. Fertilize — a tile with an immature crop, provided bone meal sits in the fertilizer slot. Till — a tile of free dirt (needs a hoe; turns it into tilled soil). This order keeps the "the farm tends itself" promise unbroken: without tilling as the fourth action, the promise would break the moment the player expands the farm. Flight. The action lands when the drone arrives, not when the target is picked: it flies at = 11 ticks per block of distance and only then does the work. A leg is never shorter than = 26 ticks — otherwise the drone would cover the tile next door faster than the eye can follow. The trip home takes as long as the trip out, plus the = 6 ticks the drone spends standing on the tile it worked (below), so one action costs at least 58 ticks (≈2.9 seconds), not a tick: the station tends the plot at the pace of a machine, not instantly. Without that it would tend a whole farm within a couple of ticks, which reads as teleportation rather than as a machine doing work. On arrival the job is re-validated — the world may have changed mid-flight (the player harvested it by hand, a piston moved it), so the target is checked again rather than trusted. Flight sound. While the drone is airborne a quiet rotor loop plays, and it comes from the drone itself — the source travels with it rather than sitting on the station. It has to: the drone ranges several blocks out and passes right over the player's head, and a buzz arriving from the pad instead would read as a bug. An 8-block audible radius and 0.22 volume make it the quietest loop in the mod, for two reasons — it is the only sound whose source comes to the player, and the only one that plays for most of a work cycle. On the pad, and during the beat spent standing on a worked tile, it is silent. Tilling sound. As it turns a tile, the drone plays the same vanilla hoe sound () a player hears tilling by hand, at the same volume and pitch. Only tilling is voiced of the four actions: it is the one with an unambiguous vanilla counterpart, which planting, fertilizing and harvesting do not have. Once the work is done the drone stands on the tile for 6 ticks before it heads home. Without that beat the action and the return leg began on the same tick: the drone touched the plot and lifted off inside a single frame, which read as a bounce rather than as a machine doing a job. The pause is only at the far end — on the pad it would shift the tick the action lands on, and that tick is what every test scenario counts to. Scan zone. A 4-block radius around the station — this is the tier-1 drone, and a machine that tends a 9x9 field straight out of the crafting table leaves nothing for a later tier to improve. Radius 4 is a comfortable plot around the dock. The target list for the zone is cached and invalidated by block updates inside the radius; a full cache rebuild happens no more often than once every = 20 ticks. Touching any zone position requires an check first — the station never forces a synchronous chunk load. Crop maturity is decided by a shared predicate reused from the Scythe (the same class that already decides whether a crop is ready to cut — pumpkin/melon stems, cactus/sugar cane base-only, berry bushes, and vanilla s are all handled identically in both places, with no risk of the edge cases drifting apart). Fertilizing goes through the standard vanilla interface (the same trio of methods already used by the Trellis for cotton) — the effect matches manual bone meal, minus the player and the click-particle simulation. Harvesting without a player. The station doesn't break a block through the path (there is no player) — instead it computes the ripe crop's drop server-side, inserts it into its own output slots, and only removes the crop block on full success. Neither an nor block-break events are created — the same conscious trade-off already accepted by the Pump when it drains a fluid source.

Slot Accepts Count Seeds (0) items tagged as seeds for the matching crop up to a stack Fertilizer (1) up to a stack Drone (6) — the station is inert without it 1 Hoe (7) any hoe (); spent by tilling and harvesting 1 Output 1–4 (2–5) insertion only by the station itself (harvest); manual/automated insertion from outside is blocked up to a stack each Four output slots, not one — a ripe crop can yield more than one item type in a single action (e.g. wheat drops both wheat and wheat seeds separately); the mod's base machine model doesn't support mixed contents in a single output slot. Inserting the drop into the output slots is a two-pass operation ("simulate room for every stack first, mutate only on full success") — no partial harvest loss when the output is full.

Type: container (station GUI). Shows: energy buffer bar, seed/fertilizer/output slots, station status (out of resources / working / everything tended this cycle — readable from a distance via the drone model's status light color).

The dock is not a full cube: a thin 1×1-block plate with a lit landing outline, two charging contacts, and yellow corner lamps (see "Appearance" below). The drone is drawn on top of it by a and has no collision/hitbox separate from the station. Field Value Shape a low-profile plate (not a full cube; occluder covers the lower part of the block) Hardness 3.0 Blast resistance 6.0 Tool pickaxe Drops with energy NBT no (buffer/inventory/drone state persist via /, not an item NBT drop)
Crafting: (iron/steel casing, electronic circuit, propellers — the exact composition is fixed during implementation). No processing recipes — the station doesn't process items.

Tier: LV. Power: any LV source, e.g. Generator. Supersedes (no code): "Crop Matron" and "Crop Harvester" one block instead of two stationary ones with the same outcome. Requires: an electronic circuit to craft, like most of the mod's LV machines.

Scythe — source of the reused crop-maturity predicate. Trellis — the mod's existing precedent. Incubator — reference for a multi-slot, index-tag-validated inventory with a wider-than-base . Pump — reference for bounded zone scanning, and the only precedent of a machine mutating a world block from its own tick with no player involved. Electric Heater — reference for "EU only on a useful tick" (demand-driven consumption).

The Incubator is a 1×2 multiblock: a squat mechanical base below and a glass dome above. Place any glass (the tag) on the base and it turns into a volumetric chamber, with the irradiated item floating and spinning inside. The machine mutates items in three ways: it duplicates (1 → 2), transforms (A → B), or creates a new mod material. Every operation costs EU (LV) and an irradiation charge: one buys 3 attempts, then burns out into which settles in the ash slot. The mode by a mutation chip in a dedicated slot — duplication / transformation / creation. Without a chip the machine does not run; the chip itself is never consumed. The outcome is probabilistic: on success a rarity grade is rolled — Common (70 %) / Rare (20 %) / Epic (8 %) / Legendary (2 %) — which colors the name and grants a bonus to further mutations. What it does How Forms the multiblock base + any block on top → dome Mutates items EU (LV) + a charge (1 = 3 attempts → 1 ) Mode chip slot: duplication / transformation / creation Mutation kinds duplicate (×2), transform (A→B), create (A→new mod item) Rarity every success rolls Common / Rare / Epic / Legendary (70/20/8/2 %) Slag 5 % of attempts yield instead of an empty failure

Hybrid model: EU from the grid (LV) plus uranium as the irradiation fuel. Uranium is not destroyed — it becomes , a feedstock for the future nuclear phase. Field Value EU buffer 8000 — holds the costliest operation in full Max input 32 EU/tick (LV) Consumption 8 EU/tick while running — four times the machine standard Fuel 1 = 3 attempts → 1 into the ash slot Without uranium in the fuel slot an operation will not start; EU is spent only while a cycle runs.

Duration and cost are tied to the mutation kind. The Incubator is the mod's most energy-hungry LV machine: the floor is 2400 EU per operation versus 200–300 for routine machines. Kind Success chance Ticks EU/attempt On failure Transform 0.75 300 (15 s) 2400 input lost, −1 charge Duplicate 0.45 500 (25 s) 4000 input lost, −1 charge Create 0.25 1000 (50 s) 8000 input lost, −1 charge Three outcomes of an attempt: Outcome Probability What happens Success chance by kind (+ gene bonus, cap 0.95) result into the output slot + a grade roll Slag 5 % input lost, drops into the output Failure the remainder input lost, output unchanged Slag is subtracted from the failure, never from the success — the success chance never drops. A grade is rolled only on success (slag is always Common). The outcome is rolled at the end of the cycle: until the last tick the result is unknown and cannot be cancelled by pulling the input. Grade. On success a rarity is rolled: Common 70 % / Rare 20 % / Epic 8 % / Legendary 2 %. A Common grade leaves no trace — the item still stacks with vanilla. Rare and above write the component and color the name (yellow / aqua / light purple). The input gene burns. The input item's grade grants its chance bonus (+5 / +10 / +15 p.p. for Rare / Epic / Legendary, the total capped at 0.95) and burns away — the result always gets a fresh grade roll. A Legendary cannot be multiplied via duplicate; it can only be spent for the higher chance.

Five slots: chip, fuel (uranium), the item to mutate, the result, and ash. The result and ash slots are read-only for the player; automation into the ash slot is pull-only. Slot Accepts Behaviour Chip (3 chips) 1 item; not consumed; sets the mode; an empty slot means the machine will not run; automation cannot take it out Fuel (= ) 1 ingot is taken the moment it lands in an assembled machine; a charge = 3 attempts Input items with a mutation recipe in the selected mode 1 stack; consumes 1/attempt (lost on failure) Result the mutation result or 1 stack; fill-only Ash 1 stack; +1 per exhausted ingot; pull-only

The screen shows: EU storage, cycle progress, the irradiation charge (0–3), the five slots and a formed indicator. The energy bar runs down the left edge; the irradiation charge is a vertical column of pips right of the fuel slot, filling from the bottom up. Top row: chip, input, progress arrow, result; bottom row: fuel and ash. The chip slot is the top left one. While it is empty, the status line names what is missing ("Needs glass on top" → "Needs a chip"). Swapping the chip resets the progress of the current operation. Both halves of the multiblock are clickable: right-clicking the dome opens the same menu as clicking the base.

A two-tier multiblock with deliberately different silhouettes: a heavy mechanical bottom and a light rounded top — not "two cubes stacked on each other". Base — a full cube with a recessed front panel, an emitter ring along the top face and cooling ports on the sides. While running, an emitter glow rises above it. Dome — a volumetric rounded chamber, placed automatically from any block. The original glass type is remembered, so: dismantling the multiblock returns exactly your glass — nothing is lost; stained glass tints the dome — 17 colors with no extra recipes: 16 stained-glass dyes plus an uncolored variant. The frame and the spire always stay the casing's dark metal. The irradiated item floats at the center of the chamber and slowly spins; while running — particles and a pulsing glow.

Base block follows the machine-assembly standard, full 3×3 grid: 1 machine casing + 2 uranium plates + 3 glass + 1 electronic circuit + 2 iron plates. The uranium plates gate entry into the mechanic behind an established uranium chain (ore → ingot → plate). The three mode chips are crafted from plus a thematic filling; a uranium plate in each is the shared "irradiating" element: Chip Recipe Mode empty chip + 2 amethyst shards + uranium plate duplicate empty chip + redstone + lapis + uranium plate transform empty chip + diamond + echo shard + uranium plate create Recipe type — three separate types, one per mode: , , . Each JSON describes one input → one output with an optional override. Fuel is not mentioned in the recipe — uranium is the machine's charge, not an ingredient.

The cost of an attempt is fixed (⅓ of an ingot + 4000 EU + 25 s), so the only balance lever is the success chance: the more valuable the item, the lower the chance. Class Chance Items Gems and precious ingots 0.45 ,, , , , Minerals and common ingots 0.55 ,, ,, , , , , , Rare organics 0.60 , , , , Basic crops 0.85 , , , ,, Ingots yes, processed parts no. Vanilla and mod ingots are duplicated (,, , ,,) — these are base materials. Anything processed (dusts, plates, casings, circuits, chips, cables, raw ore and ore blocks) is not — it would devalue the crafting chain. Uranium is not duplicated (no recipe). Rubber is a stated exception. It is a machine product, so by the rule above it should not duplicate. But oil is a finite resource — lakes do not refill and nothing turns water into oil — so without the Incubator the amount of rubber in a world is capped by the deposits you happen to find. Duplication is an expensive renewable route, not a free one: an attempt costs 4000 EU and a third of a uranium ingot at a 0.55 chance, while the same rubber made from fresh oil costs 400 EU. While there is oil left, pumping is ten times cheaper; the Incubator matters once there is not.

Like is traded for like. Upgrading by value (iron → gold) is forbidden. All 27 recipes share a 0.75 chance, 300-tick duration and 2400 EU cost. For families with many members (saplings, flowers, soils) a ring is used: each item turns into the next one around the circle until the wanted one comes up. Category Recipes Ring Minerals 3 ↔, ↔ , ↔ (all 1:1) Saplings 8 oak → birch → spruce → jungle → acacia → dark oak → cherry → mangrove → oak Flowers 8 dandelion → poppy → blue orchid → allium → azure bluet → cornflower → lily of the valley → oxeye daisy → dandelion Soils 5 dirt → podzol → mycelium → dirt; sand ↔ red sand

An ordinary item evolves into a unique mod material along a three-tier ladder. The higher the tier, the lower the chance and the costlier the operation. From tier 2 onward a failure returns the input intact (only the charge and EU burn) — otherwise no one would risk climbing past tier 1. Branch Tier 1 Tier 2 Tier 3 Diamond — energy density → irradiated diamond → diamond matrix → singularity core Crystal — optics → resonant shard → focusing lens → prismatic core Biological — agriculture → mutagen dust → living mutagen → gene matrix Nuclear — fuel → unstable isotope → enriched core → isotope concentrate Tier Chance Ticks EU On failure 1 (vanilla → mod material) 0.25 1000 8000 input is lost 2 0.15 1500 12000 input returned intact 3 0.08 2000 16000 input returned intact The nuclear branch starts from the Incubator's own ash — spent uranium becomes the entry to a chain rather than waste. The current release ships only the 4 tier-1 recipes (one per branch): → , → , → , → . Tiers 2–3 and upgrade chips from the upper materials come in the next release.

Tier: LV. Best built after the first machines (macerator/extractor), once you have a stable uranium vein and an EU grid. Introduces 7 new items: , , , , , (a by-product of 5 % of attempts — no consumers in this release, groundwork for the future) and three mode chips. Grade "genes" on materials grant a bonus to further mutation chances (+5/+10/+15 p.p.) — consumers will arrive in future agriculture/nuclear phases. Mutation advancements: first mutation, first result, first Legendary outcome.

Uranium — the fuel ingot. Nuclear theme — where goes. Teleporter multiblock — a sibling structural task. Sawmill — the reference machine with switchable modes. Solar panel — the reference for a chip slot driving machine behaviour.

The Trellis is a support for climbing plants and the mod's first crop. Cotton grows on it today, and it is the farming answer to hunting spiders for fibre: grown in a field instead of being knocked out of mobs. The name is deliberately generic — the support is meant for future plants too. The trellis stands two blocks tall — the plant climbs it. Place it on tilled soil, then right-click it with cotton seeds. From there the plant lives in two phases: Rooting — the long phase, and it is walked through once in the plant's life. The cotton slowly climbs the support until it wraps both blocks. Fruiting — a short cycle that repeats forever. The bush fills with bolls, you pick them with a right-click, and it fills again. The point: harvesting never destroys the plant. Right-clicking a ripe bush takes the cotton and returns it to its grown, boll-free state — patience is the price of the plant itself, not of every harvest.

Both phases only advance under two conditions: tilled and moist soil under the lower half (farmland next to water); enough light, as for vanilla crops. If the soil dries out or the light goes, growth pauses: the stage is never lost, the plant never dies and never reverts to a seed. Restore the water and it continues from the same stage. This is deliberate — walking away from the game must not wipe out a plantation. Bone meal speeds growth up, but buys strictly one stage per use, so it cannot turn a bare trellis into a ripe bush on the spot. Plants can be packed as densely as you like: the trellis does not tick like a machine, so a large plantation costs the world nothing.

Action Result Right-click a ripe bush 1–2 cotton fibre, 35 % chance of cotton seeds; the bush stays and fills again Right-click an unripe bush nothing happens, the state does not change Break the trellis the trellis comes back, plus the seed if something was planted Break tall or short grass 5 % chance of cotton seeds (not while shearing — the same rule vanilla applies to wheat seeds); Fortune raises the count Grass is the entry point into the chain: clearing a plain finds the first seeds in the same place wheat seeds come from. After that the plantation sustains itself, since harvesting returns seeds too.

Property Value Height 2 blocks (lower and upper half) Base tilled soil () Hardness 0.2 — breaks instantly by hand Sound grass Collision yes — the trellis blocks movement like a fence post Piston does not move it (half a multiblock must not be torn from its pair) Breaking both halves go together; the trellis drops exactly once
The trellis is sticks tied with string: Ingredients Result 4 × stick + 2 × string 1 × trellis
Cotton fibre is the feedstock for the coming Fluxweave line: it gives the farmer the same route the spider's string gives the fighter.
Incubator — seed duplication by irradiation (cotton to be added later). Rubber — an example of one spec covering several ids through an alias.

The Advanced Circuit is the second tier of the Electronic Circuit, and the first part that forces you to finish the oil chain. It's an item, not a block: you only meet it as an ingredient in MV recipes. It's built on top of a finished plain circuit: the circuit itself in the centre, four gold plates along the edges (rewiring it onto a better conductor) and four rubber in the corners (sealing the board). The icon is a near-black board with a green die in the middle, gold contacts and rows of grey pins down both flanks — next to the warm copper-brown Electronic Circuit it reads as the sterner, pricier part. The point of the tier is to tie together two paths that ran in parallel until now. Metals led to machines, oil led to insulated cables, and they only ever met on wiring. From now on you cannot reach MV without going through oil → Polymerizer → Vulcanizer. Mini-example: craft a plain circuit, hammer out four gold plates and pull four rubber off your oil line. Circuit in the middle of the workbench, gold on the sides, rubber in the corners — that's an advanced circuit. Two of them go into an Advanced Machine Casing.
Stores and consumes no energy — it's a plain crafting ingredient.

A required part of the Advanced Machine Casing — two per casing. Through the casing it lands in the price of every MV machine; the first of them is the Assembler. LV recipes are untouched: they still ask for the plain circuit and the plain casing.
Not applicable (item). Stack: 64.
— rubber (×4); — gold plate (×4); — electronic circuit (×1). Yields 1.

Tier: MV. The first component that needs metallurgy and petrochemistry at the same time. Input chains: and . Both branches have to be finished — there is no way around the oil. Rubber is the expensive input. One piece costs a bucket of oil, four sulfur dust and 800 EU across two machines, so it pays to put an Electric Heater under the Vulcanizer: the same batch of sulfur then yields three times the rubber. The gold goes in as plates, not ingots: a plate already requires a Forge Hammer or a Compressor, i.e. a finished metalworking phase.

Electronic Circuit — the LV predecessor, and an ingredient here. Rubber — the end of the oil chain, sealing the board. Advanced Machine Casing — the only consumer. Assembler — the first MV machine, reached through the casing. Material Forms — the gold plate.

The Advanced Machine Casing is the Machine Casing one tier up: mid-tier (MV) machines are built on it. It is crafted from a plain casing clad in 6 Tempered Iron plates above and below, with 2 Advanced Circuits on either side. The chain still reads plainly, but it is now a double one: iron → tempered iron → plate gives you the cladding, and oil → rubber → advanced circuit gives you the innards. Reaching MV costs a full pass through the furnace and either the Forge Hammer or the Compressor and a finished oil line, rather than replaying LV with a different texture. It does nothing on its own and holds no energy — it is a crafting part, and incidentally a building block: dark steel with four riveted panels, easy to tell apart from the pale LV casing. Quick example: already have a machine casing? Smelt 6 iron ingots into tempered iron and hammer them into 6 plates, then craft 2 Advanced Circuits. Casing in the middle of the grid, a circuit to its left and right, plates in rows above and below — that is your advanced casing.
An ordinary solid block with a metallic feel. Tougher than the LV casing — it is the step up, after all. Field Value Tool any pickaxe Drop itself

Craft: a plain Machine Casing in the middle, 2 Advanced Circuits on either side of it, and 6 tempered-iron plates in rows above and below. Where it's used: the base of MV machines. The first of them is the Assembler.

Tier: MV. The first part that exists purely for the mid tier. Requires a finished LV casing, i.e. the plate phase and the first machines behind you. Since it also requires 2 Advanced Circuits, i.e. a finished oil line: oil → Polymerizer → Vulcanizer → rubber. Before that, reaching MV was one more lap around the iron chain you had already mastered, and it did not feel like a step up. Existing LV machines are untouched: their recipes still use the plain casing.

Machine Casing — the LV predecessor, and an ingredient here. Tempered Iron — the cladding material. Material Forms — plates. Electronic Circuit — the other mandatory part of machine recipes. Advanced Circuit — the MV circuit seated in this casing. Assembler — the first MV machine built on this casing.

Evolution chips are crafting components that turn base T1 forms into T2. Two variants: Solar chip (day) — evolves the base solar panel into the daylight T2 and the base wind mill into the sky T2. Lunar chip (night) — evolves the base panel into the moonlit T2, and the wind mill into the tempest T2. Evolution carries accumulated NBT energy: the base block's charge is not lost during the upgrade. The chip itself is consumed in the process. Mini-example: place a solar panel, accumulate EU, craft a solar chip → evolve the panel to T2 — the charge carries over, the chip is spent, and daytime output quadruples.
Stores none. The chip is a one-shot evolution catalyst; all EU logic lives on the evolving block.
Applied through the evolution slot/recipe of a base T1 block (solar panel or wind mill). After evolution the chip disappears, the T1 becomes a T2 with its NBT energy preserved.
Not applicable (item). Stack: 64.

Both chips are crafted at a workbench on the same shaped 3×3 pattern: nickel in the corners, a glowing/lapis block in a cross, and an electronic circuit at the centre. Solar chip (day): = glowstone. Lunar chip (night): = lapis block. — nickel ingot (×4); — electronic circuit (×1).

Components with no tier of their own. Open the T2 era of solar and wind generation. Nickel + glowstone/lapis is a moderate early gate, reachable after a first Nether trip (glowstone) or deep-cave mining (lapis).

Solar Panel and Wind Mill — the T1 bases. Daylight / moonlit T2 panels — the results of evolution with the solar/lunar chip. Sky / tempest T2 wind mills — the wind evolution results. Electronic Circuit — the chip's central component. Nickel — the chip's corners.

The Battery is the mod's first energy carrier: a small 2 000 EU cell you can charge, discharge and carry by the handful. It is still a crafting component, too — batteries go into the Energy Pack, the Electric Drill, the Jetpack, Fluxweave armour and the rest of the powered gear. What sets it apart from every other powered item in the mod: the battery stacks, and it stacks by charge level. Batteries drained to zero stack with freshly crafted ones, equally charged batteries stack with each other, and batteries at different charges sit apart. One glance at the inventory tells you which are full and which are empty. Mini-example: charge a handful of batteries in a Battery Box before heading out. Your drill runs dry mid-dig — pull out a battery, right-click the drill, and it is full again. Back home, drop the leftovers into the discharge slot and the energy goes back into the grid.

Field Value Charge 2 000 EU per battery Stack up to 16 — a full stack carries 32 000 EU Intake 32 EU/t (the LV ceiling) Right-click transfer 500 EU per click Charge is stored per battery. A stack of sixteen therefore takes sixteen times as long to fill as a single one: the store pays for each battery, not for the stack.

the charge slot of the Battery Box — available from the very start; the charge slot of the Reinforced Energy Storage; standing on the Charging Station, which fills batteries right in your inventory. A worn Energy Pack does not charge batteries: a full stack holds more than the pack itself, so it would drain into your spares instead of powering your tools. Discharging also works three ways: the discharge slot of the Battery Box; the discharge slot of the Reinforced Energy Storage; right-click with the battery in one hand and a chargeable item in the other — 500 EU per click. This only works with a single item in each hand: charge is counted per battery, so "pour out of a stack" would have no single sensible meaning.

Recipes that build a battery into a powered item carry its charge into the result: craft a drill from two full batteries and the drill arrives with 4 000 EU. The sum is capped by the result's own buffer, and the surplus is lost. A drained battery behaves in those recipes exactly as it always did — the result comes out empty. Recipes whose result stores no EU (Battery Box, Reinforced Energy Storage, Charging Station, Electric Furnace) do not carry charge — it is simply lost. Build those from drained batteries.
Not applicable (item). Stack: 16.
Crafted at a workbench (shaped 3×3): see for the exact pattern. Key materials are tin, redstone and copper cable.
The first step of the EU-carrier line: battery → (planned) energy crystal → lapotron crystal. Arrives at LV, before the Energy Pack, and stays a component of every powered item after it.

Battery Box — charges and discharges batteries. Reinforced Energy Storage — the same at MV speed. Charging Station — charges batteries in your inventory. Energy Pack — the wearable buffer built from three batteries. Battery Pouch — the neighbouring powered item of the same tier.

The Copper Coil is a crafting component: copper cable wound around a tin core. It's an item, not a block — you only see it as an ingredient in recipes. Its first job is the Electric Drill, which takes two coils in the bottom row of its recipe. The coil is the mod's first "electrical" part — it ties two of the base material lines (copper cable and tin) into a single piece that later electric tools and devices build on. Mini-example: once you're making copper cable and have some tin, wind three ingots' worth of core with six lengths of cable to get a coil — that's halfway to an Electric Drill.
Uses no energy — it's a plain crafting ingredient.
A pure intermediate. It crafts into the Electric Drill (two coils per drill), and is expected to appear in later electric tools and devices.
Not applicable (item). Stack: 64.

Crafted at a workbench (shaped 3×3): a column of three tin ingots as the core down the middle, with six lengths of copper cable as the winding filling the left and right columns. — copper cable (×6); — tin ingot (×3, core). The recipe appears in the recipe book once you have copper cable or a tin ingot.

A component with no tier of its own. Sits between early resource gathering (copper + tin) and your first electric tool. It exists so the drill can't be built from plain iron alone — you need the mod's electrical line first.
Electric Drill — the coil's first consumer. Copper Cable — the winding. Tin — the core.

The Electronic Circuit is the mod's base crafting component — the "brain" of nearly every early (LV) machine and storage block. It's an item, not a block: you only see it as an ingredient in machine recipes. It's what makes the progression feel real — before you can assemble a machine, you first have to assemble its brain. It's built at a workbench from the mod's metals (silver and nickel) plus quartz and an emerald, so it pushes you to mine and smelt the mod's ores. The circuit itself stores no energy. Mini-example: smelt some silver and nickel, grab a piece of quartz and an emerald, and assemble a circuit at your workbench. That one circuit is the part every LV machine asks for — make a few and you're ready to craft your Macerator.
Uses no energy — it's a plain crafting ingredient.

A pure intermediate, and the early-game bottleneck: almost every LV machine and generator asks for at least one. It crafts into the Generator, the Macerator, the Solar Panel, the Pump and the rest of the early machine line and electric items. The Battery Box does not take a circuit — it crafts without one. It later evolves into the Advanced Circuit (for MV and above).
Not applicable (item). Stack: 64.

Assembled at a workbench (shaped 3×3): silver ingots in the four corners, nickel ingots top and bottom centre, quartz on the left and right sides, and an emerald as the conducting core in the centre. — silver ingot (×4); — nickel ingot (×2); — quartz (×2); — emerald (×1).

A component with no tier of its own. The early crafting bottleneck — every LV machine needs at least one, which forces you to mine and smelt the mod's silver and nickel before you automate. Priced to sting a little, not to block the first machine.
Macerator — the first machine that requires a circuit. Silver and Nickel — the ores you mine for it. Material Forms — the wider ore → dust → ingot chain.

The Empty Chip is a crafting component — the blank base that functional upgrade chips are built on. It's an item, not a block. On its own it does nothing, and it cannot be installed in a machine's upgrade slot (the slot rejects it). Its only role is the shared starting point from which the real chips are assembled — the first of which is the Mute Chip. It keeps the upgrade line consistent: you first craft a "blank", then build it up into whichever chip you need. It holds no energy and never goes into a machine as-is. Mini-example: sandwich an Electronic Circuit between two Copper Coils inside a glass frame and you have an Empty Chip — the blank you then turn into a Mute Chip by wrapping it in wool.
Uses no energy — it's a plain crafting ingredient.
A pure intermediate. It crafts into the Mute Chip and is the intended base for future upgrade chips. Don't try to drop it into a machine's upgrade slot — nothing happens, by design.
Not applicable (item). Stack: 64.

Crafted at a workbench (shaped 3×3): a full border of plain glass (top and bottom rows), with two Copper Coils flanking an Electronic Circuit across the middle row. — glass (×6); — copper coil (×2); — electronic circuit (×1).
A component with no tier of its own. The common root of the upgrade-chip line — every functional chip starts from this blank, so you make one whenever you want a new upgrade.
Mute Chip — the first functional chip built on this base. Electronic Circuit — its core ingredient. Copper Coil — its side ingredient.

An Energy Clot is what the Energy Condenser turns the grid's surplus into: energy that would otherwise simply vanish. There are three tiers — I, II and III — and they are three distinct items, not a stack of the same one. A clot cannot be bought and cannot be crafted: the only way to get one is to let the condenser's bank fill up and take what its output slot offers. The longer you wait, the higher the tier. Clot Banked EU required Times the previous one Tier I 250,000 EU — Tier II 1,000,000 EU ×4 Tier III 4,000,000 EU ×4 Mini-example: the condenser has banked 950,000 — the slot holds a tier-I clot. Take it now and that is what you get, while the 700,000 above its price burn. Wait for the million and the very same slot hands you tier II.
A clot neither stores nor gives back EU: the energy was spent the moment it formed. This is a material, not a battery — you cannot slot it into a machine to power it.

The only use is machine overclockers, and every step needs a Overclocker What goes into it Overclocker I tier I clot + an empty chip + two gold ingots + redstone Overclocker II tier II clot + Overclocker I + three gold ingots Overclocker III tier III clot + Overclocker II + three gold ingots The steps stack: each tier is built on top of the previous one, so reaching tier III costs all three clots in sequence, not just the last.
Not applicable (items). Stack: 64. They are pulled from the condenser's output slot by hand, hopper or pipe — and taking one wipes the bank completely, however full it was.
Not applicable (items).
No tier has a crafting recipe — clots are only ever grown in the condenser. There is no way back either: a clot cannot be broken down into EU.

They appear once you have surplus generation: on a hungry grid the condenser banks nothing. They gate the entire machine-speed branch — without clots no overclocker can be built at all. The way to speed this up is scale, not upgrades: more condensers and thicker wiring.
Energy Condenser — the only source. Overclocker — the only consumer. Empty Chip — the other half of the first-tier recipe.

Flux Thread and Fluxweave Cloth are two steps of one material, and the only road to the Fluxweave armour. The chain is short and one-way: The thread is plated in the Galvanic Bath — the one machine in the mod that needs water to run. The cloth is made on a crafting table: four threads in a square give one bolt. Mini-example: one thread is 25 seconds of bath time and 1000 EU. A bolt takes four threads, and a chestplate takes four bolts: sixteen threads, nearly seven minutes of the bath running without a pause.
Neither thread nor cloth stores energy. The EU goes into making the thread, and a charge only appears once the armour itself is finished.

Thread only ever goes into cloth — it has no other consumer. Cloth goes into the four armour pieces and, separately, into repairing them: the set is mended with cloth on a crafting table or an anvil. Armour piece Cloth Threads behind it Helmet 2 8 Chestplate 4 16 Leggings 2 8 Boots 2 8 Full set 10 40 Besides cloth, every piece takes an electronic circuit, a battery and tempered iron — and the battery's charge carries over into the finished item instead of burning away.
Not applicable (items). Stack: 64.
Not applicable (items).

Flux Thread: fibre (vanilla string or cotton fibre) + silver dust in the Galvanic Bath, 25 seconds and 1000 EU apiece, plus water in the tank. Fluxweave Cloth: four threads in a 2×2 square on a crafting table, no machine involved. There is no way back: cloth cannot be unravelled into threads.

Gated behind silver and the Galvanic Bath, i.e. the middle of the LV branch. The most time-expensive material of the mod at this stage — the bath is slower than any other machine, and a full set needs forty threads, close to seventeen minutes of its running time. Unlocks the only EU armour set; keep spare cloth around, because that is also what repairs a worn set.
Galvanic Bath — where the thread is plated. Fluxweave Armour — what all of it is for. Silver Ore — the source of the dust used in plating.

The Machine Casing is the base block that machines are built from. It is forged from 8 iron plates (a ring on the crafting grid) and then becomes the body of an LV machine: a machine recipe is the casing plus its defining part. This builds a clear chain: ingot → plate → casing → machine. On its own it holds no energy and interacts with nothing — it is an intermediate part and, at the same time, a rugged building block (the "grid plating" look). Mini-example: want a Macerator? First hammer 8 iron plates (or press them in a Compressor), craft a casing from them, then casing + flint + electronic circuit — and the Macerator is done.
An ordinary solid block with a metal feel. Broken by any pickaxe. Field Value Tool any pickaxe Drop itself

8 iron plates → 1 casing (crafting grid, ring , ). No reverse recipe — the casing is a part, not a storage form. Where it is used: the base of LV machines. The Macerator, Extractor, Compressor, Polymerizer and Incubator are all built on the casing (casing + defining part + electronic circuit). Generators are not tied to the casing — they are the entry point into power.
A Phase 3 intermediate: gives the iron plate its main sink and tidies up machine crafting. Machines already placed in the world keep working; only the crafting recipe of new ones changed.

Material forms — the plates the casing is built from. Forge Hammer — the hand way to make plates before electricity. Macerator · Extractor · Compressor · Polymerizer · Incubator — the machines built on the casing.

The material forms are a family of intermediate items — dust, and later plate, billet and wire — that machines and recipes turn ores and ingots into. In the first phase you only meet dust: it's what the Macerator produces, and it's the trick behind "ore doubling" (an ore block or raw ore → 2 dust → 2 ingots). The second form is the plate: a flat blank pressed from an ingot. You hammer it by hand with the Forge Hammer (ingot + hammer → plate) before electricity, and later stamp them in bulk in the Compressor (ingot → plate, 260 EU). Plates are the blank for the Machine Casing and future circuits; a spare plate can be recycled back into dust ×1 in the Macerator. Plates exist for nine pure metals and for all four alloys of the Alloy Smelter — bronze, invar, cupronickel and electrum. The third form is the reinforced plate: the upgraded tier of rolled stock, and only the four alloys have it. Two ordinary plates compress into one reinforced plate — with the same hammer on the crafting grid, or in the same Compressor (2 plates → 1, 260 EU). It eats twice the metal, so it is meant for late, heavy recipes. The other forms (billet, wire) belong to the same family and are added later, as the machines that consume them appear. The forms hold no energy — they're just intermediates. Mini-example: mine one iron ore, run it through the Macerator to get 2 iron dust, then smelt each dust in a furnace — that's 2 iron ingots from a single ore instead of the usual 1.
Uses no energy — these are plain crafting ingredients.

Dust is the hub of the ore-processing chain: Metal dust is smelted back into an ingot. That closes the doubling loop: ore → 2 dust → 2 ingots. Exactly where it melts depends on the metal: Dust Vanilla furnace and the Iron Furnace Electric Furnace Iron, copper, gold ✅ ✅ Silver, tin, nickel ✅ ✅ Uranium, palladium ✖ ✅ The blast furnace smelts dust for no metal at all — it only works with ore and raw material. Non-metal dust (coal, diamond, emerald, lapis) is compressed back into the gem/item in the Compressor — not smelted. Same loop shape: ore → 2 dust → 2 items. There's no way to duplicate material. Macerating a finished ingot gives only 1 dust, so is net-zero (you only spend energy).
Not applicable (items). Stack: 64.
Not applicable (items).

How much dust the Macerator gives depends on what you feed it: Input Dust out Ore block (stone or deepslate) ×2 Raw ore ×2 Finished item (ingot, or a pure gem/coal) ×1 The one special case is lapis: lapis ore gives ×6 dust. Vanilla lapis ore already drops 4–9, so a plain ×2 would make maceration pointless; 6 is a guaranteed yield above the average pickaxe drop, which is what justifies the energy cost.

Getting dust: macerate ore or metal in the Macerator (see that page for the per-recipe energy cost). Metal dust → ingot: smelt it in a vanilla furnace or the Iron Furnace (uranium and palladium dust excepted), or in the mod's Electric Furnace — that one melts any of them. The blast furnace does not take dust. Non-metal dust → item: compress it in the Compressor.

Items with no tier of their own. The whole point of building your first energy network: dust is what turns the Macerator from a machine into an ore-doubler. The non-metal dusts give the same deal for coal and the gems.

Macerator — produces dust (ore doubling). Electric Furnace — smelts metal dust back into ingots. Compressor — compresses non-metal dust back into gems/coal. Electronic Circuit — the other key early component.

Metal gears are a family of crafting components: stone, iron, gold and silver. All four are built from the same blank — a wooden gear — pressed with a cross of their tier's material. They are items, not blocks: they exist only as ingredients. The mod already has the wooden gear, which goes into the Wind Mill, its Wooden Rotor, the Water Mill and the Stock Display Frame. The metal gears carry that same line further up the material ladder. The iron gear already works: the Fluid Tank, the Item Pipe and the Wrench are all built on it. Note: the stone, gold and silver gears build into nothing for now — no recipe consumes them. They were added ahead of the machinery of upcoming work (MV/HV drives). Until the first consumer lands this is a dead-end branch of the crafting tree, and that is a deliberate decision, not an oversight.
They use no energy — plain crafting ingredients.

The iron gear is a working ingredient: the fluid tank, the item pipe and the wrench are built on it. The stone, gold and silver gears have no consumers yet — their niche, parts for MV/HV machinery and drives, will arrive later.
Not applicable (items). Stack: 64.
Not applicable (items).

All four are crafted the same way (shaped 3×3): a cross of the tier's material around a wooden gear in the centre. — wooden gear (×1); — the tier material (×4): Gear Material Stone Cobblestone, blackstone or cobbled deepslate (tag ) Iron Iron ingot Gold Gold ingot Silver Silver ingot For reference, the wooden gear itself is four sticks in a cross around a wooden button. Each gear's recipe shows up in the recipe book as soon as you hold a wooden gear and the matching tier material.

Components with no tier of their own. A step between the wooden gear and future machinery: stone is the cheapest, iron the workhorse, gold and silver for jobs that will call for a pricier metal. The silver gear is the only one tied to a metal of the mod itself — it gives silver a use beyond the Silver Chest.

Wind Mill — consumer of the wooden gear. Water Mill — consumer of the wooden gear (block craft). Water Mill Wheel — consumer of the wooden gear. Stock Display Frame — another wooden-gear consumer. Copper Coil — another early-game crafting component.

Mutation chips are three items that switch the Incubator between its working modes. The chip goes into a slot of its own; an empty slot means the machine will not start at all — it never picks a mode by itself. A chip is never consumed: build it once and it works forever. What gets spent is uranium and EU; the chip only tells the machine what to do with the input. Duplication chip — get a second copy of an item. Transformation chip — trade an item for one of equal worth: lapis for redstone, sapling for sapling. Creation chip — grow a unique mod material out of a vanilla item. Mini-example: with the duplication chip in place, diamonds turn into copies. Swap it for the creation chip and that same diamond becomes an irradiated diamond. Same machine, same input, different result.
Chips neither store nor draw energy. The whole cost of an attempt sits with the Incubator: uranium as charge, plus EU by mode.

The chip occupies the Incubator's top-left slot. While it is empty, the status line says outright what is missing. Swapping a chip mid-run resets the progress of the current attempt, so change modes between runs rather than halfway through one. Automation can put a chip in but not take one out: the slot allows push and forbids pull, otherwise a pipe would yank the chip out mid-operation. More than one chip will not fit. Chip Mode What it does to the input Duplication a second identical item; the more valuable the input, the lower the chance Transformation an equal-worth trade, 0.75 chance across every recipe Creation vanilla item → unique mod material, 0.25 chance on the first rung Full tables of chances, costs and item lists live on the Incubator page.
Not applicable (items). Stack: 64 in a normal inventory, 1 in the chip slot.
Not applicable (items).

All three are crafted around an empty chip, and all three have a uranium plate at the base — the chip has to withstand the very irradiation the Incubator runs on. Chip What goes in Duplication two amethysts flanking the empty chip, uranium plate below Transformation redstone and lapis flanking the empty chip, uranium plate below Creation a diamond and an echo shard flanking the empty chip, uranium plate below The creation chip is the dearest of the three: echo shards only come from an ancient city, and that is a deliberate gate in front of the strongest mode.

They need a uranium plate, which means the nuclear branch: uranium first, mutations after. The duplication chip is the cheapest way into the machine; the creation chip unlocks materials that drop and craft nowhere else. None of the three is consumed, so the full set is built once per playthrough.
Incubator — the only machine that reads them. Empty Chip — the blank all three are built on. Uranium Ore — where the plate at the base comes from.

Mutation products are materials that sit in no chest, no ore and no crafting grid: only the Incubator yields them. They come in two groups. The first rung of four ladders (creation mode, 0.25 chance, 8000 EU per attempt): From What you get Ladder Diamond Irradiated Diamond energy density Amethyst shard Resonant Shard optics Lapis lazuli Mutagen Dust agriculture Depleted Uranium Unstable Isotope nuclear By-products of the machine running: Depleted Uranium — what a uranium ingot burns down into: one ingot is three attempts and then settles in the ash slot. It is also the input of the nuclear ladder, so the Incubator's ash feeds the Incubator. Irradiated Slag — turns up in 5 % of attempts instead of a plain failure. The input is lost. Mini-example: four uranium ingots through the Incubator give twelve attempts and four depleted ingots. Put those back into the input with a creation chip and try to lift them to unstable isotopes.
None of these materials stores energy. The EU is spent by the Incubator at the moment of the attempt.

Honestly: today, hardly at all. All four first-rung materials exist, can be obtained and can be stacked in a chest — but nothing in this release consumes them. Rungs two and three of the ladders (the diamond matrix, the focusing lens, the living mutagen, the enriched core and everything above) are not implemented yet. The one working use right now is Depleted Uranium: it goes back into the machine as the input of the nuclear branch. Stockpiling the rest only makes sense if you enjoy being ready early. Building a farm of Incubators for their sake is premature.
Not applicable (items). Stack: 64. Depleted uranium is taken from the ash slot (automation: pull only), the mutation result and the slag from the output slot.
Not applicable (items).

None of them is crafted: only the Incubator with a creation chip — and depleted uranium and slag are not "made" at all, they appear as traces of the machine working. There are no reverse recipes either: a resonant shard cannot be turned back into an amethyst.

They open up together with the Incubator, i.e. after uranium and the uranium plate. The first rung is the cheapest part of the ladder, and even so three attempts in four are lost. The point of these materials arrives with rungs 2–3; until then this is a collection.
Incubator — the only source, and where the chance and cost tables live. Mutation Chips — what selects the creation mode. Uranium Ore — the machine's fuel and the start of the nuclear branch.

The Network Analyzer is a hand-held diagnostic tool — a player-friendly alternative to the command for people without operator rights. It makes and stores no energy of its own; it only reads what's happening in a network. Right-click a cable and it shows that network's stats (not the whole world): the combined EU/tick supply from producers, the combined EU/tick demand of consumers, and how much EU actually moved over the last tick. At the same time it draws the network in the world — cables and the devices on them are joined by lines, and animated pulses run along the lines showing the direction of energy flow, producer to consumer (a lot like the channel visualisation in Applied Energistics 2). Mini-example: your machines went quiet and you don't know why. Right-click the cable leaving your generator with the analyzer: the actionbar shows supply and demand, and the on-world trace lights up green at the producer, orange at each consumer — so you can see at a glance whether a segment is starved or disconnected.
Uses no energy — it never connects to a network, only reads one.
Not applicable (item). Stack: 1 (a tool, not consumed).
Not applicable (item).

The tool has two diagnostic modes. The chosen mode is stored on the item itself and survives world reloads. Traverse (default). An energy storage block counts as part of the network: the analyzer walks through it and highlights the whole connected cable system — even if, topologically, it's several separate networks joined through the storage block. Good for seeing an entire power system at once. Stop-at-storage. Shows exactly one network — the one the clicked cable is in; the walk stops at a storage block. Good for targeted diagnosis of a single segment. Shift + right-click in air or off-network (including on someone else's block) cycles the mode 1↔2 and prints the new mode's name to the actionbar. Right-click on a cable (Shift or not) — scans in the current mode. A click on a cable is always diagnostic; Shift doesn't switch it. Right-click on another network's cable — replaces the highlight with the new network. Right-click off-network (into air or a block with no network) — clears the highlight. What a scan shows: the actionbar prints a line — the number of cables, sources, consumers and storages, plus supply/demand EU/tick and how much EU moved over the last tick (aggregated across all walked networks in traverse mode). If the traverse-mode network cap is reached, an extra warning is shown. The item tooltip always shows a base hint with the current-mode line beneath it; the result of the last scan is stored on the tool and expands under [SHIFT]: cables, sources/consumers/storages, supply/demand EU/tick, and how much was transferred last tick. The highlight is a volumetric "trace", visible through walls and across several chunks (it simply isn't drawn in unloaded chunks — there's no separate timer). Coloured cube markers sit at the joints: green for a producer, orange for a consumer, light-blue for a storage block in traverse mode (to flag the "bridge node"). Animated flow pulses run along the trace from producer to consumer; on unpowered sections (a network with no producer, an isolated island) the trace is drawn statically, without animation. The tool only reads the network — it changes nothing and doesn't affect energy distribution.

Assembled at a workbench (shaped 3×3): a tin body, an Electronic Circuit as the "brain" in the centre, and copper contacts at the bottom — thematically a power-network diagnostic device. — tin ingot (×5); — electronic circuit (×1); — copper ingot (×3).
No energy tier — a diagnostic tool, useful from your very first network onward and increasingly handy as networks grow more complex.
Electronic Circuit — its central component. Tin — its body. Copper Cable — what you click it on.

The resonance chain is three items, each made from the one before it, existing for a single purpose: teaching the teleporter station to throw you at a random point in the world. Step What it is Made from Spatial Crystal the chain's raw stock ender pearl, amethyst, glowstone dust Resonance Coil a general-purpose component, the step above the Copper Coil copper coils, resonant shards, a crystal Random Jump Chip the station's upgrade an empty chip, coils, a chorus fruit, redstone The whole chain is crafted on a workbench — no machine is needed for any of it. The Resonance Coil is not a teleporter part. It is built as an ordinary component one tier above the copper coil, and the chip is merely its only consumer today. It is groundwork: the next part that needs something stronger than copper winding will take this.
None of the three stores or spends energy — they are ingredients. The energy is spent by the station, at the moment of the jump (see teleporter).

The chip is fitted by hand, not dropped into a slot. Hold it and shift-right-click a placed teleporter station. The chip is consumed and the station keeps the module for good — nothing appears on its screen, the module simply starts working. Why sneaking: a plain right-click on the station opens its screen, and the click would never reach the item at all. It is also the gesture the remote already uses to bind that same station. The module survives the block being broken: a mined station carries it on the item, along with its stored EU and its privacy flag. A base can be moved without losing the chip. There is no way to get the chip back out. One chip, one station.
Not applicable (items). Stack size: 64 each.

All three are ordinary 3×3 workbench crafts. Spatial Crystal: amethyst shards above and to the sides, an ender pearl in the middle, glowstone dust below. Resonance Coil: resonant shards top and bottom, copper coils to the sides, a spatial crystal in the middle. Random Jump Chip: a chorus fruit on top, two resonance coils flanking an empty chip, redstone below. Each recipe unlocks in the book as soon as you hold any one of its ingredients.

Components with no tier of their own, but end-game in practice: the chain needs the End (pearls, chorus fruit), the Incubator (the resonant shard) and a working HV teleporter station. The resonant shard was a dead end until this: the Incubator could make one and nothing anywhere consumed it. The coil is its first sink. Grows into: further parts that need a winding better than copper.
Teleporter — the chip's only consumer. Copper Coil — the step below. Empty Chip — the blank base. Mutation products — where the resonant shard comes from.

Rubber is the end product of the oil chain: Raw rubber is the intermediate item made from one bucket of oil. It can no longer be smelted in a furnace: finished rubber requires sulfur, EU and external heat for the Vulcanizer. Mini-example: one oil bucket gives one raw rubber. With four sulfur dust, a campfire produces one rubber, lava produces two, and an Electric Heater produces three.

Stage Input Output Polymerizer 1000 mB oil + 400 EU 1 raw rubber Vulcanizer, campfire 1 raw rubber + 4 sulfur dust + 400 EU 1 rubber Vulcanizer, lava/magma the same materials and EU 2 rubber Vulcanizer, Electric Heater the same materials + 800 EU for the pair 3 rubber Better heat saves raw materials instead of merely making the operation faster.

Rubber is the material for insulated cables and the path into MV. Until those recipes are revealed, it can be stockpiled. The Incubator can duplicate finished rubber at a very high cost, so the Vulcanizer is the main production path but not literally the only possible source of the item.
Oil Polymerizer Sulfur Vulcanizer Electric Heater

Tempered Iron is an ingot made by smelting a single vanilla iron ingot. The recipe is strictly 1:1, but the result is a different material — "tempered" iron, from which items come out slightly better than their iron counterparts. It's the source material for the mod's whole same-named line: five tools (pickaxe, axe, hoe, shovel, sword), a four-piece armour set, and a compact 9:1 storage block. The ingot itself holds no energy — it's just a crafting ingredient, like vanilla iron. Mini-example: drop a stack of iron ingots in a blast furnace and you get a stack of tempered iron — then craft the tempered-iron pickaxe, which mines a bit faster and lasts longer than the vanilla iron one.
Uses no energy — it neither stores nor transmits it.

A crafting and repair material. It builds the Tempered Iron tools (pickaxe/axe/hoe/shovel/sword), the matching armour set, and the Tempered Iron Block (9:1, for compact storage and building). Tools and armour of this line are repaired in an anvil with these same ingots, just like vanilla iron gear is repaired with iron.
Not applicable (item). Stack: 64.

The ingot is made by smelting — three ways, all 1:1 (one iron ingot → one tempered iron): Vanilla furnace — the slow, everyday route; gives a little XP, like smelting ore. Blast furnace — twice as fast as the furnace, same small XP (as always for the blast furnace). Mod Electric Furnace — runs on EU instead of fuel, no XP (XP is a vanilla furnace mechanic; the electric furnace doesn't grant it). The reverse route — breaking the storage block back into 9 ingots — is described on the Tempered Iron Block page.

A material with no tier of its own. The natural step above vanilla iron: once you're smelting iron in bulk you can temper it and craft gear that's a little better than iron on every axis, while still leaving diamond's block access untouched.

Tempered Iron Block — the compact 9:1 form. Tempered Iron tools — the main consumer of the ingots. Electric Furnace — the EU-powered way to make it. Material Forms — the wider ore → dust → ingot chain.

The Water Mill Wheel is a crafting component: the wheel you place into the wheel slot of a water mill. Without a wheel in the slot, the mill generates nothing. The wheel is a durability component: it wears out only while the mill actually produces EU (proportional to output) and breaks when spent. The wear bar shows in your inventory and in the slot. It comes in three grades — the water-side counterpart of the rotor ladder. The mill itself needs no rebuilding: a better wheel goes into the same slot and raises output right away. The grade is visible from a distance — the in-world wheel is built from its grade's material. Grade Output Durability Total life Lasts about Materials Wooden ×1.00 1000 320 000 EU 6–7 days planks, copper, sticks, wooden gear Reinforced ×1.25 3000 1 200 000 EU 25 days the wooden wheel + tempered iron plates, copper, iron gear Advanced ×1.50 6000 2 880 000 EU 60 days the reinforced wheel + tempered iron plates, electronic circuit, copper, silver gear Days are in-game days of ordinary round-the-clock operation. The wooden wheel is available at the same time as the mill itself. Each grade is crafted from the one below it, placed in the centre of the grid — no rung can be skipped. A worn wheel works as an ingredient just as well as a pristine one. Mini-example: the mill on your channel runs unattended, but once a week it stops with an empty slot. The advanced wheel outlives nine wooden ones and makes half again as much EU. Because mill output is in whole EU/t, the difference between grades shows up best on a wide channel: with all four drive cells running that is 4 → 5 → 6 EU/t. On a single jet, rounding eats part of the gain.
Uses no energy — it's a plain ingredient for the wheel slot.

Goes into the dedicated wheel slot of the Water Mill. Rendered in the world as a 3D model — tilted blade-planks, a rim, spokes and a copper axle in the style of Create (rendered on vanilla wood/copper sprites). Wears out while the mill generates EU.
Not applicable (item). Durability component: max durability 1000, so it does not stack (stack: 1).

Crafted on a workbench (shaped 3×3): planks in the corners, copper ingots top and bottom, sticks on the sides, a wooden gear in the center. — planks (any, ×4); — copper ingot (×2); — stick (×2); — Wooden Gear (×1).
A component with no tier of its own. Gates water generation: without a wheel, the mill stays silent. The wheel itself is crafted from early materials, so it's available alongside the first mill.

Component Repair Bench — clears this part's wear for one item and some EU; every repair lowers its durability ceiling, and there are four of them. Water Mill — consumer of the wheel slot. Wooden Rotor — the thematic counterpart for wind generation. Wooden Gear — the central component of the wheel.

The Wind Mill Rotor is a crafting component: the blades you place into the rotor slot of any wind mill (T1 basic, T2 sky/tempest). Without a rotor in the slot, the wind mill generates nothing. The rotor is a durability component: it wears out only while the mill actually generates EU (proportional to output, faster in rain/thunder) and breaks when its durability runs out. The wear bar shows in your inventory and in the mill's slot. It comes in three grades. The higher the grade, the pricier the craft — and the more EU the very same mill makes in the very same conditions, and the less often you have to replace the part. Nothing needs rebuilding: just drop a better rotor into the same slot. The grade is visible from a distance — each one has its own blades. Grade Output Durability Total life Lasts about Materials Wooden ×1.00 1000 480 000 EU 5 days planks, iron, copper cable, wooden gear Reinforced ×1.25 3000 1 800 000 EU 19 days the wooden rotor + tempered iron and its plates, iron gear Advanced ×1.50 6000 4 320 000 EU 45 days the reinforced rotor + tempered iron plates, electronic circuit, silver gear Days are in-game days of continuous operation at a typical output. The wooden rotor is available as soon as you can combine the basic materials from the start of the game. Each grade is crafted from the one below it, placed in the centre of the grid. You cannot skip a rung, and the top grade's price honestly includes the whole branch. A worn rotor works as an ingredient just as well as a pristine one. Mini-example: your wind farm hums along, but trekking out to replace broken rotors has worn thin? The advanced rotor lasts nine times as long as the wooden one and raises output by half along the way — one trip instead of nine, and more power. ⚠️ The bonus does not breach the generator's ceiling. A wind mill is capped in EU/t, and a better rotor does not raise that cap — it gets the generator TO the cap sooner in moderate wind. At the peak (a tall tower in a thunderstorm) all three grades hit the same ceiling and only the service life still differs. Mind the cable, too: an upgraded tempest mill reaches 24 EU/t, twice what a copper cable carries — you need a gold cable or two lines.
Uses no energy — it's a plain ingredient for the rotor slot.
Goes into the dedicated rotor slot of the Wind Mill (T1), and after evolution the Sky Mill and Tempest Mill (T2). One rotor serves any wind device in the mod.
Not applicable (item). Durability component: max durability 1000, so it does not stack (stack: 1).

Crafted at a workbench (shaped 3×3): planks in the corners, iron in a cross, a wooden gear in the centre, and copper cable above and below the centre. — planks (any, ×4); — iron ingot (×1); — copper cable (×2); — Wooden Gear (×1).

A component with no tier of its own. Gates wind generation: until you have a rotor, the wind mill is silent. The rotor itself is crafted from early materials, so it's available alongside your first wind mill.

Component Repair Bench — clears this part's wear for one item and some EU; every repair lowers its durability ceiling, and there are four of them. Wind Mill — the basic rotor consumer. Sky Mill T2 and Tempest Mill T2 — evolution consumers. Wooden Gear — the rotor's central component.

The Battery Box is the mod's first storage block: it banks EU from your generators and feeds it back to your machines. It's what lets a solar panel's daytime output keep your machines running through the night. Mini-example: solar panels by day fill the box; at night the box powers the Macerator. Without it, your machines go dark the moment the sun sets. It's a buffer, not a source — on its own it produces no EU. Both its input and output are LV, so it can never overload the LV machines connected to it.

What Value Capacity 20 000 EU Max input 32 EU/t (LV) Max output 32 EU/t (LV) Both sides are LV. Under a larger inflow it only takes its own limit — the surplus doesn't pass through, nothing breaks. The output is always LV, so it's safe for any LV machine. It connects through two opposite faces only: one accepts energy (point it at your generator), the other emits it. The four side faces don't connect. You can wire the same network into both its input and its output face — it won't circle energy around and burn it on cable loss. While the machines need more than the generators produce, the storage only gives; it starts charging once the machines are satisfied or the generators cover their appetite. That's the same "machines before storage" priority the network uses to hand out energy.

c.h: Cascade: several boxes on one network
c.t: Extending the bank is simple — place another box and wire it to the same network. The fuller box tops up the emptier one until their fill fractions match. They level out together rather than "fill the first to the brim, then start the second": two 20,000 EU boxes holding 10,000 and nothing settle at roughly 5,000 each. The cascade only runs once the machines are covered — a working machine is always served before a neighbouring store. It stops on its own at level: each tick moves half of the difference, and very small gaps are ignored, so boxes never slosh energy back and forth. A cost worth knowing about. The transfer travels by cable and pays the usual distance loss. It is a one-off price for levelling, not a constant leak — once the fractions meet, the flow stops. On a long run it is noticeable, though: across 30 blocks of copper only about half of what is sent arrives. If your bank is spread across a large base, keeping the boxes next to each other is cheaper. The same rule applies without cable: two boxes placed flush, output face to input face, behave identically. It is one behaviour, not two. Only battery boxes take part. The Teleporter is a store as well, but it banks energy from a surplus on its own and is never filled from a box automatically — so a full box cannot drain into it behind your back.

One slot for portable EU items (battery pouch, energy pack): Slot Does Charge fills a portable EU item from the buffer The slot only charges — you can't drain a charge back into the box through it. Hoppers don't use it: it's a manual, GUI-only slot.
One screen: energy storage, in/out rate, charge slot.
An ordinary solid block. Any pickaxe breaks it, and it keeps its charge when broken — you don't lose energy by moving the box around. What Value Tool pickaxe Keeps charge on break yes

Crafted at a workbench from oak planks, two batteries, copper cable and redstone: batteries go in the middle of the top and bottom rows, planks in the corners, cable on either side of the centre, redstone in the centre. It's a storage block, not a processor — no processing recipes.
The entry step of the storage line. As the base grows, the LV buffer stops being enough, and higher-tier storage blocks (MV/HV) take over later.
Generator — the typical charge source. Solar Panel — fills the box by day.

The Reinforced Energy Storage is the second step of the storage line: the same job as the Battery Box, one tier up. It holds 100 000 EU and moves 128 EU/tick in and out instead of 32.
