Mini-example: the starter box powers your Macerator overnight, but it runs dry by morning and can't absorb the full daytime output of a solar farm that has since grown. The reinforced one takes the whole flow and lasts through several nights, not one. Like its little brother it's a buffer, not a source — it produces no EU on its own. The only difference is scale: a bigger reserve and a wider throat. It's crafted from a finished Battery Box — the starter block goes in the centre of the recipe and becomes the core of the new one. The upgrade is literal, not "build it again from ore".

What Value Capacity 100 000 EU Max input 128 EU/t (MV) Max output 128 EU/t (MV) Both sides are MV. 128 EU/tick is the tier ceiling, not a promised speed: it's what the block will pass if you have something to feed it with. What actually arrives depends on the supply line: How it's wired Real inflow Copper cable (LV) 12 EU/t Gold cable (MV) 48 EU/t Flush against the source, no cable up to 128 EU/t The practical takeaway: switching to the MV store does not speed up your line by itself. To feel the difference in speed rather than only in reserve, you need a gold cable — or direct contact with a generator. Fill time from empty: about 10 minutes from a fuel generator (8 EU/t); about 1.7 minutes over a gold cable at full tilt (48 EU/t). Like the starter box, it connects through two opposite faces only: one accepts, the other emits. The four side faces don't connect. The network-wide priority is unchanged here: while the machines need more than the generators produce, the store only gives, and starts charging once the machines are satisfied.

c.h: Cascade: sharing a network with the starter box
c.t: The reinforced store takes part in the same bank levelling as the starter one, and levelling works on fill fractions, not absolute EU. That matters on a mixed bank: a starter box (20 000) and a reinforced one (100 000) settle at an equal percentage, not an equal charge — both at 50 %, say, which is 10 000 and 50 000 EU. The impression that "the big box drained the small one" is false: the small one gives exactly its share. The transfer travels by cable and pays the usual distance loss, so a bank is cheaper kept compact.

Slot Does Charge charges a portable EU item from the buffer Discharge drains an item's charge back into the buffer The discharge slot is what the Battery Box doesn't have: drop in a charged energy pack or battery pouch and it hands its reserve to the network. That makes the block an intake for energy carried home from a trip, not just a wall socket. Both slots are manual — hoppers don't use them, they work from the GUI only.

A machine window with an energy gauge: the vertical bar on the left shows the buffer fill, and the tooltip gives the exact figure in EU. Two item slots sit beside it — the upper one charges an item from the buffer, the lower one drains a charged item into the buffer. There is no progress arrow: the CESU processes nothing, it only stores. The output face is chosen with a wrench and shown by the coloured marker on the block itself, not in the window.

The block is built from the same cold steel as the advanced casing it's made of. The border and banding echo the Battery Box, so the two steps read as one line rather than two unrelated blocks. Face What's on it Top and bottom steel bands — the starter box's pattern, in metal Left and right a rack of three accumulator cells: you can see the reserve is inside Input a socket glowing blue Output (back) a socket glowing orange Input and output differ by colour, not by shape. That's a deliberate break from the starter box, where the output is a big obvious socket and the input a nondescript lens — players run cable to the socket they can see and hit the output. Here both faces are the same socket and the colour carries the role: blue takes in, orange gives out.

An ordinary solid block, a full 16³ cube (occluder). Tougher than the starter box — this is metal, not a plank crate. Breaks with any pickaxe and keeps its charge when broken. What Value Shape full 16³ cube (occluder) Hardness 4.0 Blast resistance 6.0 Tool pickaxe Sound metal Keeps charge when broken yes

It's a store, not a processor — no processing recipes. Electrum ingot Advanced circuit Electrum ingot Advanced casing Battery Box Advanced casing Electrum ingot Advanced circuit Electrum ingot Four electrum ingots at the corners are the contacts, two advanced circuits manage the charge, two advanced casings form the reinforced shell, and the starter box in the centre is the core. Electrum is not an arbitrary alloy here: it is gold with silver, the best conductor in the mod, and on a store it sits exactly where current enters and leaves. The corners used to hold rubber, but rubber is an insulator — right on a cable, and meaningless as four lumps in the corners of a battery.

Tier: MV. The second step of the storage line. Predecessor: the Battery Box (LV) — not merely "already built", but consumed in the recipe. Requires two production lines at once: alloys — electrum is smelted from gold and silver in the Alloy Smelter; oil — still required after rubber left the corners: rubber lives on inside the advanced circuit, which this recipe needs both directly and through the advanced casing. The gate still holds, just indirectly.

Battery Box — the LV predecessor, and an ingredient. MFSU — the top of the storage line. Gold cable — the supply line without which the speed gain is invisible. Advanced circuit · Advanced casing — the MV parts in the recipe.

The Charging Station is a flat plate, a quarter of a block tall, that you simply stand on. While you're on it, it charges everything you're carrying at once: tools in your hotbar and backpack, whatever is in your offhand, and your worn gear too — the Energy Pack, the Jetpack, a set of Fluxweave armour. Mini-example: you come back from the mine with a half-empty drill and a low jetpack — step onto the plate by your base entrance, get on with sorting your chests, and your gear tops itself up while you do. Not a single click needed. Charging never asks you to open a window: step on and it runs. The station does have a screen, but it is optional — a reference panel for whoever wants the numbers, not a condition for the plate to work. Ignore it and the only thing you lose is the numbers: the plate behaves identically with the screen open and closed.

What Value Buffer 20 000 EU Max input 128 EU/t Max output to the player 128 EU/t The station is a capacitor, not a machine. Its buffer is sized for a visit rather than for "one operation": it fills slowly while nobody is around and empties fast into whoever turns up. That is the only way 128 EU/t is ever reached — the grid does not deliver anywhere near that much: How it's fed Actual inflow Copper cable (LV) 12 EU/t Gold cable (MV) 48 EU/t Flush against a Battery Box (its output face) 32 EU/t The 128 EU/t input is a ceiling, not a promise. It exists so the station doesn't cap a player who has built good infrastructure: the thicker the supply, the faster its reserve comes back. Fed from copper, the station takes noticeably longer to refill after a big visit than it does from gold. Every item is still limited to its own charge rate (32 EU/t for all of the mod's portable gear), so 128 EU/t is the station's total output shared across everything at once, not the speed of any single item. How long it takes. Don't be fooled by the 128: the pace is limited not only by the station but by how fast each item can take charge — 32 EU/t. So 128 EU/t is only ever reached with four items charging at once; a single item always draws its own 32 EU/t no matter how much the station offers. Everything charges at once. The station splits its output between every item that needs charge rather than serving them in turn: a full set of armour fills together instead of two pieces at a time. The more you are carrying, the slower each piece goes — the station's total rate does not change with their number. Charge arrives in batches. The station credits you not every tick but four times a second, handing over what accrued in between. The speed is unchanged — the same amount per second — but the charge bar updates less often. This is for the game's sake: every credit rewrites the item and re-sends the slot to your client, and at twenty credits a second that read as a stuttering inventory. The first credit lands the moment you step onto the plate, so there is no delay at the start. Which means the time by the biggest thing in your loadout, not by the size of the station's buffer. Item Time (from a full station) Battery (2,000 EU each) ~3 seconds Battery Pouch (2,000 EU) ~3 seconds Electromagnet (5,000 EU) ~8 seconds Electric Drill, Diamond-Tipped one included (10,000 EU) ~16 seconds Electric Chainsaw, Shovel, Hoe, Saber (10,000 EU each) ~16 seconds One piece of Fluxweave (15,000 EU) ~23 seconds Energy Pack (20,000 EU) ~31 seconds Jetpack (30,000 EU) ~47 seconds The Battery is the one powered item that stacks, and its charge is held per battery. A stack shares the same 32 EU/t between all of them — 2 EU per battery per tick — so a full stack of 16 takes about 50 seconds, not three. A completely flat loadout — pouch, Energy Pack, drill, chainsaw, shovel, hoe, saber, electromagnet, jetpack and four pieces of Fluxweave — comes to 167,000 EU. The first 20,000 come out of the banked buffer, after which the pace drops to whatever the grid supplies, so charging the lot from empty is a matter of minutes rather than seconds. The Diamond-Tipped drill is not a line of its own in that total: it replaces the plain drill in your hands and shares its 10,000 EU buffer. Batteries sit outside the loadout too — how many you carry is up to you, and a full stack would add another 32,000 EU on its own. The point of the station isn't to beat a charge slot for speed — it's that it does everything at once, with no clicks at all: your gear fills itself while you sort out your haul. All six faces accept energy; the station never gives any back to the network.
The station has two independent feedback channels: the indicator under your feet is the primary one, for play on the move, and the screen is the secondary one, for whoever wants exact numbers.

A four-state indicator: four lamps at the corners of the plate and a coil ring at its centre, mirrored by a lit strip along its edge so the state reads both from above and from across the room. Indicator Meaning Light Dark Nobody is standing on it 0 Blue Charging 10 Green Everything on you is already full — off you go 10 Red The station is out of power 3 Red and green are deliberately distinct: they are different problems with different fixes. Green means "you're ready"; red means "the station has nothing to give, go build generation". Sparks lift off the plate while it is charging.

The station clicks like a metal pressure plate: once when you step on, once when you step off. It is an acknowledgement — the sound tells you the plate registered you even when you are facing the other way and can see neither lamps nor sparks. The click sounds once per visit, not once per tick: sprinting along a row of stations gets you one click from each, not a burst. A spectator drifting through the plate clicks nothing at all — they do not charge either.

The screen opens on right-click, including while you are standing on the plate. Stepping on does not open it: a window popping up on every step would get in the way of walking, and the whole point of the station is that you can step on it and get on with your business. There are no slots on the screen — there is nothing to put into the station, it charges what is on you. It shows four values: Row Meaning Charge The station's reserve and its buffer, in EU and per cent Delivery How many EU per tick are going to the player right now Charging How many items are taking charge at once Time left Estimated time until the gear of whoever stands on the plate is full The screen shows what the station is doing right now, not what is in the viewer's own pockets: if one player stands on the plate and another opens the screen, the second sees the station's work with the first. With nobody on the plate, the three lower rows show a dash — the station is delivering nothing, so there is nothing to report. "Time left" is measured against the gear of whoever stands on the plate rather than the station's own buffer: what the player wants to know is when they can leave. It is derived from the current delivery rate, so on a thin supply line it honestly grows — the station gives out exactly as much as it manages to take in.

The station spends energy only when a transfer actually happens. A station with no visitor, or one whose visitor is already full, spends nothing; left alone, it goes to sleep. It does refill like any other consumer, including while nobody is standing on it — that is the whole point of the reserve it banks ahead of time. But it queues for energy behind working machines: furnaces and macerators on the same network are always served first, so adding a station will not slow them down. A spectator drifting through the block is charged nothing and costs nothing.

Other mods' items while they are worn. Item energy on both loaders is addressed by inventory slot index, and worn armour from another mod has no such index. All of Ala Industrial's own portable gear charges fully, and foreign items sitting in ordinary inventory slots charge normally too. In creative mode the station still physically spends its reserve, exactly as a machine charges an item in its slot. That is not a bug.

Shape: a 16×4×16 plate — the bottom quarter of the block (0 to 4 in height). It has full collision: you stand on it rather than walk through it, and it is low enough that you step over the station instead of jumping onto it. The highlight outline matches exactly what you walk on. The block does not occlude its neighbours — without that, the faces of blocks around the plate would be culled as if a full cube stood there. It has no orientation: the station is symmetrical, there is nothing to rotate, and a cable connects to any face. Placed and broken with a pickaxe; hardness 3.0, blast resistance 6.0, metal sound. Breaking it does not preserve the EU buffer — the station loses what it had banked, like any machine in the mod.

While charging, the station gives off a soft transformer hum — the loop (pattern C keyed off the state, the quietest stationary loop in the mod: 0.18 — the player stands ON the block, the source is right at their feet. Standing on it full (green indicator) or with an empty buffer keeps it silent. The step-on / step-off clicks remain vanilla.

Copper Cable Copper Cable Copper Cable Iron Plate Battery Iron Plate Iron Plate Electronic Circuit Iron Plate The copper cables on top are the charging coil, the battery at the centre sets the buffer, and the circuit runs the distribution.

The Energy Condenser is a cube frame with a slowly turning, glowing orb inside. It catches the power that would otherwise be lost: when the generators make more than the machines eat, the surplus normally just vanishes. The condenser banks it instead, and hands the bank back as a single item — an energy clot. It cannot get in your factory's way. The grid serves it last, and it cannot pull a single unit out of a battery box. Place it on day one if you like — it will simply sit quiet until there is a surplus. Example: at noon your solar panels make more than two machines need. That difference used to go nowhere; now the orb starts spinning up, and a few minutes later there is a tier-I clot inside.

Property Value Intake 128 EU/tick Output none — energy goes in, but never comes back out as energy Bank up to 4,000,000 EU Powered faces top and bottom only The narrow intake is deliberate: a condenser standing closer to a generator than a machine would otherwise intercept the flow. Faster banking is not "give this one block a thicker cable" — it is a second condenser.
One slot, output only. Nothing can be put in; the clot is taken by hand, hopper or pipe — but only through the side faces, since top and bottom belong to the cable.
A full-cube frame; cable connects only on top and bottom. It glows brighter the more is banked. Mined with a pickaxe, drops itself.
While the condenser packs the grid's surplus into a clot, it gives off a soft harmonic ring — the loop (pattern A on , default 0.35; . Take the clot out or starve the grid and it falls silent.

The bank grows continuously — no modes, no switches. The output slot always shows the clot you would Banked In the slot under 250,000 empty, too early from 250,000 a tier-I clot from 1,000,000 a tier-II clot from 4,000,000 a tier-III clot Taking it spends the whole bank. Take it at 950,000 and you get tier I — the 700,000 above that tier's price burns with it. Wait a little longer and the same slot would have handed you tier II. That is the decision: greed against patience. To make it an informed one, the screen prints the current tier and how far the next one still is. The orb spins faster and glows brighter as the bank fills, so the state reads from across the room without opening the screen. The condenser has no upgrade panel. An overclocker in it would turn "sips the surplus" into a pump on the grid — exactly what this mechanic avoids.

The only source of energy clots, and therefore of every machine overclocker. Worth placing once you have some surplus generation: on a starved grid it banks nothing, and the motionless orb says so honestly. Time to a clot shrinks with more condensers and thicker cable, not with an upgrade to the block.
Overclocker — what the clots are for. Battery Box — storage for running the factory; the condenser is no rival to it and cannot drain it.

⚠️ Electrical safety: deals 2 damage not only on direct contact but also within 0.5 blocks of the segment — while the segment is live: energy is moving through it or its buffer holds a charge and a working generator is still on the grid . A charged dead-end spur carries no current precisely because it is already full — and that does not make it safe. A de-energised line is safe: with no live generator the leftover charge does not shock, so an open breaker still takes the hazard off everything past it. Normal armor applies; water does not amplify the hit; a solid block between the cable and the player blocks the shock. Servers can turn the mechanic off in the config. To lower the hit chance without removing the hazard, use an insulating stand — or replace the bare grade with the Insulated Copper Cable, which is safe outright. The Copper Cable is the main early-game cable and the wire of the starter chain: Solar Panel → Battery Box → Macerator. It connects neighbouring blocks into a single line and carries LV energy (up to 32 EU/tick). On a long line some energy is lost along the way — the longer the wire and the higher the flow, the bigger the loss. Attenuation is exponential: a line of any length leaves at least 1 EU from a positive packet, so the receiver's buffer always tops up to full. It is cheap to craft, which makes it handy for wiring a base before the higher-tier cables are unlocked.

The cable carries LV energy and connects to neighbouring blocks. Each wire run from a source to a consumer costs a little EU — the exact formula is given in the table. Field Value Role transfer Max voltage 32 (LV) Loss 0.02 attenuation per block; a consumer receives EU/tick when N > 0. Distance = number of cables from the nearest source Insulation can be insulated for safe adjacency Stand planks / wool / glass under a bare segment — lowers the shock chance, does not remove it The cable does not explode from overload: 32 EU/packet is only a throughput cap, and anything above it simply does not pass through. A proper MV/HV/EV flow needs a cable of the matching tier. Flow with inertia. A cable is not a teleport: every block has a small live buffer (12 EU). All energy — to machines and to storage alike — moves segment by segment (cable → cable) in a single network pass per tick, so any working cable really holds and shows the energy passing through it, a distant consumer is reached only as fast as the line fills, and a broken line keeps the remainder in the buffers on the source side. The buffer is deliberately tiny: a grid of 1000 cables holds 12 × 1000 = 12 000 EU — less than one Battery Box (20 000 EU), so a "battery made of wire" is not a thing. Throughput equals the buffer: 12 EU/tick into the cable next to the consumer (the tier voltage of 32 EU caps what a source hands out, not what a thin line carries). Even with no consumer at all a source fills the wires to capacity, after which the network sleeps. The other grades of the ladder (tin/gold/electrum) are wired the same way, each through its own config keys. Insulating stand. An already-laid bare segment can be given a stand: right-click the cable holding any wood (planks, logs, stripped), wool or glass of any colour to slip a thin plate underneath, and right-click with an empty hand to take it back off and recover the very same item. The plate shows the exact species or shade that was installed, and the stands of neighbouring segments meet flush along a run to form one continuous board. The protection is directional, and that is the point of it. The plate sits under the wire, so a player walking past at floor level or standing underneath is shielded completely — no shock at all, neither on contact nor through the proximity radius. Only one case stays risky: climbing onto the cable, which puts the player above the plate, where it merely lowers the chance of a hit. Glass protects best, wood sits in the middle, wool is the weakest. When a stand absorbs a shock the player gets the same invulnerability window an ordinary hit would give, so the chance applies per contact instead of being re-rolled every tick. Limits: a stand cannot go on an insulated grade (there is no hazard left to reduce, so it would be a decoration that does nothing) nor on a segment connected downwards, because that connection's sleeve fills the same space at the floor of the cell. If such a connection forms later, the stand is popped back out as an item. This does not get in the way of building with those blocks: sneaking with a block in hand is the vanilla way to bypass block interaction, so ordinary placement still works.

The cable settles neatly onto the top of a slab-like neighbour (a solar panel, for instance): if the neighbour is a low block, the wire drops to meet it near the floor instead of hanging in mid-air. This works with any future low block automatically — no exceptions.

A clamp-on switch that de-energises a line for maintenance without tearing the wiring out. Right- click any laid cable with the breaker item to fit it; it appears as a small housing on top of the wire. Three gestures, no GUI: right-click with an empty hand throws the switch, sneak + right-click pries it back off, and the item is returned. The state reads straight off the wire — a green band means the line is live, a red one means it is dead. The housing is a solid collar threaded onto the run; in a cell where the wiring leaves on more than one axis (a corner, a tee, the six-way star) it becomes a cube instead, because such a cell has no single axis for a collar to sit on. While the switch is open two short stubs poke out of the housing — severed ends, so the gap reads as a deliberate cut rather than a missing block. The click is pitched higher for on and lower for off, so the switch position is audible even when you are not looking at it. An open breaker takes its own segment out of the grid entirely: the network splits in two exactly as if the cable had been mined, and everything downstream loses power. Bare wire past the breaker stops shocking within a tick — which is the whole point of the switch. Closing it puts the segment back the same way a freshly laid cable joins the grid. A newly fitted breaker is closed, so installing one never blacks out a base by surprise, and removing one always restores the line whatever position the lever was left in. Breaking a cable drops its breaker (and its stand) as items rather than deleting them. Manual only — the breaker does not read redstone. Throwing it rebuilds part of the grid, and a redstone clock would run that work several times a second; automation is a separate future task.
Crafted at a workbench from copper alone — the most accessible wire for a starting base. Crafting: 3 copper ingots in a row -> 3 cables. Processing recipes: none.
Electrum Cable — the HV backbone with the ladder's lowest losses.

⚠️ Electrical safety. The bare electrum HV cable deals 10 damage (the tier ladder runs LV 2 → MV 6 → HV 10, key) not only on direct contact but also within 0.5 blocks of the segment — but only while energy is actually moving through this exact bare segment. A disconnected line and retained buffer EU are safe. Normal armor applies; water does not amplify the hit; a solid block between the cable and the player blocks the shock. Servers can turn the mechanic off in the config. The Electrum Cable is the first wire on tier HV. The tier itself was never empty: the Teleporter Station has run on it since as the mod's only HV consumer — with nothing but a gold (MV) cable to feed it. The cable replaces an earlier concept — a "glass fibre EV cable" — same role as the ladder's most expensive, most efficient wire, but on an already-existing tier and with a more grounded in-mod material: the electrum alloy (gold + silver, already smelted by the Alloy Smelter since 0.1.67 but with zero consumers so far), finished with a pinch of diamond dust that gives the wire its reliability/low losses. Electrum holds 512 EU/packet — four times gold's 128 — and carries 192 EU/tick in its segment buffer, also four times gold's 48. That is the same ×4 step every previous rung uses (copper→gold is also ×4 on both buffer and cap), so electrum is not a "cheat jump" but a natural continuation of the existing progression on the next, still-empty rung. Unlike gold (whose wider buffer is paid for with higher loss), electrum breaks that trade-off: its loss is 0.005 per block, lower even than the cheapest tin cable (0.006). This is a deliberate exception — electrum is simply better on every axis, and the price is an expensive craft (rare alloy + diamond), not operating loss. Where this already shows. The mod has no HV machines, generators or storage yet, but it does have an HV consumer: the Teleporter Station and its 500,000 EU buffer. Over a gold cable (48 EU/t) it fills in ~10,400 ticks ≈ 8.7 minutes; over electrum (192 EU/t), in ~2,600 ticks ≈ 2.2 minutes. The caveat that makes the promise honest: the station is a storage sink, and a storage sink is never fed from other storage over a cable (battery boxes only discharge into a machine's deficit). The speed-up is real exactly to the extent that your generators together exceed 48 EU/t — below that the wire is not the bottleneck. On the rest of the content (LV/MV) what helps is the wide 192 EU/t buffer itself on dense lines.

Field Value Role transfer Max voltage 512 EU/packet (HV tier) Throughput 192 EU/tick = the segment working buffer Loss 0.005 attenuation per block (lower than tin!); a consumer receives EU/tick when N > 0 Insulation shipped — insulated electrum cable (0.0025 loss) At full segment flow (192 EU/tick) the cable delivers 183/174/150/117 EU over 10/20/50/100 blocks respectively, and stays conductive even at 1000 blocks (minimum 1 EU — the shared model invariant, . The half-distance (where exactly half the flow is lost) is about 138 blocks — twice as far as tin, with 24× the buffer. The cable does not explode from overload: 512 EU/packet is only a cap, and anything above it simply does not pass through. Mixed networks. A network takes both its throughput cap and its loss from the strongest cable in it — the same rule that already applies to gold in a copper line. A single electrum segment in a gold line moves the whole network to 512 EU/packet and to electrum's 0.005 loss.

Like every other cable, electrum drops its horizontal sleeve toward a low neighbour (a solar panel, 8/16 tall, and any future half block) so the sleeve hugs the slab's side instead of floating above it. The behaviour is shared by all cables and is derived from the neighbour's shape, not its type.

The ritual recipe: five electrum ingots — the four corners and the center — and four diamond dust at the edge midpoints yield 3 cables. The price is deliberately steep, and that is a balance decision rather than flavour. This wire is laid on key routes, not used to wire a whole base. The insulated variant uses the shared recipe: six bare cables and three vulcanized rubber → 6 insulated. The Gold Cable is the top rung of the cable ladder and the mod's first MV wire. It carries 48 EU/tick — four times copper — and raises the packet ceiling to 128 EU (against LV's 32). The price of that width is higher loss: 0.03 per block against copper's 0.02. That is not an oversight but the whole trade: gold wins on short, high-power runs where throughput matters, and loses on long ones where reach matters. The formula is the same : from its actual 48 EU/tick flow, 36 EU arrives over 10 blocks and 11 EU over 50. Loss never reaches 100%, but gold still belongs close to the load; run long trunks on copper or tin.

The Distillation Column is a tower three blocks tall — the tallest machine in the mod and its first multiblock. The tower is assembled from three identical segments stacked on top of each other. Inside are three tanks: crude oil is poured into the middle, diesel — the light target fraction — condenses at the top, and fuel oil — the heavy residue — runs down to the bottom. There is nothing to configure: the layout is the same on every column and reads itself — "light at the top, heavy at the bottom". Mini-example: a pump feeds oil from a lake into the middle of the tower, a second pump draws diesel off the top, a third takes fuel oil at the base. A cable to the base — and the mini-refinery runs on its own for as long as the lake holds oil. A cold column first warms up (~10 seconds under power), and only then starts distilling. A warmed-up working tower has glowing windows and steam rising from the top — from far away the base's silhouette tells you whether the refinery is running or standing idle.

Segment Role Fluid Top condenser diesel — output Middle feedstock intake oil — input Bottom base cube (the "brain") fuel oil — output + energy input Hand-built (round 3): a single kind of segment block is crafted; stack three segments on top of each other — the tower assembles itself (the bottom one becomes the "brain" base, the upper two turn into the middle and top sections, an anvil clang is heard). A lone segment is an inert blank: it has no ports and no menu, and a click hints how to finish the build. Disassembly is mirrored: breaking any segment degrades the tower — the broken one drops as a segment item, the others revert to blanks in place, and the base keeps the tanks and the coke fouling inside. Nothing vanishes and nothing is duplicated. The GUI opens with a click on any segment of an assembled tower. The Rectification Section (a separate craftable block) is placed onto the top of the tower — the tower grows to four blocks and the losses drop from 10 % to 5 %: every distillation yields +50 mB of diesel (750/200). The steam moves up to the section. The section is an ordinary block with its own drop; take it off and the bonus is gone.

The column only consumes EU; power is fed into the base on any of its faces (sides and bottom). The middle and the top take no energy — a cable will not connect to them. What Value Internal buffer 800 EU Max input 32 EU/t (LV) Consumption 2 EU/t (working and warming up)

Three tanks of ten buckets each. The input tank accepts any oil with the conventional tag; the output tanks are filled only by the machine itself — neighbours may only extract. Status: a public block — present in the creative tab, has a crafting recipe, GUI, and is visible in JEI/REI. It's one of the most energy-hungry machines in the mod (1000 EU per bucket). The Pump is an EU-powered LV machine that moves fluids. It finds a lava or water source in the world (starting at the block in front of it and following the flow outward), or draws fluid from an adjacent tank, banks it in an internal 10-bucket tank, and pushes it on into any neighbouring receiver tank. The tank holds only one fluid at a time: if it already contains lava it won't accept water (and vice versa) until it empties. Mixing is ruled out on purpose — you can't accidentally dump two fluids into one pipe. The main use case is feeding the Geothermal Generator with lava through a pipe instead of hauling buckets by hand; the pump also moves water for future fluid chains.

The pump is a pure energy consumer: it takes EU in, emits none, and spends 1000 EU per bucket it draws. Field Value Role consumer with buffer Buffer (EU) 4000 — above, to bank enough for ≥4 buckets at once Max input (EU/tick) 32 (LV) Max output (EU/tick) n/a (does not emit) EU per bucket 1000 — one of the most energy-hungry machines The pump connects to the energy network like any consumer — the energy network finds it automatically. Energy is only spent on the tick when fluid was actually taken from the world or a neighbouring tank; filling by hand with buckets and pushing into a receiver cost no EU. As an LV machine the pump accepts up to 32 EU per tick. At 1000 EU/bucket and a 32 EU/tick limit, filling the buffer for one bucket takes ~32 ticks; the 4000 EU buffer holds the cost of 4 buckets, so even under bursty energy supply the pump rarely idles. Per-face energy role. The pump draws EU on its five working faces; the front face is energy-inert (no port there), like every other horizontal machine. A cable therefore draws an arm toward the five working faces only — not toward the front. Fluid intake is a separate subsystem and still reads the front face directly (see Intake), so the front being energy-inert does not change which way the pump draws fluid from.

The pump doesn't use the recipe system: it doesn't process items, it moves fluid. Each working tick runs three steps. Step Action Condition 0. Buckets empty a fluid bucket from the input slot into the tank the input slot has a lava/water bucket, the tank can accept, the output slot is free for the empty bucket 1. Intake take 1 bucket of fluid into the tank scanCooldown ≤ 0` 2. Push push fluid from the tank into neighbouring receivers the tank has fluid Intake. The pump looks for fluid starting at the block directly in front of it (the face it points at the player). If that block is lava/water itself, or a connected flowing puddle of it, the pump follows the flow to the nearest source. If there's no fluid in the world there, it tries to draw a bucket from a neighbouring tank. Limits on the world source search: Radius: up to 32 blocks from the pump; Visited cap: up to 512 blocks per scan (lag protection on large spills); Cooldown: 1 second (20 ticks) between search attempts — both after a hit and after a miss. A found source (lava or water) is pulled into the tank by the bucket, and the source block in the world is irrevocably removed (drained). Flowing, non-source fluid is not pumped — it only leads the search to the source, and once the source is gone it settles back by vanilla fluid rules. If the tank already holds a different fluid, the search doesn't even start — the pump won't waste a tick. Push. The pump pushes fluid out in every direction except the one it just drew from (so it doesn't pump back into the source), and tries to empty the whole tank in one tick to any neighbouring receiver — for example the Geothermal Generator's tank. While working the pump lights up (lit on any tick where something happened — intake, push, or a bucket fill).

Two slots for buckets — for manually pouring fluid into the tank. This isn't the pump's main way of working, just a handy convenience. Slot Accepts Count Input (0) lava bucket / water bucket (a lava bucket, a water bucket) 1 Output (1) empty bucket (an empty bucket, extraction only) up to a stack Filling via buckets: a bucket from the input slot is emptied into the tank (1 bucket = 1000 mB), the empty bucket drops into the output slot — same as the Geothermal Generator. This costs no EU (manual fill, not the pump). Hoppers can take empty buckets out of the output slot and put fresh fluid buckets into the input slot.

Field Value Implementation neutral (in, works on Fabric and NeoForge) Capacity 10 buckets (10 buckets = 10000 mB) Accepts allowlist: lava + water (→) Mixing forbidden — the tank is single-variant: while it holds one fluid, the other is rejected (guaranteed by the core's ) Extraction allowed from any side (→ true) Access per face; pipes and tanks of other mods connect to it on both loaders Single-variant guarantee. The tank holds at most one fluid at a time. If empty, it accepts any from the allowlist; if it already holds lava, water is rejected (and vice versa) until it empties. Mixing fluids by accident is impossible — it's built into the tank itself. Unit of volume — the millibucket (mB). Inside the tank everything is counted in millibuckets: 1 bucket = 1000 mB, and the tank's capacity is 10 000 mB (those same 10 buckets). This value is identical on Fabric and NeoForge — the player sees exactly the same volumes regardless of loader. Persistence and migration. After a reload the tank restores both its volume and its fluid type. Worlds saved under the older version of the pump (lava-only) are picked up correctly: if any fluid is present it's read back as lava — the only one the old tank knew.

c.h: Exchanging with capsules and foreign containers
c.t: The internal tank is not sealed off: it exchanges fluid with any container held in your hand. Vacuum capsule. Right-click the pump with an empty capsule and it takes exactly one bucket out of the tank; right-click with a filled one and the bucket goes in. Partial transfers never happen — a whole bucket or nothing. Vanilla bucket works the same way, one bucket per click. Containers from other mods are accepted through the standard fluid-container interface, so another mod's tank, tube or backpack fills and empties the pump without any dedicated compatibility code. The pump never accepts a fluid that differs from what is already in the tank — mixing is impossible. Empty the tank first if you need to switch fluids.

The pump has a graphical screen with two slots (for buckets) and two indicator bars. Type: GUI with two slots (buckets) and two bars: Left — fluid level in the tank (grows bottom-up). The sprite colour depends on the fluid type: red for lava, blue for water. Right — energy buffer. A tooltip on hover shows the volume in mB / fluid type and the EU / buffer capacity. Block state: the pump turns to "face the player" when placed (that face is where it draws fluid from) and lights up while working.

An ordinary solid block: a pickaxe breaks it, and on break it does not keep its energy charge (the tank and its fluid are kept — see Internal tank). Field Value Shape full 16³ cube (occluder) Hardness 3.0 Blast resistance 6.0 Tool pickaxe Sound metal Drops with NBT energy no

While running, the pump emits a wet suction of liquid being drawn into a pipe — the loop (pattern A, default 0.35). It falls silent when idle What sets the pump apart from the other pattern-A machines: a bucket transfer is atomic — it completes within a single tick rather than spanning processing ticks the way the macerator's grind does. So (and with it the loop) is held for a further ticks after the last transfer (60 ticks = 3s by default). Without that hold, both the indicator and the sound would flash for one tick and the pump could never be heard working. Under continuous pumping, new transfers restart the countdown before it expires, so the pump reads as continuously running rather than flickering.

One workbench recipe: an iron casing, two buckets, and an Electronic Circuit. The two buckets in the pattern reflect what the block does — moving fluid; the Electronic Circuit sets the machine's LV tier.

An early LV machine — placed once a stable generator and an Electronic Circuit for crafting are available. It frees you from hauling lava buckets by hand. Tier: LV Power: from an LV source, e.g. the Generator. Purpose: automatically feeding lava to the Geothermal Generator as a fluid instead of by hand; moving water for future fluid chains. Requires: an Electronic Circuit to craft.
Geothermal Generator — the main consumer of the pump's lava. Generator — the typical LV power source for the pump. Components — the Electronic Circuit for crafting.

The Portable Fluid Tank stores up to 8 buckets (8000 mB) of one fluid. It needs no EU, has no GUI, and does not push fluid automatically. Its glass walls show the actual fluid and fill level. Water, lava, and fluids registered by other mods can move through buckets, Vacuum Capsules, or the native loader fluid capability. Breaking the tank keeps its contents in the dropped item.

Property Value Capacity 8000 mB (8 buckets) Fluids at once 1 Input / output all 6 faces Automatic output none Different fluids never mix. A comparator outputs 0 while empty and 1–15 according to fullness.

The full-block footprint contains a sealed frame with 3 px top/bottom plates, four 3×3 px corner posts, and four translucent glass walls. A runtime renderer draws both the glass and the fluid inside it, using the registered fluid texture and tint. The block's shape follows that whole body — plates, posts and walls (1 px panes on each of the four sides, y 3–13). The walls must be in the shape even though a renderer, not the model, draws them: without them a click on the glass passes through and lands on the block behind the tank, so a player aiming at the tank empties a bucket of lava at their own feet. The shape is not a full cube on purpose — a full cube would have to occlude to satisfy the block standards, and occlusion paints the tank's own inside black. Empty tank items stack normally. A filled tank carries one atomic component and has a maximum stack size of one. Its inventory icon tints the inner fluid layer from the registered fluid colour, while the standard item bar shows the stored amount relative to 8000 mB.
Crafted at a table from tin ingots, glass panes, an iron gear and redstone dust.
Vacuum Capsule Fluid transport

The Fluid Pipe carries water, lava, oil and anything else between tanks, the pump and your machines, so you are not hauling buckets around. Lay the pipes in a line, use the wrench to say which side draws and which side pours, and the pipe handles the rest. It needs no power. A pipe moves one bucket per second. The pump fills slower than that, so on an ordinary line the pump is the bottleneck rather than the pipe. Fluid genuinely travels along the pipe instead of appearing at the far end: every segment holds a small amount and hands it onward. A long run therefore fills up gradually, and you can watch the fluid front make its way down the line.

Property Value Volume per segment 50 mB Throughput 50 mB per tick (1 bucket per second) Fluids at once one per segment Power use none A segment carries one fluid at a time. While it holds water, lava will not enter — you cannot build a line with two different fluids in it, and you cannot mix them by accident either. The per-segment volume is small on purpose: a pipe moves fluid, it does not store it. For storage there is the tank. Breaking a pipe loses whatever was inside it. That is less than half a bucket per segment, and in exchange there is no spill to clean up.

Sides work exactly like the item pipe — same wrench, same order — so there are not two sets of rules to remember. Mode What it does How it looks Plain connection. simple sleeve Draws fluid from the neighbouring tank or machine. wide funnel, orange end Pours fluid into the neighbouring tank or machine. narrow spout, teal end Switches this side off. no sleeve The usual tank-to-tank setup: on the side facing the first tank, on the side facing the second. Shift+right-click with the wrench does not configure sides — that dismantles the pipe, as it does with any block of the mod.

Where a pipe meets another pipe there is nothing to draw from or pour into — it is simply part of the route. The wrench there only toggles "joined" and "cut". Cut it and join it back, and the line works again.

The pipe is not a full cube: a 4×4×4 core in the middle of the block (6 to 10 on each axis) plus a sleeve towards every connected side. Placed and broken with a pickaxe, hardness 0.2, blast resistance 0.5, copper sound. The block does not occlude light and you can see neighbouring blocks through it. The fluid shows through the casing, coloured by whatever is flowing: water blue, lava orange, oil black. Fluids from other mods show in their own colour too.
Six silver ingots ringed around a block of glass — corners empty — yielding eight pipes. The glass is not decorative — it is what lets you see the contents.
The basic LV-tier pipe. Planned next: a reinforced one (higher throughput) and a filtering one (passes only a chosen fluid).

It's the no-fuss power source you reach for when there's no sun and no wind: it just runs, day or night, rain or shine. Mini-example: drop a piece of coal in, point a cable at it, and you've got 8 EU/t steady power for your first Macerator. It ignores the weather — the only thing it cares about is fuel.

The generator only produces power — it never takes any in. It holds up to 4000 EU inside and sends it out on an LV line. Feed it any vanilla furnace fuel. It burns at a steady 8 EU/t for as long as the fuel lasts; when the buffer is full, it pauses until there's room again. You craft it from a regular Generator, so it's an upgrade, not a first power source. Mini-example: pour one lava bucket in → it runs for a good while at 16 EU/t, pushing about 16 000 EU into your network. A full 10-bucket tank keeps a small base running almost unattended.

The Sky Mill is the second tier of the sky branch (T2), an evolution of the [basic Wind Turbine](windmill.md). It produces EU from the wind with open sky above, but its base grows with altitude twice as fast (its ridge takes 8 blocks per step instead of 16) and caps at 12 EU/tick. Weather affects it less than the other turbines (rain ×1.25, thunder ×1.5) — this is the steady-income turbine, not the peaky one. It is obtained only through evolution of the basic turbine with a Solar Evolution Chip; it has no crafting recipe.

The turbine only produces power and never accepts incoming energy. An 8000 EU buffer, LV-tier output. Energy is emitted from the back face only — same as T1, so the cable on the back wall keeps working after evolution. The other 5 faces are inert. Field Value Role producer with buffer Buffer (EU) 8000 Max input n/a (does not accept energy) Max output (EU/tick) 32 (LV) EU/tick 0–12 (base 0–8 on the altitude curve, peaking under the clouds × weak weather multiplier, capped at 12)

As with T1, but doubled payoff from altitude: the wind curve's ridge is reached at 8 blocks per step above sea level (instead of 16), up to 8 EU/tick, and weather multiplies it only weakly: rain ×1.25, thunder ×1.5, capped at 12 EU/tick. At y ≈ 128 the Sky Mill outputs 4 EU/tick — twice what the basic mill makes at the same height, but only half of its own full base; the full 8 EU/tick comes only in the y 188–192 band, under a clear sky — more than any other turbine in fair weather. Field Value Source wind: altitude above sea level + open sky + weather Working condition rotor installed AND open sky above the block AND blade area is clear AND buffer not full Dimensions minecraft:overworld EU/tick (base) on the wind curve; maximum 8 at y 188–192, 0 above y=248 Modifiers weather: clear ×1, rain ×1.25, thunder ×1.5; result capped at 12 EU/tick Altitude, sky and weather are recalculated roughly once every two seconds; between recalculations the rate stays the same. Blade clearance and rotor interference are exactly the same as on T1: the rotor needs a clear 2×2 square in front of the turbine, and overlapping blades with a neighbouring turbine stops both. Full rules and the diagram are in the T1 spec.

Type: container — energy bar (tooltip on hover), the central rotor slot and status indicator in the same positions as the basic turbine. While the turbine runs, the status row shows the current output in EU/tick; while it is stopped, the reason. No chip slot and no evolution progress (T2 is a leaf — it doesn't evolve further).
Field Value Shape full 16³ cube (occluder) Placement facing the player Hardness 3.0 Blast resistance 6.0 Tool pickaxe

The Sky Mill isn't craftable. The only way to get it is to grow it from a basic turbine: insert a Solar Evolution Chip and let it work under open sky with a rotor installed. The stored energy carries over on evolution. Crafting: none. The block is not available from a crafting table. Evolution (the only way to obtain it): a basic Wind Turbine + rotor installed + a sun alignment chip + accumulated open-sky time → turns into the Sky Mill, keeping the energy it had stored.
Wind Turbine — the neutral T1, the source of the evolution. Tempest Mill — the mirror of the tempest branch.

The Lightning Rod Generator is the only generator in the mod that runs on an event rather than on a steady flow. It stands there and waits for bad weather. In rain — and especially in a thunderstorm — lightning hits it, and a single strike is worth 20 000 EU: more than a bucket of lava in the geothermal generator. But a strike can only be caught into free space. Inside sits a conductor tip — a part you craft yourself, and it is the reservoir. As long as there is room in it, the strike is absorbed whole. If the reserve has not been drained yet, the strike is wasted, and the tip wears twice as hard as it would from a caught one. That is the whole point of the block: once you see a thunderstorm rolling in, spend what you have banked before it arrives. Mini-example: a rod with a copper tip under open sky catches a strike roughly every 45 seconds in a thunderstorm. One strike is 20 000 EU, and that then bleeds into the network at 16 EU/t for over a minute.

The rod only produces energy — it never accepts any. Energy passes through the block in two steps: the strike first lands in the tip's capacitor, and from there it flows at an even rate into the internal buffer and on into the network. What Value Energy per strike 20 000 EU Tip capacitor 20 000 / 25 000 / 30 000 EU (by grade) Bleed into the network 16 / 20 / 24 EU/t (by grade) Internal buffer 4000 EU Tier cap 32 EU/t (LV) Energy leaves through every side except the top. The top is the working face — that is where the lightning lands, and no energy passes through it. Cable can be attached to any side or from below, exactly as on the solar panels.

Lightning strikes by chance, not on a schedule. Three conditions have to hold at once: open sky above the block, rain or a thunderstorm, and a biome where rain actually falls. Weather How often it strikes Clear never Rain roughly once every 4 minutes Thunderstorm roughly once every 45 seconds Important: it never rains in the desert or in snowy biomes — a rod there will never catch anything at all. It is the same rule that keeps ordinary lightning out of the desert. Under a roof the block is just as useless: if there is anything at all above it, no strike will come. The lightning the rod attracts is harmless: it does not set buildings on fire, it does not hurt the player, and it does not turn a creeper into a charged one. It looks and sounds like the real thing, but it does no damage.

A tip is fitted and has room → the energy is absorbed and the tip takes wear. No tip → the strike is lost entirely. The block itself is fine; nothing breaks. The tip wore out on the strike → its reserve goes with it: the capacitor IS the part. The capacitor is full → the strike is lost, and the tip wears twice as hard as usual. Nothing explodes or burns down in the process — the punishment for being unprepared is simply that you lost a free 20 000 EU and a slice of the tip's lifetime.
Slot Takes Count Tip a conductor tip of any grade (required — without it there is no energy) 1

The screen shows the internal buffer bar on the left and the capacitor bar (blue) on the right: that bar is the caught reserve. The tip slot sits in the centre, with a status line underneath in "No conductor tip" — fit the part, or everything goes to waste; "Clear skies" — no weather about, nothing to wait for; "Sheltered" — something is above the block, or the biome gets no rain; "Armed" — bad weather is running, there is room in the capacitor, waiting for a strike; "Overload!" — a strike has just been wasted; while the capacitor is bleeding into the network, the current output is shown instead of the status. While it discharges, indicators glow on the body and the tip shines blue — a working rod is visible from far away.

A squat slab with a mast. The mast only appears once a tip is fitted — an empty rod looks like a bare pad, so an unequipped block is obvious without opening the screen. What Value Tool pickaxe Keeps its charge when broken yes Tip when broken drops
A caught strike sounds like an ordinary thunderclap. A wasted one gives a sharp crack and blue sparks above the mast.

Four crafting-table recipes: the block itself and the three tip grades. Lightning Rod Generator — a vanilla lightning rod on top, a machine body in the centre, copper cables on the sides, an electronic circuit underneath. Copper Conductor Tip — copper ingots, an iron plate, copper cable. Reinforced Conductor Tip — two electronic circuits, tempered plates and a copper conductor tip. Advanced Conductor Tip — two advanced circuits, gold plates and a reinforced conductor tip.

It is not the block that gets upgraded but the part inside it. Every next grade banks more, bleeds Grade Reserve Bleed Lasts for Copper 20 000 EU 16 EU/t 5 strikes Reinforced 25 000 EU 20 EU/t 20 strikes Advanced 30 000 EU 24 EU/t 60 strikes A worn tip is repaired by the Component Repair Bench — the same one that fixes windmill rotors.
Component Repair Bench — repairs a worn conductor tip. Tempest Mill — the other block that wants a thunderstorm; a good neighbour. Battery Box — somewhere to put the caught reserve. Copper Cable

The Moonlit Solar Panel is the night twin of the Daylight Solar Panel — the second tier of the night branch. It produces EU at night under open sky and nothing by day, so your machines don't fall silent after dark. You can't craft it. The only way to get one is to grow it from a base panel with a Lunar Evolution Chip (see Solar Panel → Progression). Mini-example: evolved from a base panel with a night chip → 3 EU/t on a clear night. Pair it with a day panel and your workshop runs around the clock — one feeds the Battery Box while the other sleeps. A unique trick of the night branch: even in rain or a thunderstorm it keeps a faint 1 EU/t trickle, so it never falls fully silent in bad weather.

The panel only produces power — it never takes any in. It holds up to 8000 EU and sends it out on an LV line. The Tempest Mill is the second tier of the tempest branch (T2), an evolution of the [basic Wind Turbine](windmill.md). Its base is slightly above T1 (step 16, cap 6), but the weather multipliers are stronger: rain ×2, thunder ×3.5, with an overall cap of 24 EU/tick (the reachable peak is 21). In clear weather it's weaker than the Sky Mill, but in rain and thunder it's an exciting "storm-catcher". It is obtained only through evolution of the basic turbine with a Lunar Evolution Chip; it has no crafting recipe.

The turbine only produces power and never accepts incoming energy. An 8000 EU buffer, LV-tier output. Energy is emitted from the back face only — same as T1, so the cable on the back wall keeps working after evolution. The other 5 faces are inert. As with T1, the base follows the wind curve (full base only at y 189–192, zero above y = 248), but the cap is a bit higher (6) and weather hits harder: in rain the base is multiplied by 2, in thunder by 3.5, with an overall cap of 24 EU/tick. In rain the Tempest Mill already beats what T1 does in a thunderstorm, and in a thunderstorm in the y 189–192 band it puts out 21 EU/tick — more than any other LV generator. That band is narrow, only 4 heights: at y ≈ 159 the same thunderstorm gives 11 EU/tick. In clear weather it's weaker than the Sky Mill (base 6 vs 8), which is the price of that peak. Field Value Source wind: altitude above sea level + open sky + weather Working condition rotor installed AND open sky above the block AND blade area is clear AND buffer not full Dimensions minecraft:overworld EU/tick (base) on the wind curve, ridge at +96 blocks; maximum 6 at y 189–192, 0 above y=248 Modifiers weather: clear ×1, rain ×2.0, thunder ×3.5; result capped at 24 EU/tick Altitude, sky and weather are recalculated roughly once every two seconds; between recalculations the rate stays the same. Blade clearance and rotor interference are exactly the same as on T1: the rotor needs a clear 2×2 square in front of the turbine, and overlapping blades with a neighbouring turbine stops both (even in a full thunderstorm). Full rules and the diagram are in the T1 spec.

Type: container — energy bar (tooltip on hover), the central rotor slot and status indicator in the same positions as the basic turbine. While the turbine runs, the status row shows the current output in EU/tick; while it is stopped, the reason. No chip slot and no evolution progress (T2 is a leaf — it doesn't evolve further).
Field Value Shape full 16³ cube (occluder) Placement facing the player Hardness 3.0 Blast resistance 6.0 Tool pickaxe

The Tempest Mill isn't craftable. The only way to get it is to grow it from a basic turbine: insert a Lunar Evolution Chip and let it work under open sky with a rotor installed. The stored energy carries over on evolution. Crafting: none. The block is not available from a crafting table. Evolution (the only way to obtain it): a basic Wind Turbine + rotor installed + a moon alignment chip + accumulated open-sky time → turns into the Tempest Mill, keeping the energy it had stored.
Wind Turbine — the neutral T1, the source of the evolution. Sky Mill — the mirror of the sky branch.

The Water Mill turns on flowing water and runs around the clock — night and storms mean nothing to it. No fuel, no tanks, no pumps: give it a current past the wheel and it produces EU for as long as the water keeps moving. Mini-example: a channel with a waterfall on either side of the wheel → 4 EU/t, non-stop. Over one in-game day that is 96 000 EU — eight times what a T1 solar panel makes in the same time (12 000 EU, and only by day). The one catch: still water does not count. Dropping the wheel into a pond or a river is not enough — it needs a real current.

The mill only produces power. Output leaves through the back face, which carries the connector; the other five faces are inert for energy. Field Value Internal buffer 4000 EU Output up to 32 EU/t (LV) Actual production 0–4 EU/t (1 per wheel side in a current)

The wheel hangs one cell in front of the block, and water is counted around the wheel, not around the mill. The four working cells mirror how real water wheels are driven: Cell What it is called Below the wheel undershot — the classic; the rim dips into the current Above the wheel overshot — water poured over the top Left and right the horizontal sweep of the rim Each cell with a current gives 1 EU/t, all four give the maximum 4 EU/t. The hub cell (directly in front of the mill) does not count: that is where the axle sits. Only flowing or falling water counts. Rivers and oceans are made of source blocks, so "put it in a river" will not work. The reliable trick: place a source one cell above the wheel's cell — falling water never becomes a source. Pouring a bucket straight into the wheel's cell is useless, because that cell then becomes a source itself.

The wheel is large (rim about 2.7 blocks) and needs room to turn. All nine cells of the wheel's plane are checked — the front column and both neighbours, each on three levels, bottom row and diagonals included. A solid block in any of them hides the wheel and stops generation: the screen reads "Blocked". Water and passable blocks (grass, flowers, snow) do not obstruct it, so a channel around the wheel works fine. The check runs every tick: remove the block and the wheel is back.

If two wheels overlap in space, both mills stop with the status "Wheel interference". Arrangement Gap needed Side by side 2 empty blocks Face to face 2 empty blocks Back to back flush is fine A neighbour without a wheel causes no trouble — but put a wheel in it and the working mill beside it stops too.

One slot for the water wheel and four upgrade slots. Without a wheel the mill produces nothing and the external model is not drawn. The wheel is a consumable. It only wears while the mill is actually producing EU (no current or an obstruction means no wear) and in proportion to output. A full wheel is worth 320 000 EU: about an hour of non-stop work at maximum, or 6–7 in-game days at a typical 2 EU/t. When it runs out the wheel breaks with a sound and generation stops until a new one is fitted. A worn wheel need not be thrown away: the component repair bench clears the wear for one item and some EU, at the cost of a lower durability ceiling — and no more than four times.

Energy bar on the left, wheel slot in the centre, indicator on the right: a white wheel means idle, blue means working. The line under the slot shows either the current output or the reason it stopped: "Wheel interference", "Blocked", "No water" or "No wheel". The line is never empty. A mill with no wheel used to say nothing, on the reasoning that the empty slot spoke for itself. In practice the player saw a working-looking screen producing nothing and got no hint at all. It is now a state of its own with its own line, like the Wind Turbine's "No rotor".
An ordinary full block, broken with any pickaxe. Field Value Shape full cube Hardness 3.0 Blast resistance 6.0 Tool pickaxe

A large open wheel turns in front of the mill: two 24-segment oak rims, eight spokes on each side, twelve buckets between the rims, a wooden hub and a copper axle. The stronger the current, the faster it spins; with no current the wheel stands still.
While the wheel turns you hear a quiet splash of water within about 12 blocks. It falls silent when the wheel stops.
Crafted at a workbench from planks, copper ingots, a copper cable and a wooden gear. The water wheel is crafted separately — the mill does not work without it.
Solar Panel — the other passive source, but it depends on the sky and the time of day. Generator — twice the output, but it needs fuel. Water Wheel — the consumable the mill cannot run without.

The Wind Turbine makes EU from the wind — no fuel, no sun, just altitude and weather. Build it high and it pays off; build it on the ground and it does almost nothing. It rewards players who climb a tower and don't mind a storm. To run, it needs three things: a Wooden Rotor in its slot, open sky above, and clear space around the blades. The worse the weather, the more power it makes. Mini-example: a turbine in the narrow band under the clouds (y 183–193) → 4 EU/t on a clear day and 8 EU/t in a thunderstorm. Lower down it drops off sharply: at y ≈ 128 you only get 2 EU/t.

The turbine only produces power — it never takes any in. It holds up to 4000 EU inside and sends it out on an LV line. What Value Internal buffer 4000 EU Output up to 32 EU/t (LV) Realistic output 0–8 EU/t (altitude × weather) Energy comes out only from the back face. Connect your cable to the turbine's back wall — the other sides output nothing.

The closer to the clouds and the worse the weather, the more power. The wind does not strengthen forever: the strongest air runs right at the cloud deck (y ≈ 192), and above it the air thins out and the wind dies away. The weather multiplies the result. Altitude / weather Output At or below sea level 0 (useless on the ground) y ≈ 100 1 EU/t y ≈ 127 2 EU/t y ≈ 175 3 EU/t y 183–193 (under the clouds) 4 EU/t — the maximum, eleven heights in all y ≈ 210 2 EU/t y ≥ 248 0 (the air is too thin) …in rain ×1.5 …in a thunderstorm ×2 Overall cap 8 EU/t So a turbine in the narrow band under the clouds makes 4 EU/t clear, 6 EU/t in rain, 8 EU/t in a storm — but it is easy to miss: twenty blocks lower or higher it is already weaker, and roofed, with blocked blades, or pushed to the world ceiling it stops altogether. Where exactly to put that tower is what the Wind Gauge is for: it reads the same wind curve and reports it in km/h before you build. If something's wrong, the screen says so in plain words: "no rotor", "roofed", "blocked", "interference" or "calm". When it's actually generating, the gear indicator lights up.

The blades spin in the block in front of the turbine and need room around them. Keep these clear: the block in front, one block to each side, and the three blocks directly below (a little pit). If anything solid is there, the turbine shows "blocked" and stops. "Clear" means air, grass, flowers, saplings or snow — anything you could place a block into. Stone, glass, leaves, fences, slabs or the turbine's own support pillar all count as blocked. You don't need to check the air above the blades — a roof is caught separately by the open-sky check.

Simple spacing rules so the blades don't collide: Same direction, side by side: leave 1 block of air between them, or both stop. Back to back: can sit right next to each other. Face to face: need at least 2 blocks between them. When two turbines interfere, both stop, no exceptions. A neighbour with no rotor causes no trouble — but the moment you put a rotor in it, a running turbine next door stops too.

While the rotor spins, the wind mill softly rustles its sails in the wind — the loop (pattern C, 0.22, fixed 12-block range). It falls silent in calm weather, under a roof, on a neighbouring rotor's interference, or with no rotor installed.

Wind Turbine — copper ingots in the corners, planks top and bottom, copper cable on the sides, a wooden gear in the centre. Wooden Rotor (required to run) — planks in the corners, iron ingots top and bottom, copper cable on the sides, a wooden gear in the centre.

The basic turbine is the neutral tier-1 form. Drop in an evolution chip (the same one solar panels use) and let it run under open sky with a rotor in, and it turns into a stronger version, keeping its stored energy: Solar Evolution Chip → Sky branch: stronger at altitude → Sky Mill. Lunar Evolution Chip → Tempest branch: stronger in bad weather → Tempest Mill. Expect roughly a day and a half (~28 real minutes). Evolution is weather-independent: the chip keeps accruing progress in any weather, as long as there's open sky above the mill, the blades are clear and the rotor is installed — so, unlike the solar panel, the wind mill evolves at night and in the rain alike. Component Repair Bench — restores a worn rotor for one item and some EU; every repair lowers its durability ceiling, and there are four of them. Sky Mill — T2 sky evolution branch. The Item Pipe carries things between chests and machines so you don't have to run them across yourself. Lay a line of pipes from one chest to another, tell it with the wrench where to take from and where to put — and it works on its own. It needs no power. A pipe moves 2 items per second. That's a touch slower than a hopper, so a full stack takes about 32 seconds. In exchange it runs any distance, branches, and lets you set each side — a hopper does none of that. Want speed: that comes with later pipes. If a pipe pulls from several chests (or feeds several), it takes them in turns — nobody is left out.

Every side of a pipe has a role. Point at the side you want and right-click it with the wrench: the role switches to the next one. Only the side you clicked changes, and what it became is printed at the bottom of the screen. Mode What it does How it looks A plain connection: takes and gives. plain sleeve Takes things out of the chest or machine next to it. wide mouth, orange tip Puts things into the chest or machine next to it. narrow nozzle, teal tip Turns this side off entirely. no sleeve You read the role straight off the block, nothing to open: an orange mouth takes, a teal nozzle gives, and a disabled side simply has no sleeve. The usual chest-to-chest setup: on the side facing the first chest, on the side facing the second. That's it — the items are moving. The main rule: configure nothing and the pipe decides; configure any side and the pipe does exactly what you configured. The moment any side on the line is given a role ( or ), every untouched side becomes just a stretch of the route: it neither takes nor gives. So "EXTRACT on the first chest, second one untouched" moves nothing — give the second side . One glance then tells you whether the line is finished: there is a mouth and there is a nozzle. Two chests with both sides left on will move nothing, and that is not a fault. means "takes and gives", so on such a line both ends are a source and a destination at once: whatever one hands over, the other would hand straight back. The pipe recognises that pair and leaves it alone — otherwise the items would ride back and forth forever. If you want a transfer, assign the sides: where you take from, where you put. You do not need to do this with a machine: it sorts its slots by side (ore goes into the input, the product comes out of the output), so "chest ↔ machine" with both sides works exactly as you would expect — what comes back is a different item, not the same one. A pipe never loses or duplicates anything: if the destination chest is full, the item stays where it is and the pipe just waits for room. Shift-right-click with the wrench does not set sides — that dismantles the pipe, like any block of this mod.

Where a pipe meets another pipe there is nothing to take or give — it's just a stretch of the route. So the wrench only toggles joined ↔ cut there, and no mouth or nozzle is drawn: a run of pipes stays smooth.
6 silver ingots ringed around an iron gear — corners empty — gives 8 pipes.
Wrench — sets each side, and takes the pipe back apart. Iron Gear — the crafting core. Silver — the body of the pipe.

The Battery Pouch is the mod's first electric item — a portable item store that works like a vanilla bundle but holds twice as much and needs a charge. It fits 128 weight of items (about two stacks of ordinary blocks) in one inventory slot, so it earns its keep on long trips and tight inventories. The catch is that while items sit inside it, the pouch slowly burns charge: 1 EU per second. When the charge hits zero a lock snaps shut — you can neither put things in nor take them out until you recharge it. The contents are never lost, only locked. Mini-example: going mining for an hour? Fill the pouch with cobblestone, ore, the odd tool, and keep your hotbar clean. Top it up at a Battery Box before you head out and it will hold the whole trip — about 33 minutes of carrying on a full charge.

The pouch carries its own small charge, separate from the energy network. You fill it at a Battery Box; it spends that charge only while items are inside and it sits in your inventory. Field Value Charge held 2 000 EU Charging Battery Box charge slot — full in about 3 seconds Drain 1 EU per second, only while items are inside and it is in your inventory Runs flat in about 33 minutes of carrying items When empty contents lock (safe) until you recharge

The pouch is one inventory slot holding up to 128 weight. How much an item costs to store depends on how stackable it is — the same rule as a vanilla bundle: Item type Weight of 1 Fits in 128 Blocks and resources (stack to 64) 1 128 items (about 2 stacks) Pearls, snowballs (stack to 16) 4 32 items Tools, buckets (no stack) 64 2 items

Putting items in: right-click a stack onto the pouch (or the pouch onto a stack) inside an inventory. Items fill an existing partial stack of the same type first, then take up new weight. Anything that does not fit stays in your hand. Taking items out: right-click the pouch in the air or on an empty slot to pull the whole top stack (last in, first out). The lock at zero charge: once the charge runs out, both putting in and taking out are blocked. Nothing is destroyed — the contents just sit there, locked, until you recharge. What drains it: 1 EU per second, but only while items are inside and the pouch is in a player's inventory. Sitting in a chest, on the ground, or in a Battery Box slot, it costs nothing. In creative: it does not drain at all — just as a vanilla tool takes no durability damage in creative. The same rule holds for the whole powered family: the Energy Pack and the Electric Drill spend no charge in creative either. The charge bar: the bar under the icon shows the charge (yellow). The tooltip lists the contents as a grid plus a fill bar showing "weight / 128 (NN%)" with the fill fraction as a percent; below 10 % it warns you, and at zero it shows a red "discharged". Nesting: a pouch cannot go inside another pouch. It can go inside a vanilla bundle or a shulker box. Rename it: at a vanilla anvil. On drop or death: the charge, the contents and a name you set all stay with the pouch.
Not applicable (item).
Crafted at a workbench: a leather body, a tin clasp, a vanilla bundle in the centre, and an electronic circuit at the bottom. The recipe shows up in your recipe book once you have all the parts.

The mod's first electric item — the entry point into powered carrying gear. Available after the Battery Box; without it the pouch cannot be charged. Higher tiers are planned for later — more weight, filters, and linking between pouches.

Battery Box — charges it from this mod's side (the charge slot). Energy Pack — the next step up: a worn pack that tops the pouch up in your inventory. Electronic Circuit — a crafting component. Tin — the clasp in the crafting.

The Electric Chainsaw is the mod's second powered hand tool and the wood-side mirror of the Electric Drill: an axe that runs on EU instead of durability. With charge it cuts faster than a diamond axe (speed 9.0 against 8.0) and spends 30 EU per block. A full buffer is 10 000 EU — about 333 blocks on one charge. Mini-example: fell a tree, then clear its canopy at the same speed — a third tool rule puts on the axe, which vanilla files under the hoe. When the chainsaw runs flat it doesn't stop; it just cuts at hand speed until you recharge, with the same drops the whole time. Like the mod's other EU items, the chainsaw has no durability and never breaks: the bar under the icon shows EU charge (gold), not wear. It charges where the Energy Pack does — in the Battery Box charge slot and from a worn pack.

Its own EU buffer, outside the energy network. Charges in the Battery Box slot and from a worn pack; spends charge cutting. What Value Buffer 10 000 EU Charging Battery Box slot / worn pack, fills in ~16 s Cost 30 EU per block broken Passive drain none Instant-break blocks — leaves in most configurations, saplings, vines — are free, just as they never wear a vanilla axe. In creative no EU is spent.

Cutting: with at least 30 EU it cuts and at speed 9.0. Each such block costs 30 EU. Flat chainsaw: below 30 EU it cuts at hand speed (1.0) but keeps its mining level and drops, and spends nothing. Efficiency does not apply there — vanilla only grants it above speed 1.0. Charging: the Battery Box charge slot and a worn Energy Pack both accept it automatically, up to 32 EU/t. Attack: hits like a diamond axe (6 damage, 1.0 attack speed); attacking spends no EU and causes no wear. Enchanting: it sits in , so the table and anvil treat it as an axe. Readout: the bar shows charge; the tooltip reads the exact numbers, or a red "Empty" at zero, and the texture switches to its unpowered variant. Log stripping is not supported. Vanilla stripping lives in , and extending would drag in , which sets and makes the tool breakable — the opposite of the "EU only, never breaks" model. Strip with an ordinary axe.
Not applicable — the chainsaw has no internal item storage (stack size 1).
Not applicable (item).

The drill's frame with a diamond axe in the middle instead of a diamond pickaxe: iron ingots on top, two batteries at the sides, two copper coils and an electronic circuit below. Charge held by the batteries carries over into the finished chainsaw. The recipe unlocks once you obtain a copper coil, an electronic circuit or a diamond axe. Repair is not applicable — there is no durability; "repair" means recharging.

The Diamond-Tipped Electric Chainsaw (is the chainsaw's second tier and the wood-side mirror of the Diamond-Tipped Electric Drill. Exactly two things differ from the base chainsaw; everything else is inherited unchanged. 1. It cuts faster. Speed 10.5 against the base chainsaw's 9.0 — the same step the drill took (8.5 → 10.0). The speed-up covers wood and leaves alike, because on the chainsaw the two sit on one and the same tool rule. The mining tier does not change — the upgrade makes the work faster, it does not unlock new blocks. 2. Switchable Silk Touch for leaves. Sneak + right-click flips the drop mode: normal mode (what a freshly crafted chainsaw starts in) — leaves drop as usual: saplings, sticks, the occasional apple; Silk Touch mode — the leaf block drops as itself, whole. Why that is worth having: in vanilla the only way to collect whole leaf blocks is shears, and shears are a separate item you have to keep in your hotbar and swap in by hand for every canopy. The tipped chainsaw does both jobs with one tool: fell the trunk, flip the mode, and harvest the canopy for decoration or topiary. Why switchable rather than permanent: permanent Silk Touch would cost the chainsaw its saplings for good, and without saplings a felled forest cannot be replanted. The toggle removes that problem — exactly as on the drill, where permanent Silk Touch would have killed ore doubling. The mode is visible without guesswork: while it is on, the item carries the enchantment glint and lists "Silk Touch I" in its tooltip (the mode is the real vanilla enchantment, not a separate parallel flag), and a dedicated tooltip line shows the state and reminds you of the sneak + right-click control. Switching plays a click and prints a line above the hotbar. The converse follows too: if you enchant the upgrade with Silk Touch yourself at a table, the chainsaw honestly reports "mode on", and the toggle will switch it off. There is one state, not two that can disagree. The mode does not affect logs. Wood drops as itself with any tool in vanilla, so Silk Touch on a trunk changes nothing. As a side effect the mode also touches the other blocks of the axe domain — mushroom blocks, the bookshelf, beehives (they drop whole, and a hive keeps its bees) — that is vanilla Silk Touch behaviour, not a separate mod mechanic. Inherited unchanged: the 10 000 EU buffer, 30 EU per block, 32 EU/t intake, the same charging places, no durability, hand-speed cutting when flat, creative behaviour, and the diamond-axe attack. Log stripping is unsupported on both chainsaws for the same architectural reason (see "How it behaves"). Recipe: — the base chainsaw in the centre, a row of three diamond dust above it (the "tip coating" itself), two bronze ingots at its sides (the body), and a gold gear below (the chain drive).
