The materials deliberately differ from the drill's (invar and a silver gear) so that the two upgrade branches do not pull on the same shortage. Charge survives the upgrade. The chainsaw's recipe uses the type — the same one the drill and the base powered tools use — so the EU in the chainsaw you put in moves into the result instead of burning away. The auto-fill button (the recipe book, and the "+" in REI/JEI) still will not find a charged chainsaw: vanilla looks for an item whose components exactly match the display stack, and the display shows an empty chainsaw. Lay the grid out by hand — it works with a chainsaw in any state.

The second powered tool after the Electric Drill: the drill covers stone, the chainsaw covers wood. Needs LV infrastructure first — without the Battery Box and a battery it can be neither crafted nor charged. LV tier. The remaining electric tools (hoe/saber/nano bow) are future work.

Electric Drill — the stone half of the pair; the same no-durability EU contract. Energy Pack — charges the chainsaw right in your inventory. Battery Box — charges the chainsaw (charge slot). Electronic Circuit — a crafting component.

The Electric Drill is the mod's first powered hand tool: a diamond-tier pickaxe that runs on EU instead of durability. With charge it mines a touch faster than a diamond pickaxe and spends 50 EU per block. A full buffer is 10 000 EU — about 200 blocks on one charge. Mini-example: mine ~200 blocks on a charge; when it runs flat, it doesn't stop — it just mines at hand speed until you recharge. Same mining level and drops the whole time, just slower. Like the mod's other EU items, the drill has no durability and never breaks: the bar under the icon shows EU charge (gold), not wear. It charges where the Energy Pack does — in the Battery Box charge slot and from a worn pack. The drill has a second tier — the Diamond-Tipped Electric Drill: the same tool, but it digs faster and can switch its drops to Silk Touch. See Diamond tip (upgrade) below.

Its own EU buffer, outside the energy network. Charges in the Battery Box slot and from a worn pack; spends charge mining. What Value Buffer 10 000 EU Charging Battery Box slot / worn pack, fills in ~16 s Cost 50 EU per block broken Passive drain none Instant-break blocks (grass, torches, flowers) are free — just as they never wear a vanilla tool. In creative, blocks drop nothing and no EU is spent.

Mining (charged): mines everything a pickaxe should, a touch faster than diamond. Diamond ore, obsidian, even ancient debris — drops match a diamond pickaxe. Each block costs 50 EU. Mining (flat): below 50 EU it mines at hand speed, but keeps the mining level and drops, and spends no EU. Charging: the Battery Box charge slot and a worn Energy Pack both accept it automatically. Combat: hits a touch harder than a diamond pickaxe (6 damage), but attacks spend no EU. Enchantments: the enchanting table and anvil treat it like a diamond pickaxe — Efficiency, Fortune, Silk Touch, Unbreaking, Mending. (Unbreaking/Mending are harmless but useless on an unbreakable tool.) Torch placement: with the drill in your main hand and torches in your inventory, right-clicking a block places a torch — the drill stays in your hotbar and the torch is pulled from your inventory (one used up). It prefers the Enriched Uranium Torch (which stays lit underwater) and falls back to a normal torch. Each placement drains 5 EU. If the charge is below that the torch is not placed: the drill shows a message above your hotbar, no torch leaves your inventory, and the charge is untouched — the torch is powered, not free (you can still place one by hand for free by moving it to your hotbar). That message only appears where a charged drill would really have placed something: where a torch cannot go anyway (no support, or water for a normal torch), a flat drill stays out of the way entirely — no message, and the click goes to your off-hand item as if the drill were not in your hand. Placing a torch this way sounds exactly like placing one by hand, for you and for anyone nearby. Where a torch can't go (no support, or water for a normal torch) nothing happens and nothing is spent. In creative neither the torch nor the EU is consumed and the charge check does not apply. No torches in your inventory and it does nothing (a torch in your off-hand still works as normal). No cooldown. In creative: no charge is spent — not on mining, not on torches — just as a vanilla pickaxe takes no durability damage in creative. The rule covers the whole powered family; see the Energy Pack and the Battery Pouch. HUD: while in hand, an icon + charge % + bar (green → gold → red) show top-left. Same H key toggles it as the Energy Pack.
Not applicable — the drill has no internal item storage (stack size 1).
Not applicable (item).

Built at a workbench around a finished diamond pickaxe — it sits in the centre and gives the drill its diamond mining tier (the drill itself digs a touch faster, 8.5 vs a diamond pickaxe's 8.0). Two batteries flank it, an electronic circuit sits below between two copper coils, and an iron body caps the top. All the power components gate the drill behind LV infrastructure. The charge held by the batteries carries over into the finished drill.

The Diamond-Tipped Electric Drill (is the drill's second tier. Exactly two things differ from the base drill; everything else is inherited unchanged. 1. It digs faster. Mining speed 10.0 against the base drill's 8.5 (and a netherite pickaxe's 9.0). The mining tier does not change — it stays diamond, exactly like the base drill: the upgrade makes the work faster, it does not unlock new blocks. 2. Switchable Silk Touch. Sneak + right-click flips the drop mode: normal mode (what a freshly crafted drill starts in) — drops exactly like the base drill, so ore comes out as raw material and still feeds the Macerator for doubling; Silk Touch mode — the block drops as itself: ore as ore, glass as glass, leaves as leaves. Why switchable rather than permanent: the base drill can already be given Silk Touch at an enchanting table, but a vanilla enchantment is one-way — it permanently locks out Fortune (the two are mutually exclusive) and it breaks the ore-doubling chain, because ore stops dropping as raw material. A toggle solves both. The mode is visible without guesswork: while it is on, the item carries the enchantment glint and lists "Silk Touch I" in its tooltip (the mode is the real vanilla enchantment, not a separate parallel flag), and a dedicated tooltip line shows the state and reminds you of the sneak + right-click control. Switching plays a click and prints a line above the hotbar. The converse follows too: if you enchant the upgrade with Silk Touch yourself at a table, the drill honestly reports "mode on", and the toggle will switch it off. There is one state, not two that can disagree. Inherited unchanged: the 10 000 EU buffer, 50 EU per block, 32 EU/t intake, the same charging places, torch placement on right-click at the same 5 EU, no durability, hand-speed mining when flat, and creative behaviour. The one control difference: sneak + right-click on a block switches the mode instead of placing a torch — torches go down with a plain right-click. Recipe: — the base drill in the centre, a row of three diamond dust above it (the "tip coating" itself), two invar ingots at its sides (the body), and a silver gear below (the head drive). None of those three materials were consumed anywhere in the mod before — the upgrade gives them their first use. The drill's charge carries over into the upgrade. There is no need to run the drill flat first: whatever EU it held, the upgrade comes out holding. Both share the same 10 000 EU buffer, so nothing is lost on the way and a full drill gives a full upgrade. This is the mod's general rule — energy moves into the result instead of burning — and every recipe whose result has an EU buffer of its own behaves the same way (see the battery). Place the drill in the grid by hand. The recipe accepts a drill in any state — empty, charged, enchanted — and laying the grid out yourself always works. The auto-fill button, though (the recipe book, and the "+" in viewers like REI/JEI), will not find a charged drill and will report missing materials. That is a Minecraft limitation rather than a mod one: auto-fill looks for an item whose components exactly match the recipe's display stack, and the display shows an empty drill. It is the same reason auto-fill never picks up enchanted or renamed items, in any recipe in the game. Laying the grid out by hand takes a couple of seconds and works with any drill.

The mod's first powered tool — a bridge between the energy progression and hand mining. Available after the Battery Box and the Energy Pack. Its second tier is the diamond-tip upgrade above, gated behind the Alloy Smelter (invar) and the Macerator (diamond dust). Other electric tools (chainsaw/hoe/saber) are future work.
Energy Pack — charges the drill in your inventory. Battery Box — charges the drill. Tempered Iron Pickaxe — the non-powered alternative earlier on.

The Electric Hoe is the fourth and last powered hand tool in the line: after the Electric Drill (stone), the Electric Chainsaw (wood) and the Electric Shovel (earth), it covers farmland. Same contract: it runs on EU instead of durability, never breaks, and when it runs flat it keeps working at hand speed with every drop intact. It does two things, and both cost 50 EU per use: Tilling. Right-click dirt, grass or a dirt path to make farmland; coarse dirt turns to dirt, rooted dirt to dirt plus a hanging root. Breaking blocks. It breaks at speed 9.0 against a diamond hoe's 8.0 — hay bales, leaves, sponge, moss, nether wart block, dried kelp. A full buffer is 10 000 EU — about 200 uses on one charge. A flat hoe behaves differently in its two roles, on purpose: it keeps breaking at hand speed with every drop intact, but it will not till — instead of farmland you get a red "Not enough charge to till" above the hotbar. The Electric Drill's torch works the same way: mining degrades gracefully, the right-click action needs power. Like the mod's other EU items, the hoe has no durability and never breaks: the bar under the icon shows EU charge (gold), not wear. It charges where the Energy Pack does — in the Battery Box charge slot and from a worn pack.

Its own EU buffer, outside the energy network. Charges in the Battery Box slot and from a worn pack; spends charge only on breaking blocks. What Value Buffer 10 000 EU Charging Battery Box slot / worn pack, fills in ~16 s Cost 50 EU per block broken, 50 EU per successful till Passive drain none In creative no EU is spent.

Tilling and the other right-click conversions cost 50 EU. Dirt, grass and paths become farmland, exactly like a vanilla hoe. The charge is only taken when a conversion actually happened — clicking a stone wall or already-tilled soil costs nothing. A flat hoe says so only over a block it could have tilled: right-clicking anything else passes straight through, with no message and no interception, so the item in your off-hand still works. Breaking: with at least 50 EU it breaks at speed 9.0. Each such block costs 50 EU. Flat hoe: below 50 EU it breaks at hand speed (1.0) but keeps its mining level and drops, and spends nothing. It cannot till — see above. Efficiency does not apply there — vanilla only grants it above speed 1.0. Charging: the Battery Box charge slot and a worn Energy Pack both accept it automatically, up to 32 EU/t. Attack: like a vanilla hoe, it is not a weapon. Attacking spends no EU and causes no wear. Enchanting: it sits in , so the table and anvil treat it as a hoe. Harvesting is not supported. That is the Scythe's job and it stays there. Readout: the bar shows charge; the tooltip reads the exact numbers, or a red "Empty" at zero, and the texture switches to its unpowered variant.
Not applicable — the hoe has no internal item storage (stack size 1).
Not applicable (item).

The same frame as the other three with a diamond hoe in the middle: iron ingots on top, two batteries at the sides, two copper coils and an electronic circuit below. Charge held by the batteries carries over into the finished hoe. The recipe unlocks once you obtain a copper coil, an electronic circuit or a diamond hoe. Repair is not applicable — there is no durability; "repair" means recharging.

Diamond-Tipped Electric Hoe (is the hoe's second tier and the line's third upgrade, after the diamond-tipped drill and the diamond-tipped chainsaw. Exactly two things differ from the base hoe; everything else is inherited unchanged. 1. It breaks faster. Speed 10.5 against the base hoe's 9.0 — the same +1.5 step the drill (8.5 -> 10.0) and the chainsaw (9.0 -> 10.5) took. The mining tier does not change: the upgrade works faster, it does not unlock new blocks. 2. Tilled plots come out already watered. Ordinary tilling — with a vanilla hoe or with the base electric one — creates dry farmland: a fresh farmland block has zero moisture. Vanilla then decides: with water within a ±4-block horizontal box, or with rain, moisture climbs back to maximum on its own; with no water, moisture drops by one per random tick, and once it hits zero with nothing growing on top, the block reverts to dirt. That is where the upgrade earns its keep: in vanilla, tilling a field far from water and not planting it straight away is close to pointless — the plots dry out and crumble back into dirt. The diamond-tipped hoe hands every fresh plot full moisture instead, which gives both faster growth (vanilla grows crops quicker on moist soil) and seven random ticks of slack before a plot can revert at all. This is a head start, not a sprinkler. Moisture then drains on the ordinary vanilla schedule; the upgrade neither tops it up nor replaces water next to the field. It does not water existing farmland either — the effect only fires on a block it just turned into farmland itself, and only when the till was actually paid for. A flat hoe cannot water anything. Note that tilling coarse dirt and rooted dirt yields plain dirt rather than farmland (that is vanilla's own table), so the perk does not apply there — there is nothing to water. Why not Silk Touch, like the drill and the chainsaw. Those upgrades got a switchable Silk Touch mode, and for a hoe it would have been dead weight: every block in its domain ( — hay, leaves, sponge, moss, nether wart block, dried kelp) already drops itself without any enchantment. There is nothing to double and nothing to suppress. So this upgrade strengthens the one thing only the hoe has — tilling. Inherited unchanged: the 10 000 EU buffer, 50 EU per block and 50 EU per till, 32 EU/t intake, the same charging spots, no durability, hand-speed operation on an empty buffer, creative behaviour, and the attack profile of a vanilla hoe (it is not a weapon). The upgrade has no config keys of its own. Crafting: — the base hoe in the centre, a row of three diamond dusts on top (the "tip" itself), two cupronickel ingots at the sides, and lapis dust below. The materials deliberately differ from both the drill's (invar, silver gear) and the chainsaw's (bronze, gold gear) so the three upgrade branches do not compete for the same bottleneck. There is no gear in the recipe on purpose: a hoe has no rotating parts and nothing for a drive to turn — the bottom slot carries lapis dust as the recipe's "water" component instead. The charge survives the upgrade. The recipe uses the type, so the EU inside the base hoe moves into the result rather than burning away. The drill's and the chainsaw's recipes work the same way. You have to lay the recipe out by hand. The recipe book's auto-fill button will not pick up a charged hoe: vanilla's ingredient lookup compares item components, and a charged hoe carries , which the showcase reference does not. This is a vanilla limitation shared by all three upgrades — details in task.

The fourth and last powered tool: drill for stone, chainsaw for wood, shovel for earth, hoe for farmland. Needs LV infrastructure first — without the Battery Box and a battery it can be neither crafted nor charged. LV tier. The remaining electric items (saber/nano bow/vajra) are future work.

Electric Drill — the stone part of the line, same cost per block. Electric Chainsaw — the wood part of the line. Electric Shovel — the soil part; the same right-click delegation trick, but its action is free while the hoe's is paid. Scythe — the harvesting tool; the hoe does not replace it. Battery Box — charges the hoe (charge slot).

The Electric Saber is the fifth item in the powered-equipment line and its first weapon: after the Electric Drill (stone), the Electric Chainsaw (wood), the Electric Shovel (earth) and the Electric Hoe (farmland), combat gets its turn. Same contract as the rest of the line: it runs on EU instead of durability, never breaks, and on an empty buffer it degrades instead of switching off. The saber has three states, and the player controls two of them: State Damage Reach Cost On the target Charged and switched on 12 4 blocks 100 EU per hit Slowness II for 2 s + sparks Switched off (shift-right-click) 4 3 blocks — — Flat 4 3 blocks — — Twelve damage beats every vanilla sword (diamond 7, netherite 8) and our own tempered iron one (6.5). A full 10 000 EU buffer lasts 100 hits; after that the saber hits for 4 — a stone sword's worth, which is still a weapon rather than a stick. A live blade also reaches one block further: an energy edge is longer than a steel one. A flat saber swings at the vanilla 3 blocks. The switch (shift-right-click) is the same ergonomic the Electromagnet has: the player decides when to burn charge. A switched-off saber spends nothing and hits like an ordinary sword — handy on the long walk home when slimes keep turning up. Like the mod's other EU items, the saber has no durability and never breaks: the bar under the icon shows charge (gold, the LV colour), not wear.

Its own EU buffer, outside the energy network. It charges in the Battery Box slot, from a worn Energy Pack and on the Charging Station, and spends charge only on hits against living targets. What Value Role powered melee weapon with an EU buffer: a consumer at a charger Buffer 10 000 EU Charging Battery Box slot / worn pack, ≤ 32 EU/tick (capped by the LV ceiling) → a full charge in ~16 s Drain 100 EU per hit on a living target Idle drain none Component (Long, persistent + network-synchronised) — shared by every powered item in the mod The drain happens server-side only, only after damage actually landed, and only for a player. Creative mode spends nothing.
Not applicable — the saber has no internal item storage (stacks to 1).
Not applicable (item).

Crafting — the line's usual frame with a diamond sword in the middle: a row of iron ingots on top, two batteries at the sides, two copper coils and an electronic circuit below. Charge held by the batteries carries over into the finished saber. The recipe unlocks once the player has a copper coil, an electronic circuit or a diamond sword (advancement ). Repair — not applicable: there is no durability to mend; "repair" here means recharging.

A powered hit. While the blade is on and the buffer holds at least 100 EU, the saber deals 12 damage, spends 100 EU per landed hit and leaves Slowness II on the target for two seconds along with a burst of electric sparks. Attack speed is 1.6 swings per second, a vanilla sword's rhythm. Reach. A live blade adds one block of attack reach (4 instead of 3). It is a real item attribute, so client and server agree on the distance and the line shows up in the tooltip next to the damage. The switch. Shift-right-click toggles the blade: a line appears above the hotbar, a metallic click plays, and the icon goes dark. A switched-off saber spends no EU, hits no harder, reaches no further and shocks nothing — but it keeps its charge. A plain right-click does nothing, so the saber never gets in the way of other interactions. A flat saber. Below 100 EU the damage drops to 4, the reach bonus and the discharge disappear and no EU is spent. There is no message: the bar, the tooltip and the darkened icon already say it. Sweep. The saber is in , so the vanilla sweep attack works. Without Sweeping Edge nearby mobs take 1 damage, like with any sword; with it the sweep is computed from the full 12 and hits considerably harder. Enchantments. That same tag brings the whole melee set: Sharpness, Smite, Bane of Arthropods, Looting, Fire Aspect, Knockback, Sweeping Edge. Unbreaking and Mending can be applied but do nothing on an unbreakable saber — exactly as on the Drill. Blocks. Like a vanilla sword: instant through cobwebs and fast through leaves, bamboo and the rest of . Breaking blocks costs no EU and does not depend on charge. Charging: the Battery Box slot, a worn Energy Pack and the Charging Station all take the saber automatically, up to 32 EU/tick. Readouts: the bar under the icon shows charge (gold, LV colour). The tooltip lists the cost per hit, the blade state and "Charge: X / 10 000 EU"; below the per-hit cost that line turns red. The texture switches to the dark variant when the saber is flat or switched off. Drop/death/relog: charge and switch position live in the item and persist. In creative: no charge is spent.

The mod's first EU weapon and the fifth item of the line; the combat branch is separate from the tool branch but shares the energy model and every charger. Available after the Battery Box and the battery: without LV infrastructure the saber can be neither crafted nor charged. The recipe also eats a diamond sword, so the saber replaces finished diamond gear rather than iron. LV tier. Ranged EU weaponry (the nano bow) is future work.

Electric Drill, Electric Chainsaw, Electric Shovel, Electric Hoe — the tool half of the same line: same energy, same chargers, same unbreakability. Electromagnet — the shift-right-click switch this one copies. Fluxweave armour — the other item whose attributes follow its charge. Battery Box — where the saber charges (charge slot). Tempered iron tools — the mod's previous combat step.

The Electric Shovel is the mod's third powered hand tool and the earth-side member of the line after the Electric Drill (stone) and the Electric Chainsaw (wood). It runs on EU instead of durability: with charge it digs faster than a diamond shovel (speed 9.0 against 8.0) and spends 20 EU per block. A full buffer is 10 000 EU — about 500 blocks on one charge. Mini-example: flatten a hillside, then right-click the grass you left to lay a dirt path — the shovel keeps every vanilla shovel interaction, and that part costs nothing. When it runs flat it doesn't stop; it just digs at hand speed until you recharge, with the same drops the whole time. One tool rule is enough: dirt, sand, gravel, clay, snow, soul sand and concrete powder all already sit under , so unlike the chainsaw this tool adds no tag of its own. Like the mod's other EU items, the shovel has no durability and never breaks: the bar under the icon shows EU charge (gold), not wear. It charges where the Energy Pack does — in the Battery Box charge slot and from a worn pack.

Its own EU buffer, outside the energy network. Charges in the Battery Box slot and from a worn pack; spends charge digging. What Value Buffer 10 000 EU Charging Battery Box slot / worn pack, fills in ~16 s Cost 20 EU per block broken Passive drain none Instant-break blocks — snow layers, grass — are free, just as they never wear a vanilla shovel. In creative no EU is spent.

Digging: with at least 20 EU it digs at speed 9.0. Each such block costs 20 EU. Flat shovel: below 20 EU it digs at hand speed (1.0) but keeps its mining level and drops, and spends nothing. Efficiency does not apply there — vanilla only grants it above speed 1.0. Dirt paths and campfire dousing work. Right-click grass, dirt, podzol, mycelium or rooted dirt to make a path; right-click a lit campfire to put it out — exactly like a vanilla shovel, and free of charge. Charging EU for it would contradict the rule this whole line is built on: a flat tool still works. Charging: the Battery Box charge slot and a worn Energy Pack both accept it automatically, up to 32 EU/t. Attack: hits like a diamond shovel (2.5 damage, 1.0 attack speed); attacking spends no EU and causes no wear. Enchanting: it sits in , so the table and anvil treat it as a shovel. Readout: the bar shows charge; the tooltip reads the exact numbers, or a red "Empty" at zero, and the texture switches to its unpowered variant.
Not applicable — the shovel has no internal item storage (stack size 1).
Not applicable (item).

The drill's frame with a diamond shovel in the middle: iron ingots on top, two batteries at the sides, two copper coils and an electronic circuit below. Charge held by the batteries carries over into the finished shovel. The recipe unlocks once you obtain a copper coil, an electronic circuit or a diamond shovel. Repair is not applicable — there is no durability; "repair" means recharging.

The third powered tool: the drill covers stone, the chainsaw covers wood, the shovel covers earth — the LV line now spans all three basic materials. Needs LV infrastructure first — without the Battery Box and a battery it can be neither crafted nor charged. LV tier. The remaining electric tools (hoe/saber/nano bow) are future work.
Electric Drill — the stone part of the line. Electric Chainsaw — the wood part of the line. Electric Hoe — the farmland part of the line. Battery Box — charges the shovel (charge slot).

The Electromagnet is an EU-rechargeable convenience item: it sits in any inventory slot (hotbar / main / off-hand) and automatically draws loose dropped items toward the player — ore drops in a mine, scattered pieces after an explosion, unclaimed drops. This is tier 1: a spherical radius of 5 blocks (up, down and sideways); each item actually pulled costs 2 EU . An idle scan, with nothing in range, is free. Pickup stays vanilla: every tick the magnet sets each item's velocity straight at the player (a seek, so items fly in from any direction — a drop below rises to you), and the player collects the item once it arrives. When flat the magnet simply goes quiet (like a drained Electric Drill mining at hand speed) until recharged. It charges wherever the mod's whole powered family does — the Battery Box charge slot and a worn Energy Pack. Toggle (shift-right-click): the magnet can be switched off so you can carry it in your inventory next to farms, sorters and pipes without hoovering their items. A freshly crafted magnet is on.

Its own EU buffer, off the grid. Charged in the Battery Box slot and by a worn pack; spends charge per pulled item. Field Value Role convenience item with an EU buffer: a consumer at a charger Buffer 5,000 EU Charging Battery Box slot / worn pack, ≤ 32 EU/tick (capped by the LV ceiling) Draw 2 EU per item pulled each scan tick; an idle scan is free Passive drain none (only for actual pulling) Component (Long, persistent + networkSynchronized) — the shared component of every powered item in the mod The draw is taken server-side only (in 26.2 is called only on a ). A creative/spectating owner pays nothing (the rule shared by every EU item) — the magnet still pulls.
Not applicable — the magnet has no internal item storage (stacks to 1). It holds only EU charge and the on/off flag (absent = on).
Not applicable (item).

Crafted on a workbench in the shape of a horseshoe magnet: an iron horseshoe body, a copper coil core at the centre (the electromagnet's winding), and an electronic circuit below (control). The top corners are the poles: redstone (power) on the left, lapis lazuli (magnetic "charge") on the right. Recipe — shaped 3×3, : top row: redstone (), empty, lapis lazuli (); middle row: iron () — copper coil — iron; bottom row: iron — electronic circuit — iron. Repair — not applicable: the magnet has no durability; "repair" is charging EU (see Energy).

Pulling (seek): every tick (= 1) the magnet gathers in a spherical radius and sets each item's velocity straight at the player's body centre at blocks/tick. Setting (not adding) the velocity overrides gravity and friction, so a drop below the player rises to it and one above sinks — the pickup itself is vanilla once the item arrives. Tariff: each item pulled costs 2 EU per tick while it flies in. If the buffer can't afford it the magnet stalls; at 0 EU it doesn't pull at all. At most 64 items are handled per pass (a guard against mass-drop lag). What it will NOT pull: items on their pickup delay () — both a fresh player -drop (so it doesn't instantly suck back what was just thrown) and "never pick up" items (delay 32767); items sitting in lava (so they aren't dragged through the fire); items out of range. Item frames / displays are untouched (the filter is strictly the class). Seek speed is capped at (0.55 blocks/tick): fast enough for items to visibly fly in, but under the vanilla pickup window so they don't tunnel through the player. Works from any slot: the magnet ticks in the hotbar, main inventory and off-hand (in 26.2 the off-hand ticks through the equipment path) — carry it anywhere, not only in hand. Toggle (shift-right-click): a shift-right-click flips on/off. State lives in the component (absent = on; disabling writes, re-enabling removes the component, so an on magnet is byte-identical to a fresh one). Toggling plays a metallic click ( on/off — an electrical sound, not a cloth one) and posts an action-bar line. A disabled magnet pulls nothing and spends no EU. Readout: the bar under the icon shows charge (yellow, LV colour). The tooltip shows short lines: a flavour line, status (green "Active" / grey "Disabled"), the charge , and a radius/tariff line. Drop/death/relog: charge and the on/off flag are stored on the item and survive. In creative: no charge is spent (the shared powered-family rule,, but pulling works.

An LV-tier convenience item: it solves the classic tech-mod pain "walking a mine — loot comes to me". Available after the Battery Box and copper coil / circuit: without LV infrastructure the magnet can be neither crafted nor charged. Filters (tag whitelist/blacklist), suppressor zones and radius tier scaling (LV/MV/HV) are future work.

Electric Drill — the EU-consumable precedent; a typical mine companion. Energy Pack — charges the magnet in the inventory on the move. Battery Box — charging the magnet (charge slot). Copper Coil, Electronic Circuit — crafting components.

The Energy Pack is a wearable energy buffer: it goes in the chest slot and, while you wear it, tops up every powered item in your inventory once a second. Today that means the Battery Pouch — with the pack on your back the pouch no longer runs flat and locks itself mid-expedition. The pack holds 20 000 EU — ten times the pouch, and as much as a Battery Box. It charges in the Battery Box charge slot, and unlike the pouch it has no passive drain of its own: EU only leave it to charge something. It is a device, not armor: no durability (it never breaks and never wears), it cannot be enchanted, and it gives a token 2 armor points — less than a leather chestplate. A chest slot filled by the pack is a chest slot not filled by armor: that is the trade. Mini-example: put a charged pack on, keep a half-empty pouch in your hotbar, and go caving for the afternoon. The pack quietly tops the pouch up every second, so the pouch's lock never snaps shut — no more running back to base just to unlock your storage.

Its own buffer, separate from the energy network. You charge it at a Battery Box; it hands energy to the items in your inventory — but only while it is worn. Field Value Charge held 20 000 EU (ten pouches; the same as a Battery Box) Charging Battery Box charge slot — full in about 31 seconds Output to items up to 640 EU per second, shared across your inventory Passive drain none — it only spends charge to feed something Order it feeds hotbar → rest of the inventory → offhand → cursor → 2×2 crafting grid Armor 2 points (less than leather)

Wearing it: the chest slot. The pack works only while worn — in a bag, a chest, or your hand it charges nothing. Charging your items: once a second the pack hands out up to 640 EU to anything in your inventory with a charge. It walks the slots in order — hotbar, then main inventory, then offhand, then the stack on your cursor and the 2×2 crafting grid — and each item takes what it has room for; the rest of the budget moves on to the next. The cursor and the crafting grid: a pouch you are holding on the cursor, or one you dropped into the 2×2 crafting grid, is charged like any other — it is still on you, and charging should not stall while you are moving things around. What it does not charge: other Energy Packs (two packs would just pass energy back and forth for nothing), items sitting inside containers — a pouch, a vanilla bundle, a shulker box — and the contents of an open chest or machine: those belong to the world, not to you. In creative: charge is never spent — not by the pack, the pouch, or the drill. Exactly as vanilla tools take no durability damage in creative. The pack still charges your items, so a charged pack lasts forever in creative; a completely empty one still has nothing to hand out. Idle: with nothing to charge — a full pouch, an empty pack, ordinary items — the pack spends nothing and its charge does not move at all. Charging the pack: in the Battery Box charge slot. The same slot takes the pouch too — it accepts any item with a charge. The charge bar: the bar under the icon shows the charge (yellow). The tooltip reads "Charge: X / 20 000 EU", or a red "Empty" at zero. On-screen readout (HUD): while the pack is worn, its icon, charge percentage and a bar (green → gold → red as it drains) sit in the top-left corner. On by default, toggled with the H key (rebindable under Controls → Ala Industrial) or in the mod's settings. Nothing shows when no pack is worn. Drained look: at zero charge both the icon and the model on your back switch to a dead look — a red indicator light instead of the green one, and pale cells. Durability and enchantments: none — the pack never breaks, never takes damage, and the anvil and enchanting table both ignore it. On drop, death, or relog: the charge lives on the item and survives.
Not applicable (item).

Crafted at a workbench from three batteries — a rechargeable cell made of tin, redstone and copper cable that holds 2,000 EU and stacks by charge level — in a leather body, with an electronic circuit on top and a tin buckle below. The battery is a carrier rather than a single-use part: the charge held by the three batteries carries over into the finished pack (the recipe is the type,, so three full batteries hand the pack 6,000 EU and it comes off the table already charged.

The next step after the Battery Pouch: the pouch carries your things, the pack keeps the pouch fed. Available after the Battery Box — without one there is no way to charge the pack. LV tier. Bigger versions (more buffer, faster output) and electric tools that draw on the pack are planned for later.
Battery Pouch — the first thing the pack feeds. Battery Box — charges the pack (charge slot). Electronic Circuit — a crafting component. Tin — the battery casing and the pack's buckle.

Fluxweave armour is the mod's first full EU set and the end of the fibre → flux thread → Fluxweave cloth chain. It is a utility suit rather than a tank: protection sits at the iron line, and what the player is really buying is the kit that switches on while the pieces hold charge. The rule that matters: charge switches bonuses on, it never switches protection off. At zero EU the set still works as ordinary armour of its material — it does not break, vanish, or lose a single point of defense.

Field Value Buffer (EU) 15,000 per piece Max input (EU/tick) 32 (LV ceiling) Passive upkeep 1 EU/second per worn, charged piece Event cost 200 EU per half-heart of set-bonus regeneration Charges in the Battery Box slot, from a worn Energy Pack, and from other mods' chargers through the item energy capability (insert only). A full buffer at 1 EU/s lasts roughly four hours of wear.

Every bonus is an attribute, not a potion effect: no particles, no HUD icons, no clash with real potions. They apply only while the piece holds charge. Slot Defense Bonus while charged Config Helmet 2 Water breathing (a chance to skip an air tick, Respiration's own mechanic) plus swim speed 3, 50 Chestplate 6 Extra toughness against heavy hits plus knockback resistance 2, 10 Leggings 5 Run speed (passive) plus a toggleable step assist 12, 60 Boots 2 Partial fall-damage softening 50 Set 4/4 — Slow regeneration below full health 200 The step assist starts switched off. A key binding turns it on (default G, under the Ala Industrial category). The flag lives on the leggings themselves, so it survives a relog and travels with the item. Auto-stepping changes how movement feels and does not suit everyone, so it waits to be asked for. The boots do not cancel fall damage, they halve it. Cancelling it outright would trivialise a core survival rule, so the percentage is clamped to 90 in code — no config value can make falling free. The set bonus requires all four pieces to be charged. Three live pieces and one flat one do not heal.

Field Value Durability never spent (wear is paid in EU) Enchanting yes, like ordinary armour (enchanting table, anvil) Repair tag → Fluxweave cloth Toughness 1.0 base, +2 on a charged chestplate Inventory bar EU charge, in the LV colour Durability formally exists — the vanilla armour helper wires it — but is never consumed: the equippable component is built with damage-on-hurt switched off. The set therefore cannot break, and the bar in the inventory shows EU rather than wear.

Not armour worn over clothes but a single suit: the sleeves run to the wrist and the helmet closes over the head and stops at the mouth line, leaving only the mouth, chin and hands bare. The weave is light and silvery, with dark panel seams at the shoulders, belt, elbows and knees. A charged suit runs at full brightness and reads at distance; a flat one darkens all over while keeping the same pattern. State is carried by brightness because this set has no gold accent.

Each piece takes four different components: Fluxweave cloth, an electronic circuit, a battery and a tempered-iron frame. No recipe collapses to one material in a silhouette. The charge held by the battery carries over into the finished piece (all four recipes are the type,: a full 2,000 EU battery comes off the table already charged, so the bonuses are available straight away with no separate charging step.

Tier: LV Requires: the Galvanic Bath, then flux thread and Fluxweave cloth, plus a circuit, a battery and tempered iron. Next: the nano set (tier 2), where night vision and hunger slowdown were deliberately deferred.
Galvanic Bath — produces flux thread Tempered-iron armour — the ordinary set without EU Energy Pack — the reference worn EU item

The Forge Hammer is an early-game hand tool for making metal plates before machine automation exists. Put the hammer and an ingot on the crafting grid and you get a plate of that metal. The hammer is not consumed as an ingredient — it stays in the crafting grid and loses 1 durability per plate. This is the deliberately "expensive by hand" path: you can hammer a plate from your very first iron, but you pay for each one in wear until you build a Compressor and start pressing them on electricity. Mini-example: you need 4 iron plates for your first machine hull and have no compressor yet. Craft a hammer from iron and sticks, put hammer + iron ingot on the grid — out drops a plate and the hammer returns to the grid a little more worn. Repeat four times (or shift-craft a whole stack at once) and the hull is built without a single machine.

Field Value Durability 128 (about 128 plates per hammer) Stack 1 Enchantable no Repair with an iron ingot (anvil) Durability 128 means roughly 128 plates from one hammer. The number lives in code (like the mod's other tools — a tool material is built before the config is read) and is mirrored in

Crafting a plate: on the crafting grid hammer + ingot → 1 plate. Works for all eight metals: copper, gold, iron, tin, silver, nickel, uranium, tempered iron. The hammer stays: after the craft the damaged hammer drops back into the same grid slot. Implemented as a craft-remainder, not a special recipe, so the recipes show in the recipe book, JEI and REI like ordinary crafts. Wear of 1/plate: exactly 1 durability per plate. Shift-crafting a stack of ingots spends exactly N durability for N plates and stops on its own when the hammer breaks. Breaking: on its last durability point the hammer breaks — the last plate is still made, and the grid slot is left empty. Enchanting: the hammer cannot be enchanted. Unbreaking could not technically work through the craft-remainder mechanic (there is no level or player in it to process a durability change), so rather than a silently useless enchant the hammer is honestly non-enchantable. Repair: with an iron ingot on an anvil.
Not applicable (item).

Crafted on the workbench (, Equipment category) from iron and a stick — a head on a handle, deliberately different from vanilla tools so it does not clash with the pickaxe recipe: is an iron ingot, is a stick. The recipe appears in the recipe book when you pick up iron or a stick.

An early-game hand tool — not tied to the mod's energy tiers. Gives access to plates before electricity: hammer them by hand first, then automate with the Compressor (ingot → plate for 260 EU). Part of Phase 3 (LV Expansion) — plates are needed in LV machine and electronics recipes.

Material forms — the plates and other intermediates this hammer makes. Compressor — the machine, mass-production path for plates. Macerator — recycles a plate back into dust (except tempered iron — it has no dust).

The Jetpack is a worn EU flight device: it occupies the chest slot (instead of armor) and carries a 30,000 EU buffer. Hold jump in the air and the engine thrusts you upward, burning 50 EU/tick: a full charge is ~30 seconds of continuous flight. Release jump — a normal fall. Out of charge mid-flight (or above the altitude ceiling) the same held jump turns into a free powerless glide: the sink rate is damped and the landing deals no damage. The glide is THIS flight's safety net: it engages only if the engine actually fired during the current flight — a jetpack that started empty falls like plain clothing, no "levitation". The buffer always burns to a clean zero: the last thrust tick takes whatever remainder is left below the per-tick cost. The safety is the engine, not the garment: letting go of jump mid-air and dropping still hurts. This is tier 1 (LV): a modest climb rate, one thrust mode, no hovering. It charges wherever the mod's whole powered family does — the Battery Box charge slot — and from an Energy Pack, though only while the jetpack sits in the inventory: the worn pack occupies the same chest slot, so the two are never worn together. Like the Energy Pack the jetpack is not vanilla armor: no durability, no enchantments, no repair; it grants 5 armor points (one under an iron chestplate's 6) through an attribute modifier — the price of the occupied slot, and protection in flight.

Its own EU buffer, off the grid. Charged in the Battery Box slot, by an Energy Pack (while carried) and by other mods' chargers; spends charge only on ticks of actual thrust. Field Value Role worn consumable with an EU buffer: a consumer at a charger Buffer 30,000 EU Charging Battery Box slot / Energy Pack / foreign chargers, ≤ 32 EU/tick (the LV ceiling) Draw 50 EU per tick of thrust; gliding and idling are free Passive drain none Component (Long, persistent + networkSynchronized) — the shared component of every powered item in the mod The draw is taken server-side only (in 26.2 is called only on a ); the server sees the held jump through the vanilla input sync, so the jetpack ships no custom packet. A creative/spectating owner pays nothing (the rule shared by every EU item, the flight and the safety still work.
Not applicable — an item (stacks to 1) holding only its EU charge.
Not applicable (item).

Crafted on a workbench (a full 3×3 grid — the priciest powered item in the mod): an iron shell, an Energy Pack at the centre (the tank and the heart of the jetpack), two batteries at its sides (the engine starters), an Electronic Circuit on top (the thrust controller), and two tin nozzles around a Copper Coil (the turbine) at the bottom. Craft — shaped 3×3, : top row: iron () — Electronic Circuit — iron; middle row: battery — Energy Pack — battery; bottom row: tin — Copper Coil — tin. Charge carries over (the recipe is the type, the EU held by the two batteries and the Energy Pack at the centre moves into the finished jetpack instead of burning away. A full Energy Pack (20,000 EU) plus two full batteries (2,000 EU each) hand the jetpack up to 24,000 EU, so it can come off the table already charged. Repair — not applicable: the jetpack has no durability; "repair" is recharging EU (see "Energy").

Thrust: the engine runs while the player is airborne and holds jump — on the ground a held jump stays a vanilla jump, the thrust picks up on the next tick. Each thrust tick: the client (player motion is client-authoritative in 26.2) adds a vertical acceleration of +0.15 b/tick² saturating at a 0.5 b/tick climb; the server, gating on the same three conditions, burns 50 EU, zeroes the fall distance and draws the exhaust (smoke + sparks) with a soft hiss every 8 ticks. Drains to zero: the engine thrusts while even 1 EU remains; the last tick takes the sub-cost remainder (the spend clamps) — there is never a dead 15–20 EU tail showing an unusable 1%. Glide (this flight's safety net): at 0 EU (or above) there is no thrust, but if the engine already fired during the current flight, the held jump caps the sink rate at 0.3 b/tick (~6 m/s) and keeps zeroing the fall distance — the landing is soft, free and silent (the client resets its own fall distance too, so no hard-landing thud plays). A jetpack that never fired this flight does not glide at all — the fall is exactly as without it. The flight session resets on touching the ground. Releasing jump is a normal, damaging fall: the distance accumulates from the point of release. "Flight never kills by accident" = keep holding jump all the way down. Altitude ceiling: above (default 320 — the overworld build limit) the engine refuses to thrust — glide only. A knob for server owners. Flight glow: while the engine thrusts, a torch-like light follows the flyer (= 10, a bit under a torch; 0 disables it) — visible at night and in caves. It is a moving block (26.2 has no per-entity lighting): placed at the player's cell each thrust tick and removed the moment the flight ends. Cleanup is leak-free — a once-per-server-tick sweep clears any light block not refreshed that tick, so no orphan light is left behind even on logout, death or unequip mid-flight. The light is only ever placed into air or water (waterlogged), never over a real block. Creative/spectator: no EU is spent (the powered family's shared rule); vanilla creative flight has priority — with ability-flight on, the jetpack stays out of the way. Indication: the charge bar under the icon (gold, the LV colour); the tooltip carries the charge and the two control lines; the chest-slot charge HUD panel in the top-left corner (shared with the Energy Pack, key H). A worn charged jetpack shows the lit model on the back, a drained one the dead model (the same way the energy pack does it). Drop/death/relog: the charge lives in the item and persists.

The mod's first vertical-mobility item: available after the Battery Box and the Energy Pack — without LV infrastructure it can be neither crafted nor charged. Pricier than the rest of the powered family (the craft consumes a whole Energy Pack): flight is a serious convenience step. Future tiers (MV/HV: faster climb, a hover mode, a bigger buffer) are separate tasks.

Energy Pack — a crafting component and the jetpack's in-inventory charger; the chest-slot neighbour. Battery Box — charging the jetpack (the charge slot). Electric Drill — the price anchor: 50 EU = one mined block = one tick of flight. Electronic Circuit — a crafting component.

The Scythe is a hand tool for quickly clearing decorative foliage and harvesting ripe crops. A right-click on a block mows down every eligible plant — leaves, grass, flowers, ferns, mushrooms, vines, roots, saplings — across a flat area in front of you, dropping normal loot exactly as if you had broken each block by hand. Holding Shift while right-clicking switches it to harvest mode: the same AOE instead cuts only mature crops (wheat, carrots, potatoes, beetroot, the torchflower crop, sweet berries, pitcher crop, cactus and sugar cane), leaving decor and unripe crops untouched. It comes in eight material tiers (wood → stone → copper → iron → gold → tempered iron → diamond → netherite); the better the tier, the wider the swath and the more blocks one swing can take. It is a building and decorating quality-of-life tool — it does not replace the axe, the hoe, or an auto-farm. Mini-example: built a base in a forest and tired of clearing leaves one by one? A diamond scythe clears a 5×5 patch in a single right-click, dropping all the saplings and sticks you'd get by hand — handy for tidying a build site without a flint-and-steel bonfire.

The mowed area is a flat box in front of you: depth runs forward in your look direction, width is the perpendicular axis (always odd, with a centre line over the block you clicked), and height is always 3 (the clicked layer plus one above and below). The block you click is the centre. Tier Area (width × depth) Max blocks per swing Durability Bonus seed chance Wood 3 × 2 12 59 — Stone 3 × 3 18 131 5 % Copper 3 × 3 24 190 8 % Iron 5 × 3 30 250 12 % Gold 5 × 3 30 32 20 % Tempered iron 5 × 4 40 350 18 % Diamond 5 × 5 50 1 561 25 % Netherite 7 × 5 70 2 031 35 % Gold is a deliberate side-grade: an iron-sized area, but fragile (32 durability) and very enchantable — the vanilla gold philosophy, where it shines with Unbreaking and Mending. That is also why it carries the most generous seed bonus short of diamond and netherite: a lucky but short-lived scythe, where the 32 durability is its own limit on how much you can reap with it. Copper is a modest step between stone and iron. Tempered iron sits between iron and diamond. Netherite is fire-resistant, like all netherite gear. The wooden scythe grants no seed bonus at all — the yield boost starts one tier up.

Trigger: a right-click, from the main hand only. Sneaking or using the off-hand does nothing special — your normal interaction still works. What gets mowed: the decorative plants listed below. Each block drops what it would if you broke it by hand — so Fortune and Silk Touch both work (the break is treated as tool-aware). Bonus seeds (harvest mode): on top of the usual drop, the scythe has a per-tier chance to yield one extra seed from the crop it just cut (see the table above). It applies only while harvesting with Shift held, and only to true crops — wheat, carrots, potatoes, beetroot and the torchflower crop. Sweet berries, cactus, sugar cane and the pitcher crop have no seed of their own, so they never grant it. The bonus is independent of Fortune and stacks with it: Fortune boosts the main drop, the bonus lands on top. Durability: soft blocks with no hardness — short grass, ferns, flowers — break for free and cost no durability; harder ones like leaves cost 1 each. You can mow plain grass forever; leaves eat into the durability bar. Per-swing cap: never more than the tier's "max blocks per swing" above. Candidates are mowed nearest-first, so what you click always breaks first. If the tool runs out of durability mid-swing, the pass stops where it is. Enchantments: being a hoe-type tool, it takes Efficiency, Unbreaking, Fortune, Silk Touch and Mending at the enchanting table and anvil. Fortune boosts the drop; Efficiency does not make the instant area any faster. Sound and flourish: one cut sound per successful swing (not per block), and a sweep particle flourish spreads across the cleared area.

c.h: What it mows (and what it does not)
c.t: It clears decorative foliage — that is its whole job: Leaves and flowers — including small flowers and the new bushes and dry grasses. Saplings and cave vines. Grass and ferns — short and tall grass, ferns and large ferns, dead bush, leaf litter. Mushrooms, moss carpets, vines, glow lichen, hanging roots and the nether root plants. In this plain (decor) mode it deliberately does not touch crops — that is what Shift + right-click (harvest mode, above) is for — nor pumpkin and melon stems, bamboo, kelp, logs, dirt, or the moss block. Cactus and sugar cane are also left alone in decor mode; harvest mode only takes the block(s) above their base, keeping the base alive to regrow. Melon and pumpkin stems are never harvested in either mode — they are not the crop itself, just a growing vine that fruits on a neighbouring block.

Holding shift switches the scythe into harvest mode. In that mode it takes mature crops and Anything in at the maximum value of its own property — wheat, carrots, potatoes, beetroot, torchflower crop, pitcher crop and so on. Unripe seedlings are left to grow. Sweet berry bushes — only ripe ones (age 2 or above, the stages that actually bear berries). Cactus and sugar cane — only the blocks above the base one standing on the ground. The base keeps growing, exactly as when you cut the top by hand. Harvest mode deliberately does not take: Melon and pumpkin stems — a stem is not a crop but a growing vine that produces its fruit on the neighbouring block, so it is left alone. Unripe crops and berry bushes — they are given time to finish growing. Decorative vegetation, dirt, logs, water and everything else. That is decor mode's job (plain right-click), and the two modes never overlap. Durability is spent per block actually cut, the same as in decor mode, and the per-swing block limit of the tier still applies.
Not applicable (item).

All eight tiers are crafted at a workbench with the same custom shape — three tier-material pieces plus two sticks, a shape deliberately different from the vanilla hoe since the scythe is stronger and is the tier material (planks, cobblestone, copper ingot, iron ingot, gold ingot, tempered iron, diamond, or netherite ingot) and is a stick. Each tier's recipe shows up in your recipe book once you've picked up its material. Repair a scythe with its matching tier material at an anvil, as you would a hoe.

A hand tool — not tied to the mod's energy tiers. Eight material steps parallel the vanilla hoes; in creative each scythe sits right after its tier's hoe in the Tools tab. Area and per-swing cap grow with the tier; gold is the fragile enchantable side-grade, tempered iron the step between iron and diamond.

Tempered Iron tools — the mod's custom tool family and the tempered iron material one scythe tier is made of. Tempered Iron Pickaxe — another tempered iron tool. Vanilla hoes — the material baseline the scythe tiers are built on.

The shielding suit is four pieces — hood, jacket, trousers and boots — and the only wearable protection against radiation. It is not armour: protection sits at the leather line, and what you buy is not numbers but the ability to walk up to uranium, or into a running reactor, and walk back. The recipe is deliberately early and cheap: leather, rubber, yellow dye and a glass pane for the visor. The reason is blunt — the first version was built from shielding alloy, so the protection arrived later than the reactor that emits the radiation. Protection you can only get after the source protects you from nothing. Mini-example: you find uranium, put it in your bag, and start feeling sick. You craft the suit out of leather and rubber, put it on, and the nausea stops. You step inside a live reactor core — the suit buys you a couple of minutes of work rather than immunity, and spends durability on every dose it absorbs.
Not applicable: the suit neither charges nor draws EU.

Worn in the ordinary armour slots. Every piece cuts its own share of the dose (25 % by default), so a partial set protects partially — and you can see it on the player: wherever a piece is missing, skin shows. Radiation weakens with distance, so the suit and a step back work together: right at a column about 5 % of the dose gets through a full set — roughly a minute and a half to a lethal level; one block out that triples, and three or four blocks out the dose barely climbs. The full set stops all ordinary background: uranium in the pockets, uranium on the ground, a reactor with no shell. At an open core a separate ceiling applies ( 95 %) — there the suit buys time, not invulnerability. Durability is spent on any contact with uranium, paced by how fierce the source is: a point a second at a live core, one every two seconds with a refined-uranium item in your pocket, one every eight with ore. The life of the suit is therefore a TIME: about three minutes in a core, about five with refined uranium carried, over twenty with ore. A broken piece stops shielding. Repaired with rubber (tag) at an anvil.

Field Value Protection (hood/jacket/trousers/boots) 1 / 3 / 2 / 1 — the leather line Toughness 0.0 Durability factor 15 (leather 5, iron 15) Enchantability 10 Repair tag → rubber Shielding 25 % of the dose per piece, capped at 95 % at an open core The stats are low on purpose. A cheap suit with iron-grade protection would be strictly better than iron armour, and players would wear it for the numbers rather than for the job. Here the numbers are honestly bad and the value is the shielding.

A rubberised yellow coverall with dark straps, a steel visor and respirator, gloves and rubber boots. In the full set no pixel of the player's skin shows — no face, hands, legs, or even the skin's own second layer: the suit is sealed, and its textures carry no transparent pixel anywhere the model shows geometry. The one exception is your own hand in first person: in Minecraft 26.2 the armour layer is not composited there for any set at all. That is vanilla behaviour, not an omission. In third person and to other players the suit is sealed completely.

Every piece is leather as the base, the mod's rubber as the shielding layer and one yellow dye; the hood additionally takes a glass pane for the visor. — 3 leather, 1 dye, 2 rubber, 1 pane — 3 leather, 1 dye, 4 rubber — 3 leather, 1 dye, 4 rubber — 2 leather, 1 dye, 2 rubber

Tier: none, early game. Requires: leather (mobs), rubber (vulcanizer), yellow dye (dandelion), a glass pane. Next: handling uranium and entering the reactor room; storing uranium in a shielding chest so the suit does not have to be worn around the clock.

Uranium ore — the first source it protects you from Reactor controller — the room it lets you step into Fuel rod assembly — the strongest source in the mod Fluxweave armour — the other utility set, powered by EU

The Soul Vessel is a glass flask in a silver frame with soul sand at the bottom. While it sits in your inventory, every hostile mob killed by you personally — your hand, your sword, your arrow — yields its soul into it. Pet kills, trap kills and other players' kills do not count. A full vessel goes into a Mob Repeller and is consumed whole, Jump Souls needed Small → medium 80 Medium → large 250 The counter shows in the item tooltip. The vessel holds at most 250 souls; any surplus above the jump threshold burns with the vessel — charge it for the specific tier you need.

Only actively hostile mobs count: monsters, plus angered endermen and zombified piglins. Passive and calm neutral mobs yield no souls. The killing blow must come from the player: a tamed wolf, a lava trap or someone else's arrow will not register the soul. With several vessels in the inventory, the first non-full one in slot order fills up. Vessels with different soul counts do not stack — each keeps its own memory.
Crafting table 3×3: 4 silver plates in the corners, 3 glass, soul sand in the centre, an electronic circuit at the bottom.

The Teleporter Remote is a handheld beacon-item: it binds to a Teleporter station via shift-right-click and then triggers a jump that takes the player to the station. The remote itself holds no EU — the energy of the jump is paid by the charged target station. One remote remembers up to 16 stations — binding the same one twice changes nothing, there are no duplicates. The "station + remote" pair is the entire teleport mechanic: a stationary anchor stores EU, the wearable remote picks the target and pays for the jump out of the station's reserve. Mini-example: bind the remote to a station at base → go mining → right-click with the remote → teleport home. EU for the jump comes out of the base, not your inventory.
Stores none. The EU cost of a jump is paid by the target station out of its own buffer, not by the remote.
Shift-right-click on a placed Teleporter station binds the remote to that station. Right-click in the world with a bound remote triggers the jump to the station (if it has enough EU).
Not applicable (item). Stack: 1.

Crafted at a workbench (shaped 3×3): an Ender Pearl in the centre of the top row, Tempered Iron in a cross, and an Electronic Circuit in the centre. — Ender Pearl (×1); — tempered iron (×3); — electronic circuit (×1).

An item-category tool, tier LV (the recipe is available before the HV station — but without a station it's useless). Tied to the HV era: teleportation only opens up after you've built and charged a station.
Teleporter (station) — the anchor the remote binds to. Electronic Circuit — a crafting component. Tempered Iron — the body material.

Tempered-iron armor is a full four-piece set — helmet, chestplate, leggings and boots. Each piece is tougher than its iron counterpart and is repaired with tempered iron (via the tag). Protection sits a bit above iron and below diamond — a middle ground between the early and late game. Mini-example: a full set of tempered-iron armor gives noticeably more protection than an iron set, while being crafted from smelted iron (cheaper than diamond gear). A solid intermediate layer before stepping up to diamond/netherite.
Not applicable (non-powered armor).
Equipped into the matching armor slots (helmet, chestplate, leggings, boots). Repaired at an anvil with tempered iron.
Not applicable (items). Stack: 1 each.
All four pieces are crafted at a workbench (shaped 3×3) from tempered iron on standard vanilla armor patterns: Helmet — Chestplate — Leggings — Boots — — tempered iron ingot.

Item-category armor, no tier of its own. Fills the gap between iron and diamond armor: tougher than iron, available earlier than diamond (via tempering iron in an electric furnace / furnace), repairable.
Tempered Iron — the armor and repair material. Tempered-iron tools — the sibling tool set. Electric Furnace — where tempered iron is smelted for crafting.

The Tempered Iron Pickaxe is the mod's first hand tool. It is crafted like a normal pickaxe — three ingots on top, two sticks below — but uses the mod's tempered iron instead of plain iron. On every stat it is a touch better than the vanilla iron pickaxe: 100 more durability, slightly faster mining, slightly more damage, and a little better at catching enchantments. It cannot mine diamond-level blocks (diamond ore, obsidian, ancient debris), though — same as iron — so the diamond progression is not devalued. It is the natural upgrade slot between an iron pickaxe and your first diamond one. Mini-example: you have iron but no diamonds yet. Smelt that iron into tempered iron, craft this pickaxe, and you have 350 durability of mining at speed 7.0 — enough to last you comfortably until you finally strike diamonds.

The baseline is the vanilla iron pickaxe. Every difference fits in one table: Stat Iron (vanilla) Tempered iron Durability 250 350 (+100) Mining speed 6.0 7.0 Attack damage 4.0 4.5 Enchantability 14 16 Attack speed same as iron same as iron Mining level iron iron (diamond/obsidian/ancient debris — no) Repair at anvil iron ingot tempered iron It drops nothing from diamond ore, diamond deepslate, obsidian and ancient debris — exactly like iron. That is the single limit that keeps it short of diamond.

Mining: mines everything a pickaxe should, at speed 7.0 — a bit faster than iron. Diamond-level blocks drop nothing and mine more slowly, exactly like an iron pickaxe. Combat: 4.5 damage, same attack speed as iron. The slightly higher damage is its only combat edge. Durability: 350 (100 more than iron), spent on mining and hits like any tool. It needs no EU — just ordinary wear. Enchanting: enchantability 16 (vs iron's 14), so it catches enchantments a little better. The enchanting table offers the full vanilla pickaxe set — Efficiency, Unbreaking, Fortune, Silk Touch, Mending. Repair: in the anvil with tempered iron, at the vanilla XP cost.
Not applicable (item).

Crafted at a workbench in the vanilla pickaxe pattern — three tempered iron ingots on top and two sticks down the centre. Repair it at an anvil with tempered iron, the way an iron ingot repairs a vanilla iron pickaxe.

A hand tool — not tied to the mod's energy tiers. It slots between the vanilla iron pickaxe and the diamond one: by durability and speed it is closer to iron, and it does not overlap diamond on block access. It appears as soon as you start smelting iron into tempered iron in bulk — a natural upgrade to carry you until your first diamond pickaxe.
Tempered Iron — the crafting and repair material. Tempered Iron tools — the rest of the tempered iron tool family. The vanilla iron pickaxe — the balance baseline.

The Tempered Iron tools are the mod's set of five hand tools: the pickaxe, the axe, the hoe, the shovel and the sword. Each is crafted like its vanilla counterpart but uses the mod's tempered iron instead of iron. Across the board they are a touch better than vanilla iron: 100 more durability, slightly faster mining, +0.5 damage, and a little better at catching enchantments. The pickaxe, axe, shovel and hoe cannot mine diamond-level blocks (diamond ore, obsidian, ancient debris) — same as iron — so the diamond progression is not devalued. They are the natural upgrade slot between iron and diamond. Mini-example: your iron pickaxe is about to break and you have no diamonds. Recraft the whole kit in tempered iron — pickaxe, axe, shovel, hoe and sword — and you have a full set that lasts longer, hits a touch harder, and enchants a little better, all before you ever see a diamond.

All five share one tempered-iron material, so the common numbers — durability, mining speed, enchantability — are shared. Damage and attack speed are per tool, as in vanilla. Stat Iron (vanilla) Tempered iron Durability 250 350 (+100) Mining speed 6.0 7.0 Enchantability 14 16 Mining level iron iron (diamond/obsidian/ancient debris — no) Damage per tool (iron vs tempered; attack speed matches iron): Tool Damage (iron → tempered) Pickaxe 4.0 → 4.5 Axe 9.0 → 9.5 Hoe 1.0 → 1.5 Shovel 4.5 → 5.0 Sword 6.0 → 6.5 The sword, like the vanilla one, mines cobweb instantly.

Harvesting (pickaxe/axe/shovel/hoe): mine their materials — stone, wood, dirt, farmland — at speed 7.0, slightly faster than iron. Diamond-level blocks drop nothing, exactly like iron tools. Axe: strips bark, lights wood on a right-click, and breaks wooden blocks faster — the full vanilla axe behaviour. Hoe: tills soil and harvests crops, like the vanilla hoe. Shovel: makes a dirt path and extinguishes campfires, like the vanilla shovel. Sword: 6.5 damage (vs iron's 6.0), mines cobweb instantly, knocks back enemies. Combat: every tool hits for +0.5 over its iron counterpart (see the table above); attack speed is unchanged. They need no EU — just ordinary wear. Durability: 350 each (100 more than iron), spent on mining and hits. Enchanting: enchantability 16 (vs iron's 14), so each tool catches enchantments a little better. The enchanting table offers the full vanilla set for each type — Efficiency, Unbreaking, Fortune, Silk Touch, Mending for the harvesting tools; Sharpness, Looting, Fire Aspect, Unbreaking, Mending for the sword. Repair: any of the five tools is fixed at the anvil with one tempered iron.
Not applicable (items).

All five are crafted at a workbench in the vanilla patterns of their tool types, with tempered iron in place of iron ingots and sticks for the handles: Pickaxe — three tempered iron on top, two sticks down the middle. Axe — three tempered iron (mirrored vanilla pattern), two sticks. Hoe — two tempered iron (mirrored vanilla pattern), two sticks. Shovel — one tempered iron on top, two sticks. Sword — two tempered iron down the middle, one stick below. Repair is not a separate recipe: any of the five tools is fixed at the anvil with a single tempered iron.

Hand tools — not tied to the mod's energy tiers. They slot between the vanilla iron and diamond tools: by durability and speed they are closer to iron, and on block access they do not overlap diamond. They appear as soon as you start smelting iron into tempered iron in bulk — a natural upgrade to carry you until your first diamond gear.
Tempered Iron Pickaxe — a separate page for the pickaxe (the first tool). Tempered Iron — the crafting and repair material for all five. The vanilla iron tools — the balance baseline.

The Vacuum Capsule is a stackable fluid container. It solves the vanilla-bucket problem: buckets don't stack, so each one eats a whole slot, and carrying any real volume of fluid becomes awkward. The capsule comes in two forms. Empty, it is an ordinary item that stacks to 64. Filled, it holds exactly 1 bucket (1000 mB) of one fluid, and filled capsules of the same fluid stack up to 16 in a single slot — so one stack is up to 16 buckets. Different fluids never merge into one stack: a stack of water capsules and a stack of lava capsules sit apart. You fill a capsule from a fluid source in the world (like a bucket) or from a machine's tank — and empty it back with the same click. Mini-example: building a lava power setup far from your pump? Stack 16 empty capsules, fill them all at the pump's tank in a few clicks, and carry 16 buckets of lava home in a single inventory slot — the kind of trip that would take 16 slots with plain buckets.

A filled capsule holds exactly one fluid — the same volume as a bucket. How they stack: Field Value Volume per capsule 1 bucket (1000 mB) Stack size, empty 64 Stack size, filled 16, of one fluid only Different fluids never merge — each fluid keeps its own stack Two capsules of the same fluid are always equal and stack together, and the contents survive a drop, death, or transfer.

Fill from the world: right-click a fluid source with an empty capsule (water, lava, another mod's fluid). The capsule takes the source and becomes filled, just like a vanilla bucket. Fill from a tank: right-click the face of a tank block — the mod's pump or geothermal generator, or any fluid port, including other mods' machines — to pull exactly 1 bucket into the capsule. No partial fills: a whole bucket, or nothing. Empty into the world: right-click with a filled capsule to place the fluid (some exotic fluids with no block form can only go into tanks, not into the world). Water evaporates in the Nether, just like from a bucket. Empty into a tank: right-click a tank face with a filled capsule to pour its bucket in; if the tank accepts a whole bucket, the capsule comes back empty. The swap: filling or emptying swaps the empty capsule for a filled one and back. In creative the source stack is not consumed, like a vanilla bucket. Name: a filled capsule has a dynamic name — "Capsule: " — and the tooltip reads "1000 mB (1 bucket)". Look: the capsule's glass is coloured after the fluid inside — water blue, lava orange, crude oil near-black, diesel golden, fuel oil dark brown. A stack of capsules is readable at a glance, with no need to hover. A fluid the mod holds no shade for (one from another mod, say) shows as a neutral grey-blue fill. Pipes and tanks: the capsule plays nicely with other mods — their pipes and tanks can fill and drain it right in a slot.
Not applicable (item).

Crafted at a workbench: a tin body and clasps, two glass-pane windows, and a copper cable with redstone at the base. The recipe shows up in your recipe book once you have all the parts, and it yields one empty capsule.

Available early: tin is a Phase 1 metal, the copper cable arrives with the energy network, and redstone and glass are vanilla. The capsule needs no tempered iron or electronic circuit, so it comes before the Battery Pouch. It pairs with the mod's fluid machines — the pump and the geothermal generator — as a portable, stackable 16-charge bucket.

Pump — pumps fluid into its tank; the capsule fills from it and pours back. Copper Cable — a crafting component. Tin — the body and clasps in the crafting. Battery Pouch — the mod's other stackable carrying item.

The Wind Gauge is a hand instrument that needs no power. It builds nothing and produces nothing: it tells you the wind speed where you are standing, so a tower site for a Wind Mill can be chosen before you build, instead of building, dismantling and moving it three times. The gauge gives no advice. No "climb higher", no "this spot is optimal", no "N blocks to the ceiling". It shows a measurement — the conclusion is yours.

Shift + right-click with the gauge in hand, in the air or against any block — it makes no difference. A line appears in the action bar and the instrument chimes: The chime's pitch rises with the reading, so a strengthening wind is audible before the line has been read: climbing a tower, you can simply listen. A dead spot gets the lowest note. A plain right-click is not intercepted, so the gauge never gets in the way of placing blocks or opening machines. The reading is always taken where the player stands, not where the crosshair points.

The reading is a wind speed in km/h to one decimal. It changes on every block of height: climb one block and the number is different. Round numbers are rare, and that is not decoration — the wind curve is non-linear, so 24.7 and 47.1 are simply what it yields at those heights. The wind follows a single curve shared by the gauge and all three mills (see the altitude profile). In short: no wind at ground level, a climb towards the clouds, the strongest air right at the cloud deck, and thinning air above it. Height (sea level 63) Clear Rain Thunder Y 63 and below 0.0 0.0 0.0 Y 85 12.6 18.9 25.3 Y 100 18.6 28.0 37.3 Y 127 28.1 42.2 56.3 Y 160 39.7 59.6 79.5 Y 175 49.3 73.9 98.6 Y 185 56.8 85.2 113.5 Y 192 (clouds) 62.5 93.8 125.0 Y 198 47.1 70.7 94.2 Y 210 32.8 49.1 65.5 Y 230 15.9 23.9 31.9 Y 248 and above 3.8 5.6 7.5 Weather multiplies the speed: clear ×1, rain ×1.5, thunder ×2. The values come from the same settings that drive the mills, so the reading cannot drift away from the generation.

One curve serves the whole mod: the gauge turns it into km/h, the mills turn it into EU/t. Four Calm — at or below sea level there is no usable wind. Climb — sea level to the branch's ridge: a fast rise that eases off, reaching 45 % of full strength. The ridge is the height at which that branch used to hit its cap (). Shoulder — ridge to the cloud deck (Y 192): the remaining 55 %, gained on an accelerating curve. That acceleration is what keeps the peak narrow: with a linear shoulder a mill sat at its cap over sixty-seven consecutive heights. Thinning — cloud deck to Y 248: a collapse to 6 % of full strength, steepest immediately above the clouds. Higher up only a trace remains: the gauge still shows it (3.8 km/h), but for a mill it is zero. The practical consequence: the windiest place in the world is a narrow band right under the clouds. Full output is available over a handful of heights only: T1 at Y 183–193 (11 blocks), the Sky Mill at Y 188–192 (5), the Tempest Mill at Y 189–192 (4). Neither "a bit higher" nor "at the world ceiling" works: a tower at Y 230 is weaker than one at Y 127.

A closed sky means 0.0 km/h, whatever the height and the weather. The gauge tests the sky as strictly as the mill does: the column above the point must be fully transparent. Leaves and cobwebs count as a closed sky — a mill under them is dead, unlike a solar panel, which merely loses part of its output under foliage. In the Nether and the End the gauge shows no number and says there is no wind here: mills do not work there, and any number would be an invention.

The climb segment by a branch's ridge, so the gauge picks one reference: the base Wind Mill (T1), the first one a player builds and the only one that exists by the time the gauge is craftable. Above the ridge every branch shares the same shoulder and the same thinning, so the choice only shapes the climb — not where the wind peaks or where it dies. The Sky Mill's ridge is the same as T1's: 8 steps of 8 blocks is the same +64 as 4 steps of 16. Those two branches differ by their cloud-deck base (8 against 4) and their weather factors, not by altitude. Only the Tempest Mill has a ridge of its own (+96), which stretches its climb — but the peak and the death of the wind are shared. One caveat if the config is edited: the scale stays continuous only while the per-block step exceeds 0.1 km/h. A heavily stretched profile, or a small, will make adjacent heights read the same.
Two sticks, a glass pane, two tin ingots and two wooden gears. No power and no circuits — a plain wooden instrument, built long before the first mill.
Wind Mill — the T1 branch the gauge is scaled to. Sky Mill — T2, same ridge, double the base. Tempest Mill — T2, a higher ridge.
The Wrench is not consumed and does two things: it sets the faces of an Item Pipe, and it dismantles the mod's blocks.
A plain right-click on a pipe face cycles the mode: . Only the face you click changes; the mode is announced in the action bar and saved in the pipe.

Shift-right-click any block of this mod — panel, machine, cable, or the pipe itself — and it comes apart neatly: it drops as an item with everything it held (stored energy and inventory contents survive), with the sound of a loosened bolt. No pickaxe needed. Shift is the dismantle key because a vanilla secondary-use click goes straight to , skipping the block's own action — which is why the face cycle sits on the plain right-click.
Iron ingots and an iron gear in the shape of a wrench.
Item Pipe — the block whose faces this configures. Iron Gear — a crafting component.

The Alloy Smelter is the first machine in the mod that combines several different materials into one new material. It has three input slots and all of them are equal: the smelter looks at the whole set of loaded ingots, not at which one sits in which slot. Mini-example: connect LV power, put three copper ingots in any input slot and one tin ingot in any other, and 7.5 seconds later you get two bronze ingots.

What Value Internal buffer 800 EU Max input 32 EU/t (LV) Consumption 8 EU/t while working Cost per operation 1200 EU Duration 150 ticks (~7.5 s) 8 EU/t is exactly what a coal-fired Generator puts out and two thirds of a copper cable's throughput, so a single smelter occupies most of a starter line. The cost is the same for every alloy: expensive alloys differ not in what the machine charges, but in how many ingots they eat and how few they return.
