Alloy Load You get EU per ingot Bronze 3 copper + 1 tin ingot 2 ingots 600 Invar 2 iron + 1 nickel ingot 1 ingot 1200 Cupronickel 1 copper + 1 nickel ingot 1 ingot 1200 Electrum 1 gold + 1 silver ingot 1 ingot 1200 The output is always smaller than the sum of the inputs — melting costs metal. Bronze stays the bulk alloy (four cheap ingots give two), while invar, cupronickel and electrum are made one at a time: they are expensive both in material and in energy per finished ingot. Inputs are accepted by the conventional tags (, , , , , ), so copper and iron from another mod are taken just like the mod's own.

c.h: How the smelter picks a recipe
c.t: There is one rule: slot order changes nothing. The smelter looks for a recipe whose components can be laid out across the occupied slots, one component per slot. Two behaviours follow from that, and both are worth knowing: A two-component recipe will not start while a third slot is occupied. The smelter will not quietly ignore the extra stack: as long as it sits in an input, no two-component alloy counts as a match. This prevents the case where a player drops in the wrong item and never works out why it is "never consumed". Running short stops the work but does not drop the recipe. Two copper instead of three, and the smelter waits for the third rather than deciding there is no recipe at all.

Slot Accepts Three inputs (left-hand column) any ingot used by some alloy recipe Output the finished alloy Inputs are served from the top and the sides, the output from the sides. The bottom face is not exposed to item automation. A hopper cannot jam the machine. An input slot refuses an item that already sits in another input slot. Without that rule a hopper full of copper would fill all three slots with copper and the smelter would be stuck for good: no recipe has that set, and a hopper cannot pull the surplus back out. With the rule the extra copper stays in the hopper — visibly backing up — and the free slots wait for tin.

The screen shows energy, progress, the three input slots in a column, and the output. The column is deliberate: identical cells stacked one above another read as "put the parts here", where the usual input → output row would suggest an order that does not exist here. The progress arrow is not the shared one-in/one-out arrow the other processing machines carry. Here it is three separate strands, one facing each input slot, converging into a single bar that points at the output. The picture is the machine's own action — three materials becoming one — and it fills with gold from left to right as the melt runs. Hover the arrow to open the list of alloying recipes.
Pickaxe; drops itself and its inventory when broken. Glows while working (the crucibles on the front face and the shaft on top heat up). Makes no sound.
Crafted at a table from bricks, iron ingots, a machine casing and an electronic circuit. Reachable before any alloy exists, or the smelter could never be built.
The Macerator and the Compressor form the ore-doubling loop: dust becomes an ingot, and the ingot then goes into the smelter. Tin, Nickel and Silver are the mod's own metals that go into the alloys.

The Assembler is the mod's first MV machine and the end of hand-crafting 64 stacks at a time. It remembers crafting-table recipes — stored on an Assembly Blueprint and stamps them out continuously for as long as materials and charge hold out. No redstone needed; the machine runs on its own. It draws materials neither from its own inventory nor from pipes, but from its own store built out of Storage Modules. Finished items go into a separate output area so product never mixes with feedstock. Unlike the vanilla Crafter, which re-solves the grid on every redstone pulse and remembers nothing, the Assembler holds a queue of three blueprints and switches between them by itself.

Field Value Role consumer Buffer (EU) 12000 Max input (EU/tick) 128 (MV) Max output (EU/tick) n/a EU/tick 12 It runs off existing generators through a Gold Cable (MV transport, 48 EU/t) — no dedicated MV generator or transformer is required to get it going. A copper LV cable (12 EU/t) is just barely enough: the machine needs exactly 12 EU/t. Energy is spent only on a working tick. Idling for any reason — no blueprint, no ingredients, no room in the output area — costs no EU at all.

Field Value What it can assemble any crafting-table recipe, shaped or shapeless Duration (ticks) 40 Cost per operation (EU) 480 Auto-eject no The Assembler has no recipe type of its own. It solves ordinary crafting-table recipes through the stock the ordinary crafting-table recipes, which means it automatically supports vanilla recipes, this mod's own recipes (they are declared as plain ), recipes from any third-party mod, and datapacks. Tags come for free: in a recipe means "any planks", exactly as at a crafting table. The mod's own machine recipes (macerating, smelting, extracting) are not run by the Assembler — those are separate recipe types and separate machines.

c.h: Picking a blueprint from the queue
c.t: Blueprints are polled round-robin, and the cursor position persists between cycles. A blueprint is skipped if any of the following holds: the store is missing an ingredient; there is no room for the result in the output area; the blueprint's recipe no longer exists (e.g. after a datapack change). If no blueprint is ready, the machine sleeps and wakes when the store or the charge changes. Round-robin was chosen deliberately over strict top-down priority: under strict priority the first blueprint with an endless supply would never hand the queue over to the others.

The order is strict; deviating breaks either the result or the return of remainders: Build the input from the blueprint grid and check every ingredient against the store. Check that the result fits the output area and the remainders fit the store. If not, do not start the operation at all — this is what protects against item loss. Spend EU and advance progress. On completion: take the recipe result, then the remainders, and only then consume the ingredients. Steps 1–2 run on copies of the store and the output area: an operation is either worked out in full or not begun, and what is written back to the world is exactly the arrays the fitting check ran on. The check and the act are the same code, so "it will fit" and "it was placed" cannot drift apart. The planning happens twice per operation — once to decide whether to start, once at the finish (the store may have changed over forty ticks) — and not on the forty ticks in between. If the plan no longer holds at the finish (the store ran dry, the recipe vanished), the machine parks on the finish line: progress and the EU already spent are kept, and it completes the moment the plan holds again.

By default the Assembler takes exactly the items recorded on the blueprint, matching by item and ignoring components (the same comparison the stock makes). A worn tool therefore satisfies a blueprint written with a fresh one. The substitution toggle — the square arrow button right of "Write" — flips this for whichever blueprint the window is showing, that is, the one ringed in the queue. The setting lives on the blueprint item itself: move the blueprint to another Assembler and it substitutes there too. With substitution on, the order is: The item the player recorded comes first. As long as the store holds it, that is what is taken. Refined Storage does not do this, and it is a standing player complaint. If it is out of stock, candidates come from the of that particular recipe slot, in the recipe's own order. Never "from the tag in general": a recipe written as (sticks, crafting table, bowl) has twelve candidates, while , whose ingredient is literally , has none at all and never substitutes. The "any planks in the blueprint, oak and birch in the store, which stairs do I get" situation cannot arise: vanilla family recipes are per-species. A stand-in is accepted only if re-assembling gives the same result — the recipe still matches and the assembled stack equals what the blueprint promises in its tooltip, components and count included. If it does not, the operation never starts: no EU spent, nothing taken from the store. The positions come from is a list parallel to the recipe's placement slots whose value indexes (or −1 for a cell the recipe leaves empty). For a those slots are the pattern cells, so the index is mapped onto the 3×3 grid through the same trim — and, for a mirrored match, the same reflection — as the remainder return. Anything that is not a (shapeless above all) has no positions by definition; there every ingredient of the recipe is offered for every filled cell, and step 3 is what keeps that honest. Why it is off by default. The stock compares items and ignores components, so with substitution on an enchanted book can be taken where a plain one was recorded, or a worn tool where a fresh one was. The button's tooltip says so, and a blueprint with substitution on carries an extra line of its own. Materials from other mods (copper, tin, silver) work exactly as far as recipe ingredients are written with common tags — that is separate work, not a property of the machine.

Recipes with containers (the bucket in a cake, a bottle) hand the item back. A remainder goes back into the very store slot its ingredient came from; if that slot cannot take it, into any free store slot; if the store is full, into the output area; and if that is full too, the operation never started (step 2). Returning it home is not cosmetic: it is what makes the Forge Hammer stay put and simply lose a point of durability instead of creeping across the store one craft at a time. It is also the reason the trimming has to be undone — the remainder list arrives in trimmed grid coordinates, and without mapping them back the "home slot" would be computed wrong. Stack-dependent remainders (this mod's hammer, which loses a point of durability instead of disappearing) work automatically, because remainders are taken through the recipe rather than straight off the item.

Slot Accepts Count Blueprints Assembly Blueprint with a recorded recipe 3 Output area output only (the machine fills it, you empty it) 6 Blank slot a blank assembly blueprint — what "Write" stamps onto 1 Upgrades upgrade modules 4 (the first one is live) Store any items 27, plus 27 per module, capped at 108 The recipe grid is not an inventory: it is nine ghost cells whose items are neither consumed nor stored — they only show what will be written to the blueprint. A 6-slot output area is a deliberate choice: a single output slot is a well-known cause of machines jamming once the result fills the one cell available. Outside automation: an item pipe fills the store and empties the output area. Feeding ingredients straight into the machine by pipe is neither needed nor supported.

Machine window (right-click the Assembler) has two tabs: "Work" and "Record". One block, one window — only what is shown changes. The window used to do two unrelated jobs side by side: the 3×3 grid a recipe is authored in sat next to the machine's live production state, and such a window does not tell you what had been recorded, what was being made right now, or which grid was which. Recording and producing are different jobs; each now has a tab, and they share no screen space at all. Switching tabs is a view switch, not a mode switch. The machine keeps crafting while you are on the recording tab: the tab touches neither the queue, nor the progress, nor the energy. There is deliberately no mode that halts production while you record — it would turn "I want to record one more recipe" into stopping the line.

What the machine is doing right now: three blueprint slots — the queue, the active one ringed; the active blueprint's 3×3 layout and its product — view only (see below); the 6-slot output area; an energy bar and a progress bar; a status line: working / no blueprint / missing materials / output full / no energy / recipe not found. You must be able to tell the reasons apart — otherwise "the machine is idle" is indistinguishable from "the machine is broken".

a 3×3 grid of ghost cells; a result preview — what that layout makes; a slot for a blank blueprint; a "Write" button — turns the blank into a recorded blueprint; the square arrow button to the left of "Write" — the substitution toggle for the blueprint on show: grey arrows for off, green for on. Grid cells are filled by clicking: hover a cell and click while holding an item on the cursor and one copy of it lands in the cell; clicking with an empty cursor clears it. Nothing is consumed — the grid shows a layout, it does not hold one. The blank sits here rather than in the blueprint queue, and that follows from the same decision: the recording tab has to stand on its own. If "Write" took its blank from the queue you would have to visit the Work tab in order to record a recipe, and the two jobs would be tangled together again. The recorded blueprint appears where the blank was; from there you pick it up and put it in the queue on the Work tab. Recording is not queueing, and the order of operations says so out loud.

c.h: A hidden tab's slots are out of reach
c.t: A slot belonging to the tab that is not on screen can be neither filled nor emptied — not by clicking, not by shift-clicking, not by dragging, not by a double-click "collect all". A hidden tab is not merely undrawn: while it is hidden, its slots do not exist as far as the game is concerned. The tab is window state, not machine state: it is never saved, and two players at one Assembler can be on different tabs without getting in each other's way.

The Work tab shows the layout of a blueprint from the queue — the one the machine is running, or the first recorded one while it is idle. Without that, a working machine looked like this: status "Assembling", the output filling up, and an empty window. The blueprint's product is drawn under the output area it is filling. The shown layout is marked borrowed and not editable: the items are dimmed, and hovering a cell adds the line "Blueprint N layout — view only". A pale cyan ring sits around the blueprint slot the layout came from, so it is clear which of the three is on display. It cannot be mistaken for your own layout: the shown blueprint is only drawn on top of the tab's artwork, and there are no slots in that area at all — there is nothing to take out of it on any client. Your own layout lives on the other tab and does not affect this one: while you lay out a recipe, the Work tab goes on showing what the machine is doing. (Before the tabs it was the other way round — your layout overrode the display, and the machine's vanished from under you.) The two rings in the queue mean different things: orange is the blueprint the current operation is running from, pale cyan is the one whose layout is on display. Usually the same blueprint, and the orange one wins there. On top of that, every written blueprint carries its product in the item's own icon — see the Assembly Blueprint. Three queued blueprints are told apart without hovering anything, and so are three sitting in a chest. Storage window — this is the Storage Module's own window, opened by right-clicking a module rather than by a button in the Assembler: the shared storage grid, 3 to 12 rows depending on how many modules are connected; no scrolling, no scrollbar, no search — the 108-slot cap was picked so everything fits one screen. The storage window is the very same one the storage module opens. With no store attached at all the Assembler behaves exactly as it does with an empty one: the status line reads "missing materials", no EU is spent, and nothing breaks.

Field Value Shape full cube 16³ Hardness 3.0 Blast resistance 6.0 Tool pickaxe Drops with energy NBT no Breaking the Assembler drops the blueprints from its slots and the contents of the output area. The store's contents stay in the modules — only connectivity is lost, and the modules idle until a new assembler is placed. Pinned by : the drops are counted exactly, so both a lost blueprint (which cannot be crafted back) and a doubled output area show up. The blueprint queue, the progress and the round-robin cursor survive a reload — takes the machine through NBT, the same path a chunk save and load takes. The cursor is the one field with no visible symptom: were it lost, the rotation would silently restart at the first blueprint and the fairness it exists for would quietly stop working. The front face is marked and, as on the mod's other machines, excluded from automation: a pipe pushed against the front will see no slots.

No processing recipes — the machine uses vanilla The composition follows the genre pattern — a tier casing, two circuits, an "identity" part and a "storage" part, with the four corners taken by the mechanics that move the parts: The corners are Iron Gears rather than more plating: the assembler is the first machine in the mod that moves parts around on its own, and the gear is the part this mod already spends on exactly that — the Fluid Tank and the Item Pipe read the same way. Filling all nine cells also puts the craft in line with the mod's other machines, where an empty corner is the exception.

Tier: MV — the first MV machine in the mod, the anchor of the MV phase Requires: a Storage Module (with no store the machine has nowhere to draw from) and an Assembly Blueprint Since it also requires a finished oil line — not directly, but through the Advanced Machine Casing, which now seats 2 Advanced Circuits, each costing 4 rubber. The assembler's own crafting grid is unchanged, but its full cost grew by those 2 circuits, and it can no longer be built before a Polymerizer and a Vulcanizer Upgrades into: nothing. On-demand autocrafting (order "make 64 X" with a sub-craft tree) is a separate future system, not an upgrade to this machine

Storage Module — the store the Assembler draws from Assembly Blueprint — the item that holds a recipe Gold Cable — powering an MV machine Item Pipe — fills the store, empties the output Sawmill — reference for a machine with switchable modes in its GUI

The Canning Machine does not pack a product into a tin — it renders food down to food value and pours that value back out as identical rations. Whatever you feed it, the same item comes out, which means your whole larder collapses into a single stack. Mini-example: load the leftovers of a harvest — carrots, bread, berries — add some empty cans and connect LV power. A dozen slots of odds and ends become one stack of rations.

What Value Internal buffer 800 EU Max input 32 EU/tick (LV) Draw 2 EU/tick while working Cost per operation 200 EU per ration Duration 100 ticks (~5 s) Energy enters through five working faces. The front face is inert.

The machine works in two independent steps, and the difference matters. Absorbing is free and instant. The machine eats food from the top slot and banks its food value inside. No EU is spent. Pressing is paid and timed. Once the bank covers one ration, a 100-tick cycle runs for 200 EU, one empty can is spent, and exactly one ration comes out. Absorbing only happens when the machine could actually press. With no cans, no power, or a blocked output, the food simply stays in its slot, untouched. It is never eaten for nothing. The banked remainder is shown in the window as the "Calories" line and survives leaving the world. Breaking the machine, however, loses it: the cans and the food drop, the banked calories do not. Finish the ration you started before you take the machine apart.

A product's value is its nutrition plus its saturation. Rich food buys more rations, poor food fewer. One ration costs 12.0 of value. What you feed it Value Items per ration Rabbit stew 22.0 0.5 Cooked porkchop, steak 20.8 0.6 Golden carrot 20.4 0.6 Cooked chicken, salmon 13.2 0.9 Bread, baked potato 11.0 1.1 Carrot 6.6 1.8 Apple 6.4 1.9 Melon slice 3.2 3.8 Cookie, berries, raw fish 2.4 5.0 Dried kelp, raw potato 1.6 7.5 Processing is always a loss: a ration costs 12.0 of value and carries 9.6. A fifth is spent — that is the price of convenience, and it is exactly what makes duplicating food impossible.

Hazardous food: raw chicken, rotten flesh, poisonous potato, pufferfish and spider eye. Processing would launder their risk away for free, which is not a fair trade. Its own ration. Otherwise the machine would grind its own output down, burning a can each pass. Anything that is not food, and food with no nutrition at all. The filter holds on the window's slots and on the faces alike: a hopper or a pipe cannot push through what you could not place by hand. Stews and honey are accepted, but their container is lost. A bowl or a bottle comes back only when you eat from it; the machine will not return one.

What Value Nutrition 8 (the same as a steak) Saturation 1.6 (a steak has 12.8) Stack 64 Time to eat 1 second (ordinary food takes 1.6) A ration fills the hunger bar like a steak but holds you three times worse: industrial food fills the stomach without feeding it for long. A full player cannot eat one, exactly like any ordinary food. Side effects of the source food are not carried over: a canned golden apple gives nutrition only. While it is being eaten, the can in your hand appears opened.
Slot Accepts Top input food Bottom input empty cans Output rations
Energy, two inputs, progress and the output. Below them sits the "Calories" line with the percentage banked towards the next ration.
What Value Tool pickaxe Keeps its charge when broken no
While running, the machine emits a light metallic clatter of tin cans on the line — the loop (pattern A, default 0.35). It falls silent when idle.
The machine itself is built from tin plates around a casing. The empty can is a bench craft too:
Tier LV. This machine gives tin its first mass consumer: a can is spent for good, so every meal eats metal again.

Not for a steak farm. With meat sorted, 64 cooked porkchops are already one slot and more calories than processing would return. That is by design. For odds and ends, and for the road. A dozen slots of assorted food — berries, carrots, bread, harvest leftovers, mob drops — collapse into one or two slots of identical rations.
Tin — what cans are made of. Compressor — makes the tin plates. Generator — a power source.

The Component Repair Bench restores worn wind mill rotors and water mill wheels instead of making you craft new ones. One repair clears the wear, costs one item of the grade's material plus EU — and permanently lowers that part's maximum durability by 20 % of its original value. The point is a choice, not free maintenance: repairing is cheaper in metal, but a part gets exactly four repairs, after which the bench refuses and it has to be replaced anyway.

Field Value Role consumer Buffer (EU) 800 Max input (EU/tick) 32 (LV) Max output (EU/tick) n/a EU/tick 8 Energy is accepted on every face except the front: that is the working face, and neither a cable nor a hopper connects through it.

Field Value Recipe type none — the bench uses no recipes Duration (ticks) 1200 / 2400 / 3600 — exactly 1 / 2 / 3 minutes (by grade) Auto-output true — a hopper collects the finished part The bench has no recipes on purpose: a repair does not turn one item into another, it changes the properties of the same item in the slot. What is repaired, and with what, by code and config. Grade Material (1) EU per repair Ticks Plain iron plate 9,600 1200 Reinforced () tempered iron plate 19,200 2400 Advanced () electronic circuit 28,800 3600 A rotor and a wheel of the same grade repair identically: the price follows the grade, not the family. Overclocker chips work as they do in any other machine — shorter operations, higher draw.

Slot Accepts Count Material (left) iron plate, tempered iron plate or electronic circuit stack Component (right) any grade of rotor or wheel 1 The component sits on the right, where other machines put their output slot, and that is not a layout mistake: a repair produces no new item, so the part goes in and comes out of the same slot. The arrow shows the material on the left being consumed into the component on the right. Automation. A hopper may only insert what the bench can actually work on — a worn part with repairs left. It may only extract what the bench has finished with: a repaired part, or one that has used up its allowance. So a "hopper in, bench, hopper out" line works and never loops. By hand you may insert any part, including a spent one — otherwise you could not read why it is being refused.

Type: container Shows: the energy bar on the left, the material slot, a progress arrow, the component slot, and a status line under the slots. The status line is never blank. On an empty bench it asks for a worn component; after that it names the single reason for the hold: "Nothing to repair", "Repair limit reached", "Needs repair material" — or "Repairing" while it works. Translucent ghost items in the empty slots show what belongs there: the three materials cycle on the left, the rotor and the wheel on the right. Once a component is loaded the left ghost stops cycling and shows exactly the material that grade needs. Hovering the arrow stands in for the recipe-viewer entry this machine cannot have: it prints the repair cost, how much durability the repair burns, and how many repairs the component has left.
Field Value Shape full cube Hardness 3.0 Blast resistance 6.0 Tool pickaxe Drops with energy NBT false
While a repair runs, the bench rings with soft rhythmic hammer taps on a small anvil — the loop (pattern A, default 0.35). It falls silent when idle.
Craft — three iron plates on top, a machine casing in the middle, an electronic circuit below, iron ingots at the sides. No recycling recipes.

Tier: LV. Evolves into: nothing. Requires: a machine casing, an electronic circuit and iron plates — so the bench arrives after the first machines, once enough mills are running for their upkeep to have become a chore.

Wind Mill Rotor — the consumable the bench restores. Water Mill Wheel — the second consumable. Wind Mill and Water Mill — the machines that wear these parts out. Forge Hammer — the mod's only other item that lives on durability; it is repaired at an anvil, not here.

The Compressor is an LV machine that squeezes raw materials into denser forms: metal dust into ingots, coal and gem dust back into items, ice and snow into denser blocks, sugar cane into paper. Its standout job is closing the ore-doubling loop for non-metals — it's the only machine that restores coal, diamond, emerald and lapis dust to a usable item, so ore → 2 dust → 2 items works for those too. Mini-example: grind a diamond ore in the Macerator to get two diamond dusts, then run both through here. You end up with two diamonds from one ore — and only this machine can do that last step.

A line of its own is exactly what the Compressor needs: it has batch recipes where one operation eats several items at once (4 glowstone dusts, 9 redstone). An incomplete batch is accepted into the slot but starts nothing — without a caption that just looks like a breakdown. Redstone shows it best: a full stack of 64 splits into batches of 9 with 1 left over, so a single item sitting in the input slot after a whole stack has been processed is normal, not a jam. The Electric Furnace is a full electrical counterpart to the vanilla furnace. It smelts everything a regular furnace can — ores, food, glass, cobblestone — but runs on EU instead of fuel and works twice as fast. On top of the vanilla recipes, the mod adds its own, mainly dust → ingot, which closes the ore-doubling loop started by the Macerator. Mini-example: grind iron ore in the Macerator to get two dusts, then drop both in here. In a few seconds you have two iron ingots — one vein, doubled, no fuel spent.

Input Output Notes Metal dust (copper, iron, gold, nickel, silver, tin, uranium) ingot the mod recipe — closes ore-doubling Raw ore (raw nickel, raw silver, raw tin, raw uranium) ingot the mod recipe Iron ingot tempered iron the mod recipe, 200 EU Anything else a vanilla furnace smelts (ores, food, sand → glass, cobblestone → stone, raw copper/gold/iron → ingot…) as vanilla the vanilla fallback, ~5 s The mod recipes (12 of them, all 200 EU) cover only what a vanilla furnace cannot do: the mod's dusts → ingots, the mod's specific ores (nickel/silver/tin/uranium), and iron tempering. Anything that is numerically the same as a vanilla smelt (cobblestone → stone, sand → glass, raw copper/gold/iron → ingot) goes through the single vanilla fallback — no duplicate recipe. The Electric Furnace category in JEI/REI lists everything the machine actually smelts — the mod's own recipes and every vanilla smelt (ores, food, sand → glass …), each priced as the Electric Furnace runs it: 200 EU · 5 s, not the vanilla "XP in 10 sec". Clicking the progress arrow opens that category alongside the vanilla one; clicking the Electric Furnace block in the item list does the same. Vanilla recipes enter the category as mirrors: they are built for display only and never join the game's recipe registry — at runtime the machine still executes the live vanilla recipe. The numbers you read and the behaviour you get therefore cannot drift apart. Every smelt is listed exactly once. The mod does not duplicate with its own recipe anything a vanilla furnace already does with the same input and output (cobblestone → stone, sand → glass, raw copper/gold/iron → ingot): those smelts live only in the vanilla fallback and reach the category as a single mirror. The Mekanism Energized Smelter and Modern Industrialization follow the same rule — a single source of truth for smelts that are numerically identical to vanilla ones (including the 200 EU · 5 s price, which the mirror takes from the same setting the machine ticks). Raw rubber is no longer included after removed its smelting recipe.

Tier: LV. The starter electric smelter and the other half of ore-doubling. Evolves into the Induction Furnace — the MV, faster, hotter evolution of smelting. Needs power from an LV source, e.g. a Generator.

Macerator — produces the dust this furnace smelts back into ingots. Induction Furnace — the MV evolution of smelting. Compressor — handles the non-metal dusts this furnace can't. Generator — the power source.

The Electric Heater sits directly below a Vulcanizer and gives it the maximum heat level — 3, that is three rubber from one portion of ingredients instead of one on a campfire. But not right away. This is a furnace that has to be lit: a cold heater is not a heat source at all, and the Vulcanizer above it simply waits for it to reach working temperature. Warming up takes about ten seconds, after which the machine starts straight at ×3. Mini-example: put the heater under a Vulcanizer, run an LV cable to it and load the ingredients. For the first ~10 seconds nothing happens, the thermometer on the heater's screen climbs and the coils of the block light up. The moment the thermometer is full the rubber starts coming — three at a time.

What Value Internal buffer 2400 EU Max input 32 EU/t (LV) Consumption 6 EU/t Warm-up 200 ticks (~10 s), 1200 EU Draw with nothing to heat 0 EU The heater is the most expensive part of the pair: 6 EU/t against the 2 EU/t of the Vulcanizer itself. That is by design — heat is exactly what it produces, and at the old rate it came out cheaper than the machine it serves and was not felt at all. Together the pair draws 8 EU/t, which still fits into a copper cable (12 EU/t). The numbers close on each other: the warm-up costs 1200 EU, one Vulcanizer batch costs exactly the same, and the buffer is 2400 EU. In other words, a fully charged heater can light itself up and run one batch even with the cable cut. Warming up spends energy in its own right — it is the only mode in which the block pays for something other than somebody else's work. But it does not start "just because power is connected": it starts only when the machine above really has nothing to do but wait for heat. A heater with no machine above it, or under a machine with no ingredients, still stands cold and spends nothing. If the machine above is sped up with Overclockers, the heater pays the same multiplier — otherwise an overclocked pair would pay less for its heat. The heater has no upgrade panel of its own: the multiplier arrives from the machine it heats. Careful with overclocking. On the third overclocker step the machine above asks the heater for 48 EU/t, while its LV input holds only 32. The buffer will carry such a pair for a while, then the heater starts falling behind. The practical ceiling for the pair is the second step.

Left with nothing to heat, the heater cools down twice as slowly as it warmed up: the full slide back takes about 20 seconds. That is deliberate slack for pauses — a hopper that held the ingredients back for a couple of seconds costs you a small slice of the warm-up, not all of it. Cooling down is free. And while the machine above is waiting for work — standing without energy of its own, say — the heater holds its temperature and spends nothing while doing so: it does not throw the warm-up away just because its neighbour temporarily has nothing to pay with.

The screen opens on right-click. It has no slots — there is nothing to put into the heater; it takes energy from the cable and gives heat upwards. The screen is there so that the warm-up can be watched and planned instead of guessed. Left Right Energy bar Warm-up thermometer The thermometer fills along an incandescence scale — dark ember through red-orange to bright gold at full warm-up. That last step is easy to spot: it is exactly what marks the machine above starting to work. Row What it means Warm-up Temperature in percent — always the real one, it is a property of the block itself Heat ×3 when heat is really being given away, and a dash while the heater is still warming up Draw How much EU per tick the heater spends, including the overclockers of the machine above At the bottom there is a status line: "No machine above", "No energy", "Warming up", "Up to temperature", "Cooling down" or "Cold". The first two are highlighted in red: those are what the player fixes.

A heat source for the block directly above it only, and only once it is up to temperature. An LV consumer of EU; it accepts energy on its available side faces. The glow changes with temperature — four steps from dark to red hot. The state is readable in the world without opening the screen. A fully warmed block lets heat break out of the seam with the machine. The particles only appear at full warm-up: they are the "×3 is running" signal, not a constant background. Mine with a pickaxe; it drops itself.
Crafted at a table from redstone dust, a gold ingot, iron ingots, — a machine casing, — an electronic circuit.

Vulcanizer — the first heat consumer; the heat level multiplies its yield. Thermal Centrifuge — the second consumer. For it the heater is not the "best of the sources" but the only one: lava and campfires will not start it at all. Overclocker — it sits in the machine above, but the heater pays for it too. Lava and magma blocks give free level 2 with no warm-up at all; a campfire gives level 1. While the heater is lighting up, lava under the machine would already be working — that is the price of ×3.

Mini-example: drop a poppy in, get two red dyes back instead of the one the crafting table gives. Hook a few up to a flower farm and dyes stop being a chore.

The Galvanic Bath is an LV electroplating machine: fibre and silver dust are submerged in water, a current is passed through them, and the silver plates onto the fibre as a conductive track. The result is flux thread, the half-product of the Fluxweave material. It is the first machine in the mod to consume items and a fluid at once, and it is the entry point to the EU armour line. Fibre means vanilla string or cotton fibre — one recipe accepts both through the tag. Choosing between a spider farm and a cotton trellis is a matter of playstyle, not progression.

Field Value Role consumer Buffer (EU) 800 Max input (EU/tick) 32 (LV ceiling) Max output (EU/tick) n/a EU/tick 2 Throughput: accepts up to 32 EU/tick on every face except the front, which is energy-inert and draws no cable arm. Anything above the limit is simply not transferred; nothing breaks.

Field Value Duration (ticks) 500, i.e. 25 s Water per operation 4000 mB, i.e. 4 buckets Tank capacity 10,000 mB (10 buckets) Auto-eject no The water is not part of the recipe JSON. No recipe family in the mod takes items and a fluid at the same time, so the water volume is a fixed config cost the machine checks and debits itself. A datapack can override the fibre, the silver and the energy cost, but not the water volume. The tank is one-way: water can be poured in but never pulled out. What enters is feedstock, not storage, so a neighbouring pump cannot siphon it back.

The Iron Furnace is an upgraded fuel furnace that sits between the vanilla furnace and the Electric Furnace. It's faster than vanilla and smelts everything vanilla does, but still runs on solid fuel (coal, planks, charcoal…) rather than EU. It's an early upgrade for the player who hasn't built a power grid yet but wants to speed up smelting. It fully reuses the vanilla furnace UI — only the title differs. Recipes and behaviour match the vanilla furnace: anything that smelts in a vanilla furnace smelts here too — the mod's ores, raw materials and metal dust included. Mini-example: wrap a vanilla furnace in eight iron ingots → get an Iron Furnace. Smelting is noticeably faster, fuel consumption is the same. An intermediate step before the Electric Furnace.
Uses no EU. Fuel is solid (as in a vanilla furnace). This is the key difference from the Electric Furnace, which runs on EU.

Placed like a normal furnace. Right-click opens the same UI (smelt slot, fuel slot, flame bar and progress arrow). It takes every vanilla smelting recipe — and the ones the mod adds: ore → ingot, raw material → ingot, metal dust → ingot, iron ingot → Tempered Iron. What it can't do: recipes that exist only for the Electric Furnace (that one has a recipe type of its own). Today that means smelting uranium and palladium dust — available in the Electric Furnace only.

Cubic block with a front face (lit/unlit states — lit while working). Tier: LV (by the mod's classification — early machine), but actually runs without EU. Hardness and tool: same as a vanilla furnace (stone pickaxe).
While lit, the furnace plays the vanilla fire crackle — the same ambience as the ordinary furnace (an irregular one-shot via, not a loop). No custom sample.
Crafted at a workbench (shaped 3×3): vanilla furnace in the centre, surrounded by 8 iron ingots. — iron ingot (×8); — vanilla furnace (×1).

Early machine (tier-stone), no EU. Slots into the chain: vanilla furnace → Iron Furnace → Electric Furnace → Induction Furnace (concept). Each step is faster than the last. Doesn't need a power grid — you can drop it in any cave/mine where you have fuel.
Electric Furnace — the next step: switching from fuel to EU. Iron Chest — a sibling "upgraded vanilla" block.

The Macerator is the early-game ore-doubling machine. Feed it ore or metal and it grinds the stuff into dust — and a mined ore block gives you two dusts instead of one, which is the whole point of building one. It's the first machine worth running a cable for. Mini-example: drop an iron ore block (or the raw drop) in, let it spin, and out come two iron dusts. Smelt those and one vein has just paid out two ingots instead of one. The ingot stays ×1 (net-zero, otherwise you could loop "ingot → dust → ingot" for free doubling). This is the first machine worth building an energy network for.

The Macerator only consumes EU and holds a little buffer so it keeps grinding smoothly even when the supply is uneven. The Macerator itself is crafted at a workbench: a piece of flint on top, cobblestone along the sides and bottom corners, an Electronic Circuit in the centre, and a Silver Ingot at the bottom-centre. What it grinds, and what you get back: Ore block and raw ore → 2 dust. Doubling is granted for both inputs — this is the macerator's main payoff: two ingots from one vein instead of one, whether you mined the block or the raw drop. Finished ingot → 1 dust. Net-zero, so doubling cannot be looped ("ingot → dust → ingot"). Input Output Why Ore block (iron, copper, gold, tin, silver, nickel, uranium — regular + deepslate) ×2 dust the doubling payoff — two ingots from one vein Raw ore (the raw drop from the ore) ×2 dust the second doubled form — macerate both the block and the raw Finished ingot ×1 dust an intermediate form, ×1 (otherwise doubling would loop) The same scheme covers non-metal dusts (coal, diamond, emerald, lapis): ore → ×2 dust, the pure item → ×1. One exception worth knowing: lapis ore → 6 dust (vanilla lapis ore already drops 4–9, so a plain ×2 would have made grinding pointless).

The Polymerizer is the first machine in the mod that eats a fluid rather than an item. Inside it sits a ten-bucket oil tank; one run drinks exactly one bucket and hands back a lump of raw rubber. The raw rubber is then combined with sulfur dust in a Vulcanizer. Mini-example: run a pipe from a pump sitting on an oil lake, give the machine power, and it will grind oil into rubber on its own for as long as there is oil in the tank. You can also fill it by hand: put a bucket (or a capsule) into the top slot — the fluid moves into the tank and the empty container drops into the slot below it.

The Sawmill is an LV wood-processing machine. It saws a log (or planks) at a higher yield than hand-crafting, and can cut into four different products — it has 4 switchable modes (GUI buttons): planks / sticks / slabs / stairs. Every species yields its own species; sticks are species-agnostic. It is the cheapest operation in the mod by energy — sawing wood is easier than milling stone. Mini-example: put an oak log in "Planks" mode — in ~4 seconds you get 6 oak planks instead of the vanilla 4. Switch to "Sticks" — the same log gives 18 sticks.

The screen has its own GUI: energy buffer, input and output slots, and between them a saw blade progress indicator that fills left to right. A row of 4 mode buttons with ghost icons (plank/stick/slab/stairs) sits below the slots; the active mode is highlighted and each button has a tooltip. The status line between the slots and the mode buttons explains why the machine stands idle: "Not enough material", "No matching recipe", "Output is blocked", "No energy". An empty machine gets no line at all — an empty slot speaks for itself. The energy line does not appear the moment the buffer runs dry, but only once it has stayed empty for a while: a machine that barely has enough power runs one tick on, one tick off, and a caption blinking along with it would lie about a stall.

The Thermal Centrifuge is the second ore-doubling step. The macerator already turns one ore block into two dusts; the centrifuge splits each dust in two again, into uranium concentrate, which is then pressed in the Compressor — two concentrate into one enriched uranium (U-235). A full line yields four concentrate, that is two enriched uranium, from one ore block, against a single ingot from a plain smelt. The concentrate is pressed rather than smelted: the furnace already accepts uranium dust, and a second route through it would be both illogical (concentrate is something you squeeze, not melt) and confusing — two similar recipes in one machine. Placing it and feeding it is not enough, though. This is the first machine in the mod you have to switch on and spin up: it needs a redstone signal and a hot Electric Heater directly below it. Quick example: place the heater, the centrifuge on top, run a cable to it, drop in uranium dust and flip a lever. The rotor starts picking up speed and the heater starts warming. The heater gets there first, in about ten seconds, while the rotor takes twice as long to spin up — and only then does the dust turn into concentrate. Remove the lever and the machine stops and loses its spin.

Field Value Role consumer Buffer (EU) 800 Max input (EU/tick) 32 (the LV ceiling) EU/tick (working and spinning up) 4 EU/tick while idling at speed 1 Twice the price of an ordinary machine in this mod: the centrifuge doubles the rarest resource there is, and it never works alone — the heater below is part of the deal. Together the pair draws 10 EU/tick, which still fits a copper cable (12 EU/tick), but with almost nothing to spare. That is deliberate.

The redstone signal must be held, not pulsed. This is the opposite of the Mob Repeller, where a signal pauses the block: here the signal is the motor's start button, and reading its absence as "keep running" would make no sense for a machine whose whole identity is a spinning rotor. State Condition Draw Stopped no signal 0 EU Spinning up signal present, not yet at speed 4 EU/tick Idling at speed at speed, nothing to process 1 EU/tick Working at speed, with heat, input and room in the output 4 EU/tick A full spin-up takes 400 ticks — twice as long as the heater takes to warm up. The heater gets there first, and the machine visibly waits on its own mass: that is the heavy-rotor feel the centrifuge exists for, the reason it is unlike every other machine here. If there is not even enough power for the idle draw, the rotor sheds speed at half the rate it gained it: a short brownout does not throw you back to zero. Cutting the signal is a full stop: the revolutions go to zero at once rather than winding down. The lever is an honest master switch for the whole line.

Only the Electric Heater will do. Lava, magma and campfires — all good enough for the Vulcanizer — will not start the centrifuge: its output multiplier is fixed, so a scale of heat tiers would be a dial with nothing to turn. While the heater below is still warming, the machine says so on its status line, separately from the case where there is no heater at all.
Field Value Duration (ticks) 200 Cost per operation 800 EU Yield 1 uranium dust → 2 uranium concentrate Auto-eject no

Heat multiplies the output but not the batch price, so a stronger heat source is the main way to stretch the sulfur you have found. The Electric Heater stands apart in this table: until it has warmed up it is not a heat source at all, and the machine above it waits. Bronze is the cheapest and the most mass-produced of the mod's four alloys. The Alloy Smelter melts it out of copper and tin — two metals you have usually piled up well before the smelter itself is built. Mini-example: put three copper ingots in any input slot of the smelter and one tin ingot in any other. Seven and a half seconds later the output holds two bronze ingots. Slot order does not matter. Bronze is the only alloy the smelter returns two ingots at a time, which is why it costs half the energy per ingot the other three do. There is no bronze ore: the alloy comes out of the smelter and nowhere else, and a vanilla furnace will not make it. Form How you get it Ingot alloying 3 copper + 1 tin ingot in the Alloy Smelter → 2 ingots Plate hammering an ingot with a Forge Hammer on a crafting table, or the Compressor, 260 EU Reinforced plate hammering 2 plates on a crafting table, or the Compressor: 2 plates → 1, 260 EU

The only route is the Alloy Smelter. What Value Load 3 copper ingots + 1 tin ingot You get 2 bronze ingots Cost per operation 1200 EU Duration 150 ticks (~7.5 s) EU per ingot 600 Four ingots in, two out: melting costs metal, and that holds for every alloy in the mod. Copper and tin are accepted through the conventional tags and , so copper from another mod is taken just like the mod's own.

Bronze is no longer a dead end: an ingot is forged into a bronze plate — by hand with a Forge Hammer or in bulk in the Compressor — and two plates press into one reinforced bronze plate, the blank for heavy parts. The ingot itself goes into the Diamond-Tipped Electric Chainsaw. Per ingot bronze is the cheapest of the four and the easiest to put into steady production, which makes it the natural alloy to learn plate rolling on.
Alloy Smelter — the only source of bronze. Tin — the second metal in the recipe; the copper is vanilla. Invar, Cupronickel, Electrum — the other three alloys from the same smelter.

Cupronickel is a one-to-one copper-and-nickel alloy made by the Alloy Smelter. It is the simplest of the four recipes: one ingot of each metal, no multipliers. Mini-example: put one copper ingot in any input slot of the smelter and one nickel ingot in any other. Seven and a half seconds later the output holds one cupronickel ingot. Slot order does not matter. The smelter returns a single ingot per operation, so the full 1200 EU is spent on that one ingot. There is no cupronickel ore: the alloy comes out of the smelter and nowhere else, and a vanilla furnace will not make it. Form How you get it Ingot alloying 1 copper + 1 nickel ingot in the Alloy Smelter → 1 ingot Plate ingot + forge hammer on a crafting table, or the Compressor, 260 EU Reinforced plate 2 plates + forge hammer on a crafting table, or the Compressor, 260 EU

The only route is the Alloy Smelter. What Value Load 1 copper ingot + 1 nickel ingot You get 1 cupronickel ingot Cost per operation 1200 EU Duration 150 ticks (~7.5 s) EU per ingot 1200 Two ingots in, one out: melting costs metal, and that holds for every alloy in the mod. Copper and nickel are accepted through the conventional tags and , so copper from another mod is taken just like the mod's own.

Cupronickel now has a cupronickel plate — the forge hammer or the Compressor — and a reinforced version made from two plates. The ingot itself goes into the diamond-tipped electric hoe. In material terms it is the gentlest way to spend nickel — one cheap copper per ingot instead of two iron as in invar — but nickel is still wanted by electronic circuits, so stockpiling the alloy only pays off while nickel is spare.
Alloy Smelter — the only source of cupronickel. Nickel — the bottleneck of the recipe; the copper is vanilla. Bronze, Invar, Electrum — the other three alloys from the same smelter.

Diesel is the light fraction of oil distillation and the target product of the Distillation Column: 700 mB out of every bucket of crude oil. It does not occur in the world — the column is its only source. Golden-yellow and runny; unlike oil it behaves like water — it does not burn in the world, does not slow you down and does not drown you. Mini-example: a pump set against the top of the column drains diesel into a portable tank — or put an empty bucket into the diesel slot of the tower's interface.
What Value Physics like water: spreads, does not burn, harmless Regenerates no — two sources never spawn a third Collection bucket, capsule, pump Tag (still + flowing)

Arrives together with the column — iteration 2 of the oil branch. Its purpose is fuel: the liquid fuel generator (the branch's next task) will burn it at 12 EU/t (12 000 EU per bucket) — exactly the throughput of one copper line. The tag (diesel + fuel oil + lava) has already shipped — for the generator's tank filter.
Distillation Column — the only source. Oil — the feedstock. Fuel Oil — the second, heavy fraction of the same distillation.

Electrum is a one-to-one gold-and-silver alloy made by the Alloy Smelter. By materials it is the most expensive recipe the smelter has: both input metals are valuable, and neither of them is ever spare in a chest. Mini-example: put one gold ingot in any input slot of the smelter and one silver ingot in any other. Seven and a half seconds later the output holds one electrum ingot. Slot order does not matter. The smelter returns a single ingot per operation, so the full 1200 EU is spent on that one ingot. There is no electrum ore: the alloy comes out of the smelter and nowhere else, and a vanilla furnace will not make it. Form How you get it Ingot alloying 1 gold + 1 silver ingot in the Alloy Smelter → 1 ingot Plate ingot + the Forge Hammer on the crafting grid, or the Compressor, 260 EU Reinforced plate 2 plates + the same hammer on the crafting grid, or the same Compressor, 260 EU

The only route is the Alloy Smelter. What Value Load 1 gold ingot + 1 silver ingot You get 1 electrum ingot Cost per operation 1200 EU Duration 150 ticks (~7.5 s) EU per ingot 1200 Two ingots in, one out: melting costs metal, and that holds for every alloy in the mod. Gold and silver are accepted through the conventional tags and , so silver from another mod is taken just like the mod's own.

Electrum now has an electrum plate — the Forge Hammer or the Compressor — and a reinforced version made of two plates. The ingot itself stopped sitting idle long ago: it goes into the Electrum Cable — the high-voltage line with the lowest losses — into the Reinforced Energy Storage and into the Electrum Chest. The trade-off is real all the same: silver goes into the electronic circuit and through it into nearly every machine and generator, so every ingot spent on electrum is a machine left unbuilt.

Alloy Smelter — the only source of electrum. Silver — the second metal in the recipe and the main competitor for it; the gold is vanilla. Bronze, Invar, Cupronickel — the other three alloys from the same smelter.

Fuel oil is the heavy residue of distillation: 200 mB out of every bucket of oil, running down into the bottom tank of the Distillation Column. Thick and dark-brown; more hassle by volume and less by yield — exactly what a bottom fraction should be. Like diesel, it behaves like water in the world: it does not burn and does no harm. Mini-example: a third pump at the base of the tower pulls fuel oil away into a separate tank — or put an empty bucket into the fuel oil slot in the interface.
What Value Physics like water: spreads, does not burn, harmless Regenerates no Collection bucket, capsule, pump Tag (still + flowing)

A by-product of the column — it accumulates on its own while diesel is being distilled; if you do not take it away, a full bottom tank will halt the distillation. Its purpose is cheap fuel: the liquid fuel generator will burn it at 6 EU/t (6 000 EU per bucket) — half as strong as diesel. Included in the tag alongside diesel and lava.
Distillation Column — the only source. Diesel — the target fraction of the same distillation. Oil — the feedstock.

Invar is an iron-and-nickel alloy made one ingot at a time by the Alloy Smelter. Iron you always have; nickel is the scarcest metal in the mod, so how fast you can make invar comes down to nickel and nothing else. Mini-example: put two iron ingots in any input slot of the smelter and one nickel ingot in any other. Seven and a half seconds later the output holds one invar ingot. Slot order does not matter. The smelter returns a single ingot per operation, so the full 1200 EU is spent on that one ingot. There is no invar ore: the alloy comes out of the smelter and nowhere else, and a vanilla furnace will not make it. The only route is the Alloy Smelter. Nickel, meanwhile, is already spent on electronic circuits, so every ingot you divert into invar is a circuit you did not build: stockpiling the alloy pays off when nickel is spare.

Nickel is the mod's scarcest and deepest metal, held in reserve for the entry into the MV tier — it will become the alloy for MV machine casings and advanced circuits. Its ore spawns in stone and in deepslate, deeper and rarer still than silver, and is mined with any stone pickaxe or better. Mini-example: the same two routes as tin and silver — furnace gives 1 ingot per ore, the Macerator gives 2. But nickel is the rarest of the three, so macerate every block and raw drop: you will not find many. There is no vanilla nickel, so the ingot is a mod item. Nickel already does work today: it goes into the electronic circuit (alongside silver), and that circuit is a required component of both evolution chips (day and night), which turn the solar panel and the wind mill into their reinforced T2 versions. Form How you get it Ore (stone / deepslate) mined in the world; pickaxe drops raw, Silk Touch gives the block Raw the pickaxe drop from the ore; smelts into an ingot Dust a block of ore or the raw grinds into 2 dust; a finished ingot grinds into 1 Ingot smelting the raw, the ore, or the dust
Nickel is the scarcest of the three metals: small veins sitting deeper than any other, near the bottom of the world. You will only find it while mining deep, and even then rarely.

It behaves like a vanilla ore: it needs a stone pickaxe or better, the drop scales with Fortune, and Silk Touch yields the ore block itself. Field Value Tool stone pickaxe or better (wood/gold drop nothing) Drop raw nickel ×1 (Fortune multiplies; Silk Touch → the block)

Two routes out of one vein. Furnace route (no machines): smelt the raw (or the ore) into an ingot — 1 ingot per ore. Macerator route (doubling): grind a block of ore or the raw into 2 dust, then smelt each dust into an ingot — 2 ingots per ore. Re-processing a finished ingot grinds back down to 1 dust (no doubling). The doubling applies to both the whole ore block and the raw — macerate either form.

Nickel is already in demand at LV: it goes into the electronic circuit, without which no machine or generator can be built. That same circuit is a component of both evolution chips that launch the T2 evolution of the panels and wind mills. Its role as the alloy behind the MV machine casing and the advanced circuit will be added later, at the MV tier — so spare nickel won't sit idle.

Electronic Circuit — nickel goes into its recipe. Alignment Chips — the day and night evolution chips are built on the circuit. Tin — the structural sample for an ore material (same processing). Macerator — unlocks the doubled-yield route. Silver, Uranium — the mod's other rare metals.

Oil is the mod's first fluid and the only resource you can neither craft nor smelt — you find it. It sits in the world as lakes: mostly deep underground, occasionally breaking the surface as a rare patch. A deposit is finite: every block of oil you scoop out is gone for good and never regrows the way water does. Mini-example: you find a small black pool underground and scoop it with an empty bucket — one bucket of oil. Scooping by hand takes a while; put a Pump next to it and it drains the whole deposit into its own tank. Form How you get it Oil in the world find a lake — underg or on the surface (rare) Oil bucket scoop with an empty bucket, pour it back with a right-click Oil in a tank drain the deposit with a Pump Oil in a capsule scoop with a Vacuum Capsule

Oil generates everywhere in the Overworld — biome makes no difference. There is none in the Nether or the End. Deposits come in four sizes, from a puddle to a vein worth mounting an expedition for. A surface patch — the smallest find. Turns up about once every 150 chunks. Its job is to tell you oil exists at all, not to be a mining source. A lake in the mines — the real source. Sits in the Y −40 … −8 band, never closer than five blocks to the surface, in roughly one chunk in fifty. That is the same depth as lava lakes, so oil often sits right next to lava — which is harmless in itself (see "Flammability"). A deep reservoir. Three times wider than the mine-depth lake and lower down — Y −50 … −30, roughly once every 40 chunks. This one is worth hauling a pump and a tank down for. An oil vein — the rarest thing in the ground. Roughly once every 600 chunks, and you can spot it from the surface: a one-to-three-block spout of oil erupting out of the ground with a black patch spreading around it. Below the spout a one-block-wide shaft runs down almost to bedrock, where a huge oil-filled dome is waiting. One vein holds roughly as much as twenty mine-depth lakes. Oil never generates inside structures: villages, mineshafts, strongholds and the Ancient City. Dig inside those without worrying. A deposit's volume, in oil source blocks (= buckets, 1 bucket = 1000 mB): Deposit On average Up to Surface patch ~8 buckets (8 000 mB) 38 buckets Mine-depth lake ~160 buckets (160 000 mB) 448 buckets Deep reservoir ~1 200 buckets (1.2 M mB) 2 786 buckets Vein dome ~3 700 buckets (3.7 M mB) 5 497 buckets The deep reservoir — not just "considerably more" than the mine-depth lake — is the world's main oil source (76 % of all oil in the ground). It is a one-shot resource: drain it and go look for the next one. Exact figures and the method behind them are in

Oil is a thick fluid. It spreads slower than even lava, and shorter than water — its level drops twice as fast, so a spill stays compact. Field Value Spread slower than lava; a spill is a third the length of a water one Source regrowth none — the deposit is finite Moving inside heavily slowed: you wade through oil, you do not swim in it Falling no fall damage while you are in the oil Breath never spent — oil does not drown you Boats boats do not float on oil Harvesting fluid containers only (bucket, capsule, pump); a pickaxe does nothing Inside oil your view suffers badly: a dark, beaded film clings to the screen and nothing is visible past about nine blocks. You can still find your way — swimming to the edge of a pool or riding a shaft down both work — but it is not pleasant. Going under is safe, though. Oil breaks your fall and never takes your breath, so you can ride the shaft of an oil vein all the way down — slowly, but in one piece. Getting back out is on you: oil will not push you up.

Oil burns. It catches from fire — not from lava: a neighbouring fire block turns oil into fire, and the flame walks the pool block by block until the whole spill is gone. You can light a deposit by hand with flint and steel — a click on the oil lights it instantly. Lava on its own does not ignite oil, and that is deliberate. Underground lakes often generate flush against lava lakes, and without this rule any deposit you found would burn away the moment you broke the first block next to it. The spread across a pool obeys the vanilla game rule: with it turned off on a server, a stray fire will not run through your oil. Lighting it by hand always works. Flammability can be switched off entirely with the mod setting (on by default). With it set to oil is completely inert — neither fire nor flint and steel will light it, which is handy if you keep oil next to your production line.

Oil is the start of the rubber chain: oil → raw rubber → vulcanization → rubber. The Polymerizer takes 1000 mB of oil and 400 EU and returns raw rubber; a Vulcanizer combines it with sulfur dust to make rubber. Rubber itself is not consumed by anything yet — its users (insulated cables and MV components) arrive with the next phase, so it is worth stockpiling what you make. The practical takeaway: drain a deposit you find into a tank and mark the spot — it will not come back.

Crude oil is not burned — it is fractioned. The Distillation Column turns 1000 mB of oil into 700 mB of diesel and 200 mB of fuel oil; both fractions will feed the liquid fuel generator (diesel — 12 EU/t, fuel oil — 6 EU/t). The net yield per bucket of oil is about 8 200 EU (9 600 EU out minus the pump and the distillation). Per unit that is weaker than coal (12 800 EU) and lava through a geothermal (15 000 EU) — and that niche is deliberate: lava is the king of specific power, oil wins on the sheer availability of lakes. A lake found next to your base is a power plant that feeds itself: three pumps around the tower close the "lake → column → generator" chain without a single bucket in your hands.
Pump — the main way to drain a deposit. Vacuum Capsule — a portable fluid container. Polymerizer — turns oil into raw rubber. Rubber — what the oil is mined for.

Palladium is the first and so far only material the mod puts in the Nether. The ore sits in small veins in the lower part of the dimension and needs a diamond pickaxe — one tier above uranium, which only asks for iron. Mini-example: look for it at the same depths where you would dig for ancient debris, but keep your eyes open too: unlike debris, palladium shows up on a cave wall about half the time instead of always hiding inside solid rock. There is no vanilla palladium, so the whole line is a mod addition. Processing is exactly the same as for the mod's other metals: the furnace gives an ingot, the Macerator doubles the yield, the Compressor makes a plate. High-tier consumers will come separately — just as with uranium, the ore reaches the world first and its uses follow later. Form How you get it Ore mined in the Nether; pickaxe drops raw, Silk Touch gives the block Raw the pickaxe drop from the ore; smelts into an ingot Dust a block of ore (or the raw) grinds into 2 dust; an ingot or plate grinds into 1 Ingot smelting the raw, the ore, or the dust Plate pressing an ingot, or hammering it by hand

Only in the Nether — there is no palladium in the Overworld or the End. The ore generates in the lower third of the dimension, at roughly the same heights where people hunt ancient debris, and it hides in any of the three host rocks: netherrack, basalt and blackstone. Veins are small, a couple of blocks each. Bring a diamond pickaxe or better: iron and anything below it drops nothing.

It behaves like a vanilla ore: the drop scales with Fortune, and Silk Touch yields the block itself. The rock is tougher than the Overworld ores, but nowhere near ancient debris — palladium breaks in seconds rather than standing a siege. Field Value Tool diamond pickaxe or better (iron and below — no drop) Drop raw ×1 (Fortune multiplies; Silk Touch → the block)

Two routes out of one vein, as with the other metals. Furnace route (no machines): smelt the raw (or the ore) into an ingot — 1 ingot per ore. Macerator route (doubling): grind the ore block (or the raw) into 2 dust, then smelt each dust into an ingot — 2 ingots per ore. An ingot becomes a plate in the Compressor, or by hammering it with the forge hammer. Ingots and plates grind back into 1 dust (no doubling).

Palladium was added to the world before its consumers existed — exactly the order uranium followed: the ore lives in worldgen and accumulates in your chests first, the uses arrive in later phases. For now the chain closes on itself: ore → raw → dust → ingot → plate.

Uranium — the previous step on the mod's rarity ladder, and the same "ore now, consumer later" pattern. Tin — the structural template for an ore material (same processing). Macerator — unlocks the doubling route. Compressor — presses the ingot into a plate. Silver, Nickel — the mod's other rare metals.

Silver is the mod's rare, deep metal, held in reserve for electronics: the material the mid-tier circuits and MV-tier components will be built from. Its ore spawns in stone and in deepslate — deeper and far rarer than tin — and is mined with any stone pickaxe or better. Mini-example: just like tin, a furnace gives you 1 ingot per ore, while the Macerator route grinds a block of ore (or the raw) into 2 dust (2 ingots). But silver is scarce — it pays to macerate every block and raw drop you find rather than furnace it. There is no vanilla silver, so the ingot is a mod item. Silver is not a "bank-it" metal: all of the mod's LV electronics and logistics are already built on it. The electronic circuit takes a silver ingot, and that circuit goes into the generator, macerator, pump and solar panel; silver also goes into the item pipe, the silver chest, the silver gear, the stock display frame, the electric furnace and the sawmill. Silver is rare and deep: small veins sitting lower than tin, roughly in the band where you would also hunt for gold. Expect to find it only while dedicated deep mining.

It behaves like a vanilla ore: it needs a stone pickaxe or better, the drop scales with Fortune, and Silk Touch yields the ore block itself. Field Value Tool stone pickaxe or better (wood/gold drop nothing) Drop raw silver ×1 (Fortune multiplies; Silk Touch → the block)

Two routes out of one vein. Furnace route (no machines): smelt the raw (or the ore) into an ingot — 1 ingot per ore. Macerator route (doubling): grind a block of ore or the raw into 2 dust, then smelt each dust into an ingot — 2 ingots per ore. Re-processing a finished ingot grinds back down to 1 dust (no doubling). The doubling applies to both the whole ore block and the raw — macerate either form.

Silver is a key material already at LV, not a "bank-it" metal. The electronic circuit is built on it (and through it, almost every machine and generator), as are the item pipe, the silver chest and the silver gear. The higher MV tier will later demand silver in still larger amounts, so a spare ingot is never wasted.

Electronic Circuit — silver's main LV consumer. Item Pipe — silver-based logistics. Silver Chest — the 45-slot storage block. Tin — the structural sample for an ore material (same processing). Macerator — unlocks the doubled-yield route. Nickel, Uranium — the mod's other rare metals.

Silver Plating is a decorative building block made from 4 silver plates: a neat 2x2 metal tile with corner bolts. It gives the silver plate a use as cladding. The cycle is reversible (block → 4 plates) with no loss. Mini-example: clad your base walls in silver plating for a clean industrial look, and when you need the plates again — uncraft the block.
An ordinary solid block with a metal feel. Broken by any pickaxe. Field Value Tool any pickaxe Drop itself
4 silver plates → 1 block. 1 block → 4 plates (crafting grid, shapeless) — reversible, no loss.
A decorative block: a use for the silver plate as cladding. It carries no mechanic.
Material forms — the silver plate the block is built from. Tempered Iron Plating — the second decorative plate block. Machine Casing — the "working" block from iron plates.

Steam is the working fluid of the reactor room: the reactor makes it, the steam nozzle vents it. It is the one mod fluid with no world form: there are no steam pools, no steam block, and you cannot scoop it into a bucket. It exists only inside tanks and pipes — wherever the room has pushed it. That gives it its one rule of handling: steam cannot be set aside outside the network. Oil, diesel and fuel oil can be poured on the ground and picked up later; steam is either in a tank or gone. Mini-example: put a portable tank against the room and run the steam along a pipe — a Vacuum Capsule can pull it out of the tank as well, but there is nothing that will pour it back into the world.

What Value World form none — there is no steam block Physics none: steam does not flow, does not drown, does not burn Bucket none Capsule can be filled from a tank, cannot be emptied into the world Storage and carrying tank, fluid pipe, capsule Tag

Arrives together with the reactor room — before it there is no steam in the game and nowhere to get any. Steam has no recipe and cannot have one: it is not an item, it is the contents of a tank. No machine in the mod other than the room accepts steam today — the fluid machines run on oil and its fractions.
Reactor Controller — the brain of the room that makes the steam. Reactor Port — where fluids enter and leave the room. Oil — the opposite case: a fluid that does have a world form.

Sulfur is an early mineable non-metal used to vulcanize rubber. Its ore appears in stone and deepslate, requires a stone pickaxe or better, and drops raw sulfur. The Macerator turns one ore block or one raw sulfur into two dust; a regular furnace gives one dust without doubling. Mini-example: find sulfur ore between Y −32 and 32, mine the raw sulfur, and macerate it. One raw sulfur yields two dust — half the batch for a single Vulcanizer operation. Sulfur has no ingot form: it is a non-metal, and dust is its final technological form here. Form How you get it Ore (stone / deepslate) mine it in the world; a pickaxe drops raw sulfur, Silk Touch gives the block Raw sulfur the normal ore drop Dust macerate ore or raw sulfur ×2; smelt raw sulfur ×1

Sulfur veins appear in the Overworld between Y −32 and 32, with the highest concentration around the middle of the range. Sulfur is rarer than tin but more common than silver: it supports the early rubber chain without becoming either a bottleneck or unwanted surplus.

Sulfur ore behaves like a vanilla ore: it needs the correct pickaxe, Fortune increases the drop, and Silk Touch yields the block itself. Field Value Tool stone pickaxe or better Drop ×1; Fortune multiplies, Silk Touch → block Hardness 3.0 in stone, 4.5 in deepslate

Macerator: sulfur ore, deepslate sulfur ore, or raw sulfur → 2 sulfur dust for 300 EU. Furnace: raw sulfur → 1 sulfur dust in the standard 200 ticks, with 0.7 XP. Vulcanizer: four sulfur dust are consumed with one raw rubber; heat changes the rubber output, not sulfur consumption. The Distillation Column does not produce sulfur. Ore is the only primary source, and is deliberately excluded from Incubator duplication recipes.

Sulfur is available before MV and breaks the circular gate where rubber would be required to reach the machine that produces sulfur. A furnace provides a machine-free route, but only the Macerator doubles the mined resource. Sulfur is the most expensive input of the rubber chain, and Vulcanizer heat is what saves it: a typical run of 16 insulated cables costs 8 rubber, which is 32, 16, or 12 dust at ×1, ×2, or ×3 output — nearly three hours of mining between a campfire and an Electric Heater.
Rubber — the material produced by vulcanization. Macerator — doubles sulfur dust output. Oil — the primary source of raw rubber through the Polymerizer.

The Tempered Iron Block is a storage block: 9 tempered-iron ingots compressed into a single full block. It exists to save chest space — instead of 9 stacks of ingots, you keep one stack of blocks. Mini-example: short on chest room? Craft a stack of ingots into blocks, and when you need the ingots back, uncraft the block — the cycle is strictly lossless, just like the vanilla iron or gold block. On its own it produces no energy and does nothing — it is simply a compact form of the metal and a decorative building block. Form How you get it Block (full cube) crafting 9 ingots → 1 block; uncrafting 1 block → 9 ingots
An ordinary solid block with the same feel as the vanilla iron block. Any pickaxe breaks it. Field Value Tool any pickaxe Drop itself (the block drops itself)

No processing recipes — just two workbench recipes that move metal in and out of the block form. The cycle is strictly reversible and lossless. 9 ingots → 1 block (workbench, 3×3 grid of ingots). 1 block → 9 ingots (workbench, shapeless — put the block in to get the 9 ingots back). The source ingot is tempered iron.
For now the block is a compact storage form and a decorative building block. Future uses (beacon compatibility, an MV casing from a tempered block, and so on) are planned but not yet in the game.
Tempered Iron — the ingot the block is assembled from. Tempered Iron tools — the main consumer of the ingots. Tin, Silver, Nickel, Uranium — the mod's other materials.

Tempered Iron Plating is a decorative building block made from 4 tempered-iron plates: a "tech panel" with a screen and lines. It gives the tempered-iron plate a use as high-tech cladding. The cycle is reversible (block → 4 plates) with no loss. Mini-example: dress up a control room or reactor hall with the tech panel for a futuristic look; uncraft the block back into plates whenever you need them.
An ordinary solid block with a metal feel. Broken by any pickaxe. Field Value Tool any pickaxe Drop itself
4 tempered-iron plates → 1 block. 1 block → 4 plates (crafting grid, shapeless) — reversible, no loss.
A decorative block: a use for the tempered-iron plate as cladding. It carries no mechanic.
Material forms — the tempered-iron plate the block is built from. Silver Plating — the second decorative plate block. Machine Casing — the "working" block from iron plates.

Tin is the mod's earliest metal and the backbone of its LV tier: the wires and circuits your first machines run on. Its ore spawns in stone and in deepslate at middling depths, and is mined with any stone pickaxe or better. Mini-example: one vein, two routes. Smelt the ore in a furnace and you get 1 ingot. Run the same ore block (or the raw drop) through a Macerator first and you get 2 dust — which smelt into 2 ingots. The macerator route is twice the yield per ore. There is no vanilla tin, so the ingot is a mod item. Form How you get it Ore (stone / deepslate) mined in the world; pickaxe drops raw, Silk Touch gives the block Raw the pickaxe drop from the ore; smelts into an ingot Dust a block of ore or the raw grinds into 2 dust; a finished ingot grinds into 1 Ingot smelting the raw, the ore, or the dust
Tin is the most common of the mod's metals, generating across middling depths (roughly the same band as copper). You will run into it routinely while early-game caving.

It behaves like a vanilla ore: it needs a stone pickaxe or better, the drop scales with Fortune, and Silk Touch yields the ore block itself. Field Value Tool stone pickaxe or better (wood/gold drop nothing) Drop raw tin ×1 (Fortune multiplies; Silk Touch → the block)

Two routes out of one vein. Furnace route (no machines): smelt the raw (or the ore) into an ingot — 1 ingot per ore. Macerator route (doubling): grind a block of ore or the raw into 2 dust, then smelt each dust into an ingot — 2 ingots per ore. Re-processing a finished ingot grinds back down to 1 dust (no doubling). The doubling applies to both the whole ore block and the raw — macerate either form.

Tin is the gateway to LV machinery: tin and copper wire are assembled into the Electronic Circuit, and every LV machine needs at least one. That makes tin the early-crafting bottleneck — keep a steady supply flowing into your first Macerator and furnace.

Electronic Circuit — what tin wire builds into. Canning Machine — tin's first mass consumer: a can is spent for good, so every meal eats metal again. Macerator — unlocks the doubled-yield route. Silver, Nickel, Uranium — the mod's other metals.

Uranium is the mod's rarest metal, reserved for the nuclear track (RTG, reactor, enrichment). Its ore spawns in tiny veins at the very bottom of the world, and unlike the other ores it needs an iron pickaxe or better — wood, gold and stone drop nothing. Mini-example: same two processing routes as tin — furnace for 1 ingot per ore, Macerator for 2. But uranium is roughly seven times rarer than diamond, so each block and each raw drop matters; macerate, don't furnace. There is no vanilla uranium, so the ingot is a mod item. Uranium is not sitting idle: its dust goes into the enriched uranium torch, the ingot is part of the teleporter's recipe, and the incubator spends the ingot as an irradiation charge during mutations (one ingot covers three attempts, leaving behind depleted uranium). There is a second processing route as well — through the Thermal Centrifuge. Instead of smelting the dust into an ingot you can split it in two: dust → 2 concentrate → (Compressor, two into one) → 1 enriched uranium. Together with the macerator's doubling that gives two enriched uranium from a single ore block instead of one ingot from a plain smelt — but it takes a line with a heater and a redstone signal. Form How you get it Ore (stone / deepslate) mined in the world; pickaxe drops raw, Silk Touch gives the block Raw the pickaxe drop from the ore; smelts into an ingot Dust a block of ore (or the raw) grinds into 2 dust; an ingot grinds into 1 Ingot smelting the raw, the ore, or the dust Concentrate the dust splits in two in the Thermal Centrifuge Enriched uranium (U-235) two concentrate pressed into one in the Compressor
