Uranium sits at the very bottom of the world, in tiny veins, about seven times rarer than diamond. Bring an iron pickaxe (or better) — anything weaker drops nothing.

Unlike the mod's other ores, uranium needs an iron pickaxe or better — wood, gold and stone pickaxes drop nothing. Otherwise it behaves like a vanilla ore: the drop scales with Fortune, and Silk Touch yields the ore block itself. Field Value Tool iron pickaxe or better (wood/gold/stone drop nothing) Drop raw uranium ×1 (Fortune multiplies; Silk Touch → the block)

Two routes out of one vein. Furnace route (no machines): smelt the raw (or the ore) into an ingot — 1 ingot per ore. Macerator route (doubling): grind a block of ore (or the raw) into 2 dust, then smelt each dust into an ingot — 2 ingots per ore. Re-processing a finished ingot grinds back down to 1 dust (no doubling). The doubling only applies to the whole ore block (or raw).

Uranium is reserved for the nuclear track — the reactor and the RTG — which arrives in later phases. But even now it has consumers: the dust goes into the Enriched Uranium Torch, the ingot is part of the Teleporter recipe, and the Incubator spends the ingot as an irradiation charge during mutations (one ingot — three attempts, leaving depleted uranium). A spare ingot can also be sold to the industrialist villager for emeralds. The first step of the nuclear track is already done: the Thermal Centrifuge yields enriched uranium (U-235) — the material that makes a heater line worth building. Since it has a consumer: it goes into a fuel rod, and the rod into a reactor column.

Enriched Uranium Torch — a use for uranium dust. Teleporter — its recipe takes a uranium ingot. Incubator — spends the ingot as an irradiation charge. Tin — the structural sample for an ore material (same processing). Macerator — unlocks the doubled-yield route. Silver, Nickel — the mod's other rare metals.

The Fuel Rod Cladding is a fuel rod with no uranium in it: an iron sleeve on a shielding base, everything the rod is except the fuel. It arrives by two routes — crafted at a workbench, or handed back by a reactor column once the rod has given up its 144,000 EU — and both routes end in the same recipe: one cladding plus one enriched uranium is a fuelled rod again. It is the key item of stage 4 of the epic. Before it, a burnt-out rod simply vanished, so every refuelling cost exactly what the first one did: three iron ingots, four nuggets and a shielding plate — a third of a palladium ingot per rod, forever. Palladium is mined in the Nether alone, and a reactor running at the HV ceiling eats 256 rods an hour. The cladding turns that stream into a closed loop: casings are crafted once, and after that only the uranium is bought.

Route What happens 3x3 craft , x1 at a time — the sleeve without its fuel A burnt-out rod in a column the moment a uranium rod runs out of durability, the column replaces it with an empty one where it stands Right-click empty-handed on a column claddings are handed back first, ahead of the fuelled ones Breaking the column everything racked drops, claddings included The rack does not throw the casing away by itself: a spent rod stays where it stood and is visible from outside — dark, against the lit fuelled ones. A column that has worked itself out looks worked out from across the floor, and that same look tells the player there is something in there to collect.

The recipe is shapeless: two items in any cells of the grid. That is deliberately the cheapest recipe in the nuclear branch to perform — refuelling a reactor happens dozens of rods at a time, and laying out a 3x3 for each one would be a punishment for scale.

c.h: It goes back into a column
c.t: A cladding can be put back into a reactor column, and that is not a pointless action: it is how casings are stored where they will be needed. The column keeps two counts: — how many rods are standing in it at all — and — how many of those carry uranium. The reactor counts only the second: an empty casing produces no EU, no heat, and takes no part in adjacency.

c.h: The price of a refill against a rod from scratch
c.t: Item From scratch Refill Enriched uranium 1 (half a uranium ore) 1 (half a uranium ore) Iron 3 ingots + 4 nuggets (~3.4 ingots) — Shielding plate 1 (1/3 palladium ingot + 1 tempered iron) — Processing EU ~1,610 ~1,210 Palladium 1/3 ingot 0 A reactor at the HV ceiling burns 256 rods an hour (see The difference between the columns reads like this: without casings coming back — 256 shielding plates an hour, which is roughly 85 palladium ingots an hour, which is several trips to the Nether an hour; with them — zero palladium after the first batch; however many casings you crafted are however many keep circulating. How many casings have to be in circulation not by power but by room size: one per slot. A 3x3 layer of nine columns needs 36; a 3x3x3 room packed full needs 108. After that they return by themselves.

Craft — x1 at a time. This is exactly the old uranium-rod recipe with an empty middle: sleeve, rivets and shielding base everything but the uranium pellet. That is why it reads by itself: the middle is filled by the second, shapeless recipe. Refill — shapeless, cladding + enriched uranium -> fuel rod.

Tier: none (the item carries no energy). Needs: a shielding plate — that is palladium, and therefore the Nether. It needs no uranium: a stock of casings can be made long before the first uranium vein. Unlocks: refuelling the reactor without palladium. The first batch of casings is the only palladium the fuel cycle will ever take.

Fuel Rod — what one enriched uranium turns it into. Reactor Column — what hands it back, and where it goes again. Reactor Controller — what wears rods down, and how fast. Uranium — the chain from ore to enriched uranium. Reactor Casing — where the shielding plate in the recipe comes from.

The Reactor Column is what the reactor is loaded with, and what cools it. A transparent rack for four rods stands inside a reactor room, is filled by right-clicking with a fuel rod in hand, and is emptied with an empty one. It has no menu at all. Since stage 3 it also has two tanks — water and steam. Water arrives by pipe, boils and carries heat away; steam leaves by pipe. The water level, like the rod count, is visible from outside, on the model itself. This is the central decision of stage 2 of the epic: the fuel does not sit in a slot, it stands in the room. An empty rack and a full one are told apart from across the floor, "top up the reactor" is an action in the world rather than in a window, and a half-spent core is visible at a glance instead of as a number in a GUI.

c.h: It stores items, not a counter
c.t: Before stage 4 the rack held a number of rods and one shared "how much is left in the burning one". Exactly two things followed, and a player met both in the first hour: a started rod was destroyed when pulled out (there was nowhere to write down what was left of it), and a burnt-out one vanished — so every refuelling cost a fresh shielding plate, and therefore palladium. Now the rack holds four items. Both consequences went away with their cause: Before Now A half-burnt rod was lost comes back with its durability and carries on from the same point A burnt-out rod vanished becomes a fuel rod cladding and stays standing in the rack One shared burn counter every rod carries its own durability (see the rod spec)

Action What happens Right-click with a rod in hand the rod goes into the first free slot, metal sound; in creative the item is not consumed Right-click with a cladding in hand the same: a casing can be parked in the rack for later Right-click on a full rack nothing is taken — the item stays in hand Right-click empty-handed the rack hands one rod back, spent casings first Right-click with any other item falls into the same branch as an empty hand: a rod is taken out anyway Breaking the block everything racked drops, whole and half-burnt alike The fifth row is not a slip but a forced decision: in 26.2 an from does not fall through to, so "take a rod out with a pickaxe in hand" would otherwise silently do nothing. It returns .

That order is the whole interaction. A player walks up to a worked-out column for the casings, to refill them, and least of all wants to first fish back out the live rods they put in ten minutes ago. The order is fixed: empties first, and only once there are none left, the fuelled ones, top down. The drop on removal is handled by rather than a player-only break hook: a creeper opening the rack is exactly when losing the contents would hurt most.

c.h: Wear is applied to every fuelled rod at once
c.t: The controller charges EU against the column, and the column converts them into durability points — on all fuelled rods simultaneously, one point per round. While the banked draw is short of a whole round it is carried to the next tick; as soon as it is enough, every fuelled rod takes +1 damage. A rod that reaches 1000 is replaced by an empty one right there in its slot. It works that way because "one at a time" was simply untrue: four rods sit in the same neutron flux and all four produce power, yet only one of them aged. The player saw four working rods and one draining bar. The arithmetic did not drift for it: the column still spends exactly one rod's worth of energy per rod, it just takes it out of all of them at once. The practical consequence: a column of four rods works itself out all at once. For twenty minutes (in a lone rack) all four are full, then all four become casings together. A rack loaded piecemeal evens out too: a fresh rod outlives its half-spent neighbours, because the round is charged against all of them and the ones that drop out stop paying. Fuel is spent only when the energy is wanted. If the controller's buffer is full and nothing is drawing, the racks do not wear at all — the same principle by which the charge pad spends EU per transfer rather than per tick.

c.h: The fill level is visible from outside
c.t: The blockstate carries two counters, not one: Property What it means How it is drawn = 0…4 how many rods stand in it at all, casings included occupied slots = 0…4 how many of those carry uranium lit rods; the rest are dark casings Two properties are needed not because it looks nicer. With a single counter that counted fuel alone, a worked-out column reported zero — and the casings in it became not only invisible but unreachable: the interaction code read the blockstate to decide whether there was anything to take out. Such a rack could be neither emptied nor refilled, only broken. The block entity counts its own contents and brings the blockstate into line on every change (), so the model cannot disagree with what is inside.

Two extra boolean states — and — turn on when another rack stands directly above or below. Joined racks lose the cap and the base plate between them and the seam is filled by a connector piece, so a column of three assemblies reads as one tall rack rather than as three boxes stacked on each other. The same trick a cable or a pipe uses in this mod. The join is not purely cosmetic: fluids travel along it (see "A stack is one vessel"). It does not affect output or heat — adjacency does (see Balance), and the controller counts that on all three axes regardless of how the assembly looks. The outline follows the model: a lone rack is 12x14x12, one joined above is 12x16x12. Otherwise the selection box of a stacked assembly would hang two pixels below the geometry the player can see. The states are recomputed in rather than: that is the vanilla hook for exactly this, and it runs on world edits and structure placement too.

Since stage 3 the column has two tanks, and together they are half of the reactor's cooling loop. Tank Capacity What it takes What it gives outward Water 4000 mB (4 buckets) water only nothing Steam 4000 mB nothing steam The tanks are mirrored on purpose. Water can only be poured in: reactor coolant is not a reserve to borrow from. Allow it to be pumped out and a player would park a pump on a hot core and pull the coolant back, which is both free steam and a meltdown on demand. Steam, conversely, can only be taken: nothing can push it into a column from outside.

c.h: The face rule: steam up only, water everywhere else
c.t: Face What is published there Top the steam tank The other five the water tank That way one pipe is always unambiguous: one face, one fluid, one direction. And the rule survives stacking, which "steam leaves through the top of every column" would not: the lower columns of a stack have no free top face at all. A pipe collecting steam must stand above the column in extract mode; a pipe supplying water goes on any other side, in insert mode.

c.h: A stack is one vessel; the column next to it is another
c.t: The port a pipe talks to reports for the whole vertical stack, not for one block: total amount, total capacity, filled from the bottom up, steam drawn from the top down. Every tick the controller also re-settles the stack's contents — water sinks, steam rises. Without this a two-block column simply would not fill: water sinks into the bottom block, that block reaches capacity first, and a pipe asking "is there room?" got "no" from a vessel that was half empty, and stopped. ⚠️ Columns standing side by side are separate vessels. The controller used to even the tanks out across the whole room, and one pipe watered the entire hall. That was convenient and untrue: coolant appearing inside a rack nothing is plumbed to reads as a bug however useful it is. Plumb the columns you want cooled; the easiest way is to build them in stacks and pipe into one block of each.

The column does not boil water by itself — the controller does, and only once the reactor has passed the coolant loop's target (60 % of the scale). Below that the shell sheds all of its heat on its own and the loop spends nothing: water is a safety system, not a radiator. The target sits deliberately below the amber band (= 70 %), so a healthy water-cooled reactor reads green and amber means "something is wrong" again. One millibucket of water carries = 2 units of heat away and turns into 1 mB of steam — one to one by volume. Boiling runs into two limits at once: how much water the column holds, and how much room is left in it for steam. A loop choked with steam therefore stops cooling as surely as a dry water tank — the water is there, the gauge is full, and the temperature climbs. That is not a bug; it is the one and only reason the exhaust (steam nozzle) is mandatory.

c.h: The water level is visible from outside
c.t: The blockstate carries = 0…4 — quarters of the tank, a separate part of the multipart model. The rounding rule is special: anything above zero shows at least one quarter. A column with a mouthful of water left must not look the same as a dry one — the reactions those two states call for are completely different.

The assembly has a block entity, but no tick of its own. The reactor is one machine, not a floor covered in machines: the controller drives every assembly in its room from a single tick, so a hall with thirty racks costs the server what one block entity costs, not thirty. The split of duties: the rack is state and the rules for changing it (what stands in the slots, how much is left in the rods, what to hand back when broken); the controller is the schedule. One practical consequence worth knowing: the controller sweeps the room not every tick but once every = 40 ticks (2 s). A rod inserted by hand enters the calculation on the next sweep — up to two seconds of delay, unnoticeable next to a rod that burns for minutes. An empty rack no longer drops out of the calculation. All columns go into the controller's list, not just the loaded ones: a column is part of the machine because it stands in the room, not because somebody has fuelled it yet. The old fuel filter left a discharged rack without cooling and out of the settling pass, which is why water pumped into the bottom of a stack never rose past the first loaded column. Adjacency is still counted by fuel: two empty racks side by side accelerate nothing.

Step What the controller does Every 2 s sweeps the room interior, collects all columns, sums the fuelled rods, counts adjacency pairs Every producing tick splits the output between columns in proportion to the fuelled rods in each Inside a column the share is converted into durability points and charged against all fuelled rods at once Every tick re-settles the fluids inside each vertical stack The remainder of the division goes to the first column with fuel rather than being dropped: a room whose rod count does not divide the output evenly still pays for every EU it made.

Field Value Shape a rack 12x14x12 (lone), 12x16x12 (joined above) — not a full cube Occlusion — the casing is transparent and the rods inside have to be drawn Hardness 3.0 Blast resistance 6.0 Tool pickaxe Sound metal Blockstates = 0…4, = 0…4, = 0…4, , BlockEntity yes, with no tick of its own NBT the rack contents as items, (draw not yet charged), , (tank contents, mB) Rod durability lives on the items themselves, so the rack's NBT has no field for it — and there can be no disagreement between "how much is left" and "what is standing there". Only amounts are saved from the tanks: each tank holds exactly one fluid by construction, and a "which one" field could only ever disagree with the code. The block's hardness is deliberately below the shell's (5.0 / 30.0): the assembly lives inside a protected room and needs no armour of its own — a reactor has to be opened through a wall anyway.

Craft — x2 at a time. The recipe describes the item: glass walls to see the charge through, an iron frame, and a shielding plate at the core. Two per craft, because racks are needed by the dozen and a one-at-a-time recipe would turn loading a hall into workbench drudgery.

Tier: none (the block has no energy at all). Needs: reactor glass and a shielding plate — that is palladium, and therefore the Nether. Unlocks: the reactor controller producing power. Without a single loaded assembly, a sealed room stays a diagnostic device.

Fuel Rod — what goes into it. Fuel Rod Cladding — what it hands back. Reactor Controller — what burns it and counts its adjacency. Reactor Port — how water gets into the room and steam gets out. Steam Nozzle — where the steam goes, and why boiling stalls without it. Steam — what appears in the column's upper tank. Reactor Glass — half the recipe and the same "see what is inside" idea. Reactor Casing — the walls the rack stands inside.

The Reactor Button is the smallest block in the set and the only one without which the room becomes a trap. The airlock door opens on a redstone pulse alone: outside, anything can send one; inside, there is nothing to send it with — a sealed room by design has neither openings nor wires leading out. So the source of the pulse has to stand inside, and it has to be made of the same material as the walls. The button is a real vanilla , not a look-alike: the press, the pressed shape, the redstone pulse and the auto-release are exactly those of any button in the game. Only the material, the sound family and the press duration are ours. The player does not have to relearn how a button works.

c.h: How it differs from a vanilla button
c.t: Property Reactor Button Vanilla stone Material shielding alloy stone Pressed by hand yes yes Pressed by an arrow no yes Triggered by a wind charge no no Press duration = 20 ticks (1 s) 20 ticks Place / break sound metal stone Click sound the stone button's click (from ) the same was chosen because the button is metal, and it happens to carry exactly the behaviour wanted here: a hand can press it, an arrow cannot. For a button that governs a seal the second half matters more than it sounds — a stray skeleton arrow opening the airlock of a reactor hall is not a funny detail but a hole at the one narrow point of the whole build. The press duration matches the vanilla stone button and is half of (40 ticks). That is not a coincidence: the door catches a rising edge rather than a held signal, so the pulse only has to be long enough to arrive reliably, even when the button is wired through a run of redstone dust.

Field Value Part of the shell no Occupies a shell cell no — it hangs on the face of a block that is already there If placed where a shell block belongs that cell becomes a breach: the scanner knows six shell blocks, and a button is not one of them What it attaches to wall, floor or ceiling ( / /), like a vanilla one That is the key distinction of the whole set: six blocks make up the shell, and the button hangs on it. Inside the room it goes on the casing next to the doorway; outside, wherever is convenient. It spends no cell, so the same wall can be both sealed and fitted with a button. There is no rule that a button must be present, and none is planned. A room without one forms — but a player can already walk in, shut the door behind them and have no way to open it, and that is entirely their own decision.

Field Value Role none Buffer (EU) 0 Max input / output (EU/tick) n/a The button runs on redstone, like the door it controls. EU here would be an unnecessary dependency: the control that opens the exit must not depend on whether the room has power.

Field Value Shape the vanilla button overlay on a block face; it sinks in when pressed Collision none — you walk through it exactly as through a vanilla one Hardness 0.5 Blast resistance 0.5 Tool none required (it drops however it is broken) Sound metal Piston reaction destroyed Blockstates ,, blockstate none — the button is not shell, and the flag sweep does not touch it Hardness and blast resistance are deliberately not the shell's 5.0 / 30.0 even though the material is the same. The button must not outlive the explosion that took the wall: a surviving button on the site of a blown-out wall is debris pretending to be a working control. Let it go with whatever it was attached to. The button has no flag — exactly like vanilla's buttons. That is not an oversight: a button's occlusion shape is its own little overlay, it covers nobody's face, and it has no collision at all, so it does not affect light either.

Craft — shapeless, ×2 at a time. The recipe is trivial on purpose. The button is a convenience item, not a progression milestone, and making the player assemble it out of rare parts would put an obstacle where an obstacle is pointless: without one they cannot use the room they have already built. The stone button in the recipe is not filler but a way of not reinventing a mechanic: the player takes the button they already know and dresses it in shielding alloy.
Tier: none. Requires: one shielding plate (the chain is described under casing) and a stone button. Unlocks: the ability to leave a closed room — that is, the ability to use it at all.

Reactor Airlock Door — what the button exists for; the "pulse, not a held signal" contract is described there. Reactor Casing — the material chain and the full composition of the shell. Reactor Controller — the one that tells a shell block from a foreign one; to it, the button is a foreign block. Thermal Centrifuge — the mod's other redstone-controlled block, with the opposite contract: there the signal must be held.

Reactor Casing is the wall, floor and ceiling of a reactor room. It is neither a decorative block nor "reinforced stone": a Nuclear Reactor room is not a single block with a grid of slots but a building you actually put up, and the casing is what you put it up out of. Plain stone, an iron block and vanilla glass all read to the room scanner exactly as air does — a hole.

c.h: What the shell is made of
c.t: The shell is the six faces of an axis-aligned box. Every one of its cells must be one of seven blocks; any other block, and any air, is a breach: Block Role in the shell How many Reactor Casing wall / floor / ceiling everything else Reactor Lamp light from the inside; to the scanner, plain casing any number, zero included Reactor Glass a window that is still wall at most (30 %) of the shell Airlock Door the only way in at least one Reactor Inlet where a pipe crosses the wall: water in, steam out any number, zero included Reactor Outlet the socket a cable plugs into; casing as far as the scan is concerned any number, zero included Controller the room's brain exactly one, vertical wall only The casing is the only one of the seven with no conditions of its own: it fits any cell of any face, including the edges and corners that are off limits to the door and the controller. The lamp inherits exactly those properties — the scanner classifies it as casing — and therefore does not count against the glass cap: lighting a room is not the same as spending its window budget. The reactor button stands apart: it is not part of the shell and occupies no cell — it hangs on a wall from the inside and exists only to send a pulse to the door. Putting it where a shell block belongs does not work; the scanner reads that cell as a breach.

The limits are on the interior — what the player walks into, not the footprint of the build: Field Value Minimum (interior) 3×3×3, shell 5×5×5 = 98 blocks Maximum (interior) 12×12×12, shell 14×14×14 = 1016 blocks Shape axis-aligned box only L-shapes, stepped rooms and domes are unsupported — not because they are "forbidden", but because wherever the wall has to run straight there is a block that is not shell, and the scanner honestly calls that a breach and names its coordinates. Growing a room means taking it apart and laying a bigger one. There is no upgrade in place — and no loss either: every shell block drops itself when mined with a pickaxe. They are the player's property, not consumable structure segments like the sections of the Distillation Column.

Casing, glass, reactor inlet, lamp, door and controller all carry a blockstate, and the first four carry an one as well. While the room is unfinished they are drawn with a bright bezel along the edge, so every individual block is visible. The moment the controller accepts the shell, it repaints all of it, and the wall starts reading as one surface rather than a stack of crates. Cell of a formed shell How it looks A face (one coordinate outside the box) yes no bezel-less — a continuous panel An edge or corner (two or three outside) yes yes the bezel stays Any cell of an unformed shell no no bezel on every block Edges keeping their bezel are not an exception but the other half of the idea. A 14×14 wall without a single seam turns into a featureless slab; the bezel along the edges draws the outline of the build, and the room reads as one object with defined corners rather than as a blur. What How it is done Who sets the flags the controller alone; the block never touches them What gets rewritten only the cells whose value actually changed Update flag 2 — the properties are cosmetic, no neighbour needs waking Which box is cleared the one the controller remembered, not the one the current scan measured (see below) Shared faces culled between blocks of the same kind, so a large window draws no interior grid The vanilla renderer has no connected textures, so the seam is removed in the art itself: every shell block has three texture variants — unformed, formed face, formed edge. The bezel is what draws the grid, so dropping it on the faces and keeping it on the edges is what glues the wall together and outlines it. Why the box is remembered. A failed scan measures nothing, so a sweep driven by the current scan result can only ever switch the flag ON: punch a hole in a finished room and it stays seamless and lit. That is exactly what the first play session found. The controller keeps the last box it accepted (and writes it to NBT so it survives a chunk unload) and, when a scan fails, clears precisely that box. The point is wider than cosmetics: is also an outdoor indicator. A finished room is visible from across the base without opening a screen, and on the same flag the lamp turns the light on inside. The door carries the flag too (the controller writes it into every shell cell) but its model does not change with it, and neither the door nor the controller has at all the seamless effect covers four blocks: casing, glass, reactor inlet and lamp.

Field Value Role none Buffer (EU) 0 Max input / output (EU/tick) n/a The casing neither carries nor stores energy. A cable that runs into the wall stops there; getting power inside is what the Reactor Inlet is for.

A full cube and an occluder: a wall hundreds of blocks wide must not make the client draw its inner faces. Field Value Shape full cube 16³ (occluder) Hardness 5.0 Blast resistance 30.0 Tool pickaxe (required for drops) Sound metal Blockstates , — both cosmetic, see "The seamless look" The blast resistance of 30.0 is deliberately far above the machine family's 6.0. The room is the thing standing between a meltdown and the rest of the world; if a creeper under the wall could open the shell, the whole sealing mechanic would rest on luck.

Craft — ×8 at a time. One block costs an eighth of that grid: a quarter of a shielding plate, three quarters of a tempered iron plate and an eighth of a machine casing. It was not always so: the first version of the recipe asked for 4 shielding plates per 4 blocks — a whole plate per block. The first play session showed that nobody survives to a room worth having at that rate: the smallest box ate some 44 palladium ingots (it is 19 now), almost all of it on blank wall that does nothing in play. The scarce palladium has been moved to where it reads as the substance of the build (door, controller, reactor inlet), and the mass of the wall is paid for in cheap tempered iron.

The casing is expensive not in itself but through an alloy the mod did not have before: . There is no way back to dust, as with every alloy in the mod. The chain needs no new machine at all: the Macerator, the Alloy Smelter, the Compressor and the Forge Hammer have all been here for a long time. What the reactor demands is not equipment but a trip to the Nether.

Tier: none (a passive block). Requires: palladium, tempered iron, a machine casing. Unlocks: the reactor room itself — the Controller has nothing to scan until there is something to build the shell from. A side effect that matters: before palladium was mined "for later", with not a single consumer. The shielding alloy is its first, and immediately its main one.

Nuclear Reactor — the room as a whole and how it works. Reactor Glass — the window and its 30 % cap on the shell. Reactor Lamp — the same casing, but it glows inwards. Airlock Door — a mandatory part of the shell. Reactor Button — not part of the shell, but there is no way out without it. Reactor Inlet — how pipes and cable cross the wall. Palladium — the material the Nether trip is for.

The Reactor Controller is the only intelligent block in the shell and the room's only machine. While the room is being built it finds the shell around itself, checks it and reports what is wrong and where. Once the shell is closed it becomes the reactor: it collects the fuel assemblies, works out output and heat, boils the coolant, re-settles the fluids inside every stack of columns, wears the rods down and pushes EU out. The controller goes in place of one casing block in a vertical wall, facing outwards: the front face carries the screen the player reads, and the redstone goes to the same side. The cable goes on any other face. A room with two controllers does not form — a room has exactly one brain. What the reactor does not have yet. The heat gauge is computed and shown, but 100% has no consequences: the reactor neither melts down nor explodes. There is no radiation around a running core either. Both are separate work; for now overheating only costs you the output.

Requirement Why In a vertical wall (not the floor, not the ceiling) the front face is a panel to be read, and the wire arrives there in stage 2; in a ceiling nobody sees it Not in an edge or a corner of the shell a cell on an edge has no interior side to look into Facing outwards the room's interior lies behind the controller; turn it around and you get "Controller not in a wall" Exactly one per room a second controller in the same shell yields "Second controller" together with its position All four conditions are checked by the same scan and produce the same class of answer — a status plus a place. There is no separate "setup mode": place it, read the screen, fix the thing.

The scanner works in two passes, and that is not an implementation detail but the reason its messages are useful. Six rays from the cell in front of the controller — along ±X, ±Y, ±Z, to the first shell block. A ray that finds nothing means "the room is unbounded in this direction" — either it is too large, or there is a hole in the wall you could fly through. The ray reports where it gave up, so the player at least knows which way to look. A walk of the whole perimeter implied by those six hits. This is the pass that finds a single missing cell anywhere in a 14³ shell and names its coordinates. The same walk counts controllers, remembers door cells and tallies the glass share — one pass answers all four questions. A ray reaches + 1 steps, not exactly the limit. The extra step is not slack but the condition under which "too large" can exist as a status at all: a ray capped at exactly the limit can never see the far wall of a room that is one block too wide, so every oversized room would report "unbounded". With the extra step, "you built it one block too wide" and "there is no wall there" stay different answers. Why not a plain flood fill: a flood fill cannot tell "this room is too large" from "this room leaks" — both simply run until the cap. Two passes give two different answers to two different questions. The order of the checks is a usability decision as well, not a coding one: controller placement (is there an open cell in front of its face); bounds — the six rays; size (, then ); seal — the first non-shell cell of the walk (, the walk stops there); the controller itself found as a wall cell rather than an edge one; a second controller; a door, then a doorway; the glass share. Each answer is actionable on its own, and the player fixes one thing at a time instead of being handed a list. The glass cap comes last on purpose: it is the one "soft" problem — a room that hits it is sealed and correctly built, it simply does not count as containment — and reporting it ahead of an actual hole would be the wrong order of priorities. When it re-scans Condition Periodically every (default 40 ticks = 2 s) On a neighbour change at once: a wall broken nearby, a port placed, a door blown up The periodic pass is mandatory: only fires for the six blocks touching the controller, and a room can be 14 blocks across. A block mined on the far wall is nobody's neighbour here, and without its own timer the controller would never notice. For the same reason the controller never goes to sleep.

Ten states. Nine of them are a job to be done; the tenth is "done". State Meaning Shows a place Shows a size sealed, within the size limits, with a way in — yes the controller is in the floor or ceiling, in an edge, buried, or turned the wrong way yes — a ray ran past the limit without finding a wall — — interior below along some axis — yes interior above along some axis — yes a perimeter cell is not a shell block yes — the shell is sealed but has no door — — there is a door but no doorway (no two door cells stacked at floor level) — — another controller stands in the same shell yes — glass exceeds (30 %) of the shell's cells yes — is appended to the end of the enum rather than slotted in next to where it belongs by meaning, and that is not sloppiness: the order of the constants is the wire format — what travels to the screen is an ordinal. Inserting in the middle would rename every state after it. The position reports is not a "guilty" cell — the share is guilty, not any one block but the first glass cell in perimeter-walk order. It is there so the smoke leads the player to the glazed part of the shell: a 14×14 room is large, and "too much glass" without a direction is a message with no action attached.

A finished room is one machine, and the controller executes its whole tick. The fuel assemblies have no tick of their own at all: a hall with thirty racks costs the server what one block entity costs.

On the same sweep as the shell check (once every = 40 ticks), the controller walks the room interior and records every reactor column — loaded and empty alike. The same pass sums the rods that carry uranium and counts the adjacency pairs. Empty columns go into the list deliberately. Filtering on fuel looked harmless and was not: an empty rack fell out of the water loop and out of the stack settling pass, which is why water pumped into the bottom of a column never rose past the first loaded assembly. A column is part of the machine because it stands in the room, not because somebody has fuelled it yet. Adjacency, on the other hand, is counted by fuel: two empty racks side by side accelerate nothing, or the bonus would be paid for scaffolding. Sweeping a 12³ interior is 1728 block reads: absurd sixty times a second, cheap once every two seconds. The price is latency: a rod inserted by hand enters the calculation on the next sweep, so no later than two seconds. Next to a rod that burns for minutes, that is invisible. Adjacency pairs are counted over , , — each pair exactly once — but both racks of the pair get the bonus, hence the x2 in the output formula.

Quantity How it is worked out Potential (at 100 %) , where Output x depth‰ / 1000`, but never more than the room left in the buffer Heat , where full heat , Fuel spent exactly EU a tick, split between the columns in proportion to their rods Heat scale , clamped to 0…10,000 (the full gauge) The ceiling is applied before the throttle, not after. The potential is clamped to 512 EU/t first, and only then scaled by depth. The other order looked equivalent and was not: on any core whose potential had already cleared 512, every stop of the slider produced the same 512 EU/t — the control did precisely nothing at the exact scale it was built for. Fuel is counted in EU, not in time. The controller charges the columns with exactly the energy it produced, and a column converts that into durability points on its rods (144 EU per point; the details are in the rod spec). Hence the model's central property: a rod is worth 144,000 EU everywhere, and no layout makes uranium cheaper. It was not always so. Before stage 4 fuel was driven by an "effective depth" — the fraction of its potential the room actually delivered — and on a large room that fraction truncated to its floor of 1 ‰. Two absurdities followed from the same line: a rod lasted about a thousand real days, and heat became and grew without bound as the room grew (a 12x12x12 hall came out at roughly 105,000 heat a tick — more coolant than the shell has surface to admit). Heat has an adjacency coefficient of its own, and it is the larger one — = 40 % against = 25 %. That is the key number of stage 3: a dense core heats up faster than it strengthens, so a layout that raises power raises the price of cooling with it. The stage-2 rule "heat = output / 3" no longer holds: it is two thirds on a lone column, 0.79 on two adjacent ones, and it approaches 1.07 on a very dense core at the HV ceiling a room makes more units of heat than it makes EU. That same division is also what bounds the heat from above. Both terms carry the same rods and the same adjacencies, so the heat-per-EU ratio converges as the room grows instead of diverging: A dense room at the ceiling runs between 500 and 546 heat a tick (six columns in a 2x3 block make 500, a 12x12x12 hall 546), and none runs hotter than 546: the more sparsely the columns stand, the less heat the same ceiling costs. A big room buys autonomy, not power. Everything past 512 EU/t delivers the same 512 EU/t; what grows is the time between refuellings, because the same stream is divided among more rods. The room's appetite is identical for every layout that reaches the ceiling: 256 rods = 128 uranium ore an hour. The per-layout figures are in Heat is settled every tick, even with the reactor shut down: cooling has to work, or "scram and wait" would not be a way out. A full scale drains to zero in 395 ticks (19.8 s). A full scale still has no consequence — that is and.

Control What it does Redstone signal on the controller present — the reactor runs; removed — emergency stop. A lever by the door kills the core without dismantling anything Depth throttle five stops, 0 / 25 / 50 / 75 / 100 %; 0 % is the same stop, from inside the screen There are deliberately no other controls: two is exactly as many as fit in the head of a player standing in a smoking hall. The throttle rides the vanilla container-button channel, like the dome toggle on the repeller: the button id is the requested depth in percent, so no payload of its own is needed. The value is clamped on the server, not in the screen. The throttle works at every scale: it cuts a figure that has already been clamped, so 50 % on a 3x3 layer gives 256 EU/t — and exactly half the heat, half the water and half the uranium per hour. In stage 2 that was not so (the ceiling was applied last, and above it every stop was identical); the discrepancy was closed in stage 3.

c.h: Cooling: the shell on its own, water only past the threshold
c.t: The cooling curve has two terms, and the second is the important one: The proportional term is what gives the reactor an equilibrium instead of a switch. With a flat loss a core had exactly two outcomes: production below it and the gauge never leaves zero, above it and the gauge climbs to the top and stays. The first of those is what a player's first reactor looked like, and it looked broken. Now every core settles where production and losses meet: Core Heat, units/t Equilibrium Gauge Water 1 column (4 rods) 16 1500 15 % not needed 2 columns side by side 57 6625 dry 66 % dry, 60 % on water optional (3 mB/t if plumbed) 3 in a row (12 rods) 124 above the ceiling 60 % on water needed The shell's ceiling is 84 units/t (). Anything producing less holds itself; above it the loop begins. Water is a safety system, not a radiator. It engages only past the loop's own target the coolant target (60 % of the gauge = 6000 units) and takes two things away: this tick's inflow, and a twentieth of whatever overshoot has already piled up. The target sits deliberately below the amber band (= 70 %): the loop has to bring the reactor back to green, not park it on a warning. The first term holds the line, the second walks back to it. Without the second, a runaway core would freeze exactly where it was caught — indistinguishable from a loop that does nothing. Without the first, the loop would have to undo the whole in one tick: an early version demanded fifteen hundred millibuckets a tick and drained the room in eight of them. Rounding up rather than down is deliberate: truncation returned 0 for any heat below the exchange rate, and a reactor idling just under the threshold would have held its temperature on no water at all. A starter reactor needs no plumbing. One column of four rods makes 16 heat a tick and settles at 15 % of the scale, dry. Two adjacent (57/t) already clear the loop's target — which answers to 52/t — but settle at 66 % on their own anyway, below the amber band; a pipe holds them at 60 % for 3 mB/t. The water loop becomes truly mandatory at the third column (124/t, 36 mB/t): the shell sheds no more than 84/t, and everything above that climbs to the top of the scale. Nothing forces pipes early; scale does. A water-cooled reactor sits at 60 % of the scale — its heat bar is green, and the amber band means "something is wrong" again: the supply is not keeping up, the exhaust is blocked, or the core was pushed without a loop. Before stage 4 the loop aimed at the warning line itself, and a healthy reactor glowed amber forever. The controller boils, not the column: it walks its list of columns and asks each one for as much as it has not gathered yet. Whatever could not be boiled stays as heat and goes on the scale. That is the entire failure mode of a starved loop: not an error message, a rising bar.

Every tick the controller tidies the fluids inside each unbroken vertical stack of columns: all the water gathers at the bottom, all the steam at the top. A stack therefore behaves as one vessel, and a pipe plugged into any block of it fills the whole thing. Without this a stack simply would not fill: water sinks, the bottom block reaches capacity first, and a pipe asking "is there room?" got "no" from a vessel that was half empty. ⚠️ Columns standing side by side are not connected. The controller used to even the tanks out across the whole room, and one pipe watered the entire hall. That was convenient and untrue: coolant appearing inside a rack nothing is plumbed to reads as a bug however useful it is. Plumb the columns you want cooled — the easiest way is to build them in stacks.

Type: a screen with no slots at all — the controller is read, not loaded. The lack of inventory is deliberate: empty slots would invite hoppers into a block with nothing to hold. No upgrade panel: the controller is not a processing machine, and four hidden upgrade slots would promise what it cannot do. No progress arrow: the reactor has no operation that "runs". There are two layouts, and they are never shown together. The controller's panel is much taller than the family default (176x228 instead of 176x166): the art draws two framed boxes — the readout down to y = 87 and the throttle's own frame from y = 96 — with the inventory label at y = 116. A status line, the data rows, two gauges and five throttle buttons fit inside those; together with the shell diagnostics they do not fit at all. They also answer different questions at different times: while the shell is open the reactor has no numbers at all, and once it is closed the fault line has nothing to say. Layout When Rows Building any status but the status; "Room" — the interior size ; "Problem" — the direction to the offending cell (only for the states that point at one); the charge gauge Running the status; "Rods"; "Output" in EU/t; a heat gauge; a coolant gauge carrying the boil rate in its label; the depth throttle as five buttons; the charge gauge The running layout, top to bottom: the status headline ( = 21), two text rows ( = 35, step 12), two gauges ( = 61, step 13), the throttle strip ( = 98, five 28-px buttons) and the charge gauge ( = 116). The buffer's charge gauge is drawn in both layouts — the only element that is. A reactor that has been scrammed, and a room that has just been breached, still hold whatever they banked, and that is exactly when a player wants to know how much is left. It also answers "where does the energy go": the reactor banks what nothing is drawing, and until this bar existed a working reactor gave no sign of that anywhere on the panel. The charge bar spans the full width of the content area and the figure is written on it rather than beside it. Beside it was the first try, and it broke on its own success: at 200,000 EU the label outgrew its column and ran under the gauge. A number that only misbehaves once the reactor is doing well is the worst kind. Why heat and coolant are bars rather than rows. Five text rows, three bars and a throttle fit nowhere, and the numbers that want watching continuously read better as a filling bar than as a figure to parse. The "Output" row never shows a dash. A sealed, fuelled, silent reactor is the worst state this machine can be in, and every cause has a different fix, so instead of a zero it prints the reason for the idle in red: not sealed, no fuel, rods withdrawn, no redstone, buffer full. A dash left the player guessing between five different faults. The coolant label carries both the level and the rate: "Coolant 62 % · 243 mB/t". The level says whether the loop is holding, the rate says what one inlet line has to keep up with, and a player sizing their plumbing needs both at once. There is no separate row for the rate. The heat bar is green while there is head room, amber from (70 %) and red halfway from there to a hundred (85 %). The threshold comes from the config rather than being hardcoded in the screen: otherwise the gauge would disagree with the machine it displays. The coolant bar's colour is the blocked-exhaust indicator. The rule is short and rests on three Colour When What it means teal water above zero, steam below 90 % the loop is turning over amber steam ≥ 90 % the steam has nowhere to go: the exhaust is missing, clogged, or the nozzle faces a wall red water at zero the loop is dry: supply cannot keep up, or has stopped The amber case is the only one worth the code. With the exhaust blocked the coolant bar sits reassuringly full while the temperature climbs: the water is there, and there is nowhere to boil it to. Without the hint that reads as a broken mod rather than as a plumbing mistake. The steam percentage is shown nowhere as a number — there is no room on the panel, and it would be one gauge too many — but the sync channel carries it precisely for this colour. There is no way to hit the throttle in the building layout — it is not drawn there, and a click cannot move control rods the player cannot see. Both layouts are laid out as a "label → value" table rather than as free-flowing lines. The columns are fixed: labels start at (just clear of the 11-pixel room pictogram baked into the atlas at x = 8), values and gauge bars at = 98 (bars are 70×5). That is a direct consequence of the first version of this screen, where label and value were one string and the Russian text ran into the pictogram. Separate columns take the layout's dependency on translated length away — however long a label turns out to be, the value still starts in the same place. A value that does not fit its column is shrunk, not clipped: clipping would hide exactly the part the line is read for (the block count or the direction). The same trick has long been used by the machine family's status line. A dash instead of zeros. While the room has not been measured, the size row shows "—", not "0 × 0 × 0". Zero is a measurement too, and showing one where no measurement happened is a lie; a dash honestly says "nothing to show". The same goes for the problem row: a direction is printed only for the states that really point at a block (, , , ); for and the "place" is the controller itself, and an offset would be noise. shows no direction, even though it technically has a position. That is a post-playtest fix: its "place" is wherever the ray gave up, up to 13 blocks out in open ground, and a lone controller puffing smoke into a hillside turned out to be worse than silence. It pointed at a spot with nothing to fix. The location is a direction, not coordinates. The offset is measured from the controller itself and reads as "4 east, 2 up": the player reading the screen is standing at the controller, and that sentence gets them to the right block faster than three numbers do. Axes with no offset are dropped — a breach straight overhead reads "2 up" rather than "0 east, 2 up, 0 south". Technically it is also the only option: a menu sync channel carries a signed 16-bit number, an absolute world coordinate does not fit, while an offset is at most ±14 by construction. The state is visible from outside too: on a formed room the controller's front face is lit (the blockstate), on an unformed one it is dark. The build can be checked without opening the screen.

Text alone is not enough in a build of a thousand blocks, so the controller also answers with sound and particles. A multiblock that silently starts working leaves the player wondering whether it did. Event What happens The room came together (was not formed → is formed) (0.6, pitch 1.6) at the controller + 12 particles above it The room came apart (was formed → is not) (0.5, pitch 1.4) at the breach, exactly once While the problem is unfixed 16 smoke particles at the offending cell on every scan The failure sound plays on the transition only, never in a loop, and that matters. The scan runs every two seconds; an alarm repeating every two seconds until the player finds the block turns a hint into a punishment. It is needed once because a wall is usually opened by a creeper, and at that moment the player is looking somewhere else. After that the particles do the work: they are unobtrusive, and they are visible the second the player turns round. Smoke is now the only particle a breach gets. It used to come with angry-villager puffs, and the play session threw them out: over a wall they read as cartoon clouds rather than as a fault marker. The assembly sound is the same the distillation column plays when its tower forms. That is deliberate: "a multiblock came together" should sound the same across the mod, whichever multiblock it was.

The controller is the only thing that sets the and blockstates, and it sets them on the whole shell, not just on itself. It also turns the room's lights on (details in "The seamless look" and in the lamp spec). Field Value What is walked the perimeter cells of an explicitly given box Which box on success the one this scan measured; it is also remembered Which box on failure the last remembered one — whatever the controller once accepted What is written only cells whose value actually changed set to Light a at level 15 appears in each interior cell facing a lamp (and is removed on teardown) flag 2 Why the box is passed in rather than taken from the scan result. A failed scan measures no box — its . A sweep driven by the result could therefore physically only ever switch the flag on: a breached wall left the room seamless and lit as if nothing had happened. The first play session found exactly that. The controller now remembers the last box it accepted and clears it when a scan fails. The box is written to NBT (…): a chunk can unload whole and reload with a hole in it, and a controller that forgot its box would leave the shell looking "formed" forever. The saving is not a micro-optimisation: the sweep runs on every scan, that is every two seconds for every controller in the world. Reading a thousand blockstates is cheap, rewriting a thousand is not, and a needless would additionally fire neighbour updates on every pass. Flag 2 without flag 1 is chosen for the same reason: the properties are cosmetic, so the client must hear about them and no neighbour needs to.

Field Value Role producer, tier HV Buffer (EU) = 200,000 Max input (EU/tick) 0 — a reactor is not charged from outside Max output (EU/tick) 512 = the HV ceiling Faces every face but the front pushes out (→ ); the front is The front face is energy-inert by rule R-NRG-03: it carries the panel the player reads, and a cable sticking out of the middle of an interface would spoil both the look and the sense of it. The 200,000 EU buffer is a damper rather than a store: a grid that cannot take the power this instant must not stall the core mid-tick. At the ceiling that is 391 ticks (19.5 s) of output, and exactly as long to fill from empty. One electrum cable carries 192 EU/t per segment, so a reactor running at the ceiling is drained by three independent lines — or by machines placed flush against its faces.

Field Value Shape full cube 16³ (occluder) Hardness 5.0 Blast resistance 30.0 Tool pickaxe (required for drops) Sound metal Blockstates (horizontal), Block entity yes (the scan, the reactor and the sync channel) The verdict is not written to disk: the room is the save. After a world load the very first scan re-derives the state from whatever stands around. A stored verdict could survive a world edit that took the walls away, and then it would be lying. Only what cannot be re-derived from the world lives in NBT: the bounds of the last accepted box (…), the accumulated heat and the throttle position. The box is not a verdict but an address: it is what gives the next failed scan something to clear (see "Painting the flags"), and it cannot lie — if it is stale, the sweep merely clears flags where there were none. Heat and depth are machine state: a reactor that forgot them on chunk unload would cool for free and come back at full power on its own.

Craft — ×1 at a time. The control circuit is a separate item: 4 palladium plates, a resonance coil, 2 advanced circuits, an electronic circuit and redstone The coil took the place of the unstable isotope that stood here in the first version. The isotope is a product of the Incubator, and the incubator branch has been dropped from the reactor's requirements: it sent the player into the mod's biological wing for a single item and made the nuclear branch a hostage of somebody else's chain. The resonance coil fits the role better — it already sits at the "endgame electronics" rung, the thermal centrifuge leads to it, and in required progress it is the isotope's equal.

Tier: HV — a producer of up to 512 EU/tick. Requires: shielding and reinforced shielding plates (the chain is described under casing), an advanced machine casing, advanced circuits, palladium plates, a resonance coil. Unlocks: the reactor room itself — without a controller a pile of blocks stays a pile of blocks.

Reactor Casing — what it scans the room out of, the geometry and the crafting chain. Airlock Door — a precondition of the status. Reactor Glass, the Lamp and the Reactor Inlet — the other blocks the scanner counts as wall. Reactor Column — what it burns, boils and re-settles. Fuel Rod and the Fuel Rod Cladding the fuel it wears down and the casing that is left. Steam — the loop's working fluid. Steam Nozzle — the end of the loop; until it works the coolant bar turns amber and the heat climbs. Reactor Button — the one block of the set the scanner does not count as wall. Resonance Chain — where the coil for the control circuit comes from. Distillation Column and the Incubator — the mod's two earlier multiblocks; both check a fixed shape, and the volumetric scanner was written here for the first time.

The Reactor Airlock Door is a two-block-tall shell block and the only way into the room. A room without one does not form: the controller reports "No door" and refuses to call the build finished. That is not a formality — a sealed box you cannot enter would be a bug rather than a building, and it is better said while you are still laying blocks than afterwards. The door deliberately does not behave like a vanilla iron door. It cannot be opened by hand and cannot be left open: it opens on a redstone pulse alone and shuts itself. There is no "open forever" state.

Action What happens Right-click by hand nothing A rising redstone edge (button, pressure plate, lever) the door opens for (default 40 ticks = 2 s) The signal is held on a lever the door still closes on its timer; holding does not hold it The signal is cut nothing: the falling edge is ignored on purpose A fresh edge while the door is open the closing timer starts over A player or mob stands in the doorway the close is deferred and retried every (default 10 ticks) Why this way. A vanilla iron door stays open for exactly as long as the signal lasts — its fate hangs on whether somebody forgot a lever. For a door that holds a reactor room's seal that is a poor contract. A pulse door turns a broken seal into a two-second event instead of a state that can last for hours. Waiting for whoever stands in the doorway is required for the opposite reason: the room this is all for is a place the player is meant to be inside. A door that slams shut on the player would be a trap at the one narrow point of the whole build. The door is always placed shut, even if a signal is already live nearby: otherwise a new door would appear open and the shell would be unsealed at the very moment it was built. The sounds are the vanilla iron door's, on opening and on closing. How to send the pulse from inside. Outside, anything will do — a button, a lever, a pressure plate. Inside a sealed room the signal source has to be as sealed as the room, which is why the reactor button shipped alongside the door: the same shielding alloy, a press of = 20 ticks (1 s), half of, so the pulse comfortably fits inside the opening window. A vanilla button works too, but it is wood or stone — exactly what stops existing inside an active room in stage 4. A button on the wall occupies no shell cell and breaks no seal.

c.h: The doorway: where a door counts as an entrance
c.t: It is not enough for the controller that a door merely exists in the shell. It needs a doorway — two door cells stacked, with the lower one at the room's interior floor level. Anything else is a window, not a way in. Situation Controller status No door anywhere in the shell — "No door" A door exists but no doorway (lying in the floor or ceiling, standing above floor level) — "No doorway" At least one doorway condition satisfied There may be any number of doors: two — an entrance and an exit — is an ordinary layout. The requirement is exactly one: at least one real doorway.
Field Value Role none Buffer (EU) 0 Max input / output (EU/tick) n/a The door runs on redstone, not EU. The drive inside it needs no power — it was paid for at the crafting table.

Field Value Shape a leaf 3/16 of a block thick, full height and width of the cell; swings 90° to the hinge when open Size 1×2 (lower and upper halves are one object) Occlusion (not a full cube) Hardness 5.0 Blast resistance 30.0 Tool pickaxe (required for drops) Sound metal Piston reaction destroyed Blockstates , ,, ,, The two halves live and die together: break either and the player gets one door while the other half disappears. Mobs may path through the door only while it is open. The door carries like the rest of the shell — the controller writes it into every cell of a finished room (see "The seamless look"). Unlike casing and glass, it does not change how the door looks: the leaf has no seamless texture of its own. The property exists for uniformity — neither the scan nor the flag sweep should have to know which shell block happens to have a cosmetic variant. is stored for exactly one purpose — telling a rising edge from "the signal is still on". Without it, every neighbour update with the lever on would read as a fresh pulse, and the door would re-open the instant the player watched it close.

Craft — ×1 at a time, on a 2×3 grid. The recipe reads as the block's construction: two vanilla iron leaves — one for each of its two cells of height — dressed in shielding alloy, with a drive in the middle turning a pair of leaves into an airlock. The drive is a separate item: 3 shielding plates, 2 iron ingots, an electronic circuit, 2 tempered iron plates and a piston

Tier: none. Requires: one shielding plate, two reinforced shielding plates (see casing — the full chain is described there), two vanilla iron doors and a control rod drive. Unlocks: the ability to complete a room — without a door the controller will not accept it. The drive appears here for the first time but not the last: it is also part of the controller, and in stage 2 it gets its real meaning — regulating how deep the fuel rods sit.

Reactor Casing — the rest of the shell and the material chain. Reactor Controller — what checks for a door and a doorway. Reactor Button — how the pulse is sent from inside the room. Reactor Glass — a window, which is not a door. Thermal Centrifuge — the precedent for "redstone as a machine's control", with the opposite contract: there the signal must be held.

Reactor Glass is casing you can see through. To the room scanner it is wall in the full sense: a glass cell is sealed, and a window of any reasonable size does not stop the room forming — as long as glass stays under 30 % of the shell. Vanilla glass will not do — the scanner reads it as a breach, like any foreign block. That is not pedantry for its own sake: a glass wall on a reactor has to be the same shielding alloy, or the "window" would become a cheap way to build the room out of whatever is at hand.

Field Value Counts as wall yes, on a par with casing Where it may go any cell of any face: walls, floor, ceiling, edges, corners How many at most = 30 % of the shell's cells Above that status — "Too much glass — weak structure" Unlike the door (at least one required) and the controller (exactly one, vertical wall only), glass is not tied to any particular cell: its single restriction is a share.

Field Value Config key Default 30 (percent) What is counted glass cells against all shell cells, floor and ceiling included The test — integer, no floating point When it runs last: after the seal, the second controller, the door and the doorway What the controller shows status and the position of the first glass cell of the walk The integers are not pedantry: comparing scaled integers gives the same answer on both sides of an exact share, whereas in double would behave differently in mathematically identical rooms. Overflow is impossible by construction — a shell holds at most 1016 cells. A practical yardstick on the smallest room (98 shell cells): 30 % is 29 panes, a little more than one solid 5×5 face. One wall can be all glass with a couple of windows to spare; two solid glass faces are already over the line. The position the controller points at is not the "guilty" cell — there is none, the share is guilty — but the first glass cell in perimeter-walk order. It is there so the smoke in the world leads the player to the glazed part of the shell instead of leaving them to guess where it is. Why the cap exists at all. Glass is half the palladium of casing (see "Balance"), and without a limit the optimal strategy would be a glass box: cheaper, prettier, and you can see inside. The cap gives the choice its meaning back — a window stays a window rather than a cheaper way to build the room.
Field Value Role none Buffer (EU) 0 Max input / output (EU/tick) n/a

A full cube, but not an occluder — otherwise the glass would cull its neighbours' faces like a solid block and there would be nothing to look at through it. Hardness and blast resistance are the casing's: a window is not the shell's weak spot. Field Value Shape full cube 16³,, translucent ( in the model) Hardness 5.0 Blast resistance 30.0 Tool pickaxe (required for drops) Sound glass Blockstates , — cosmetic: a face of a formed shell loses its bezel, an edge keeps it Shared faces culled between adjacent glass blocks Sound is the only thing that separates glass from casing by feel: it is placed and broken with a glassy ring rather than a metal clang. Light passes through it. Culling shared faces matters most for the glass: without it a 5×5 window would draw a grid of interior panes like a stack of separate cubes, and the "a formed room is one surface" effect would break at the first window. Vanilla glass does exactly the same thing.

Craft — ×8 at a time. The number that matters here is one shielding plate for eight blocks — 0.125 of a plate per block. For casing it is 0.25 per block: glass is exactly half the palladium. That is precisely why it has a share cap and casing does not.

Tier: none (a passive block). Requires: shielding plates (that is, palladium and tempered iron) and ordinary colourless glass. Unlocks: nothing new — it is an alternative to casing, not a step beyond it.

Reactor Casing — the base shell block; the room geometry is described there. Reactor Controller — the one that counts glass as wall and measures its share. Reactor Lamp — a glowing shell block; it does not count towards the glass cap even though glass appears in its recipe. Incubator — the mod's precedent for "glass as part of a structure".

The Reactor Lamp is casing that glows. It came out of the most obvious problem of the first play session: a formed room is a sealed box without a single opening, and inside it is pitch black. Light has to be brought in somehow, and an ordinary torch will not do — a torch is not a shell block, so the cell it occupies reads to the scanner as a breach. The lamp solves this the way multiblocks solve such things: it is a shell block and takes the place of any casing cell. The light appears only while, so a lit room is both lit and signalling "the build was accepted" at the same time. One subtlety that makes the "The light" section worth reading in full: the block does not glow. The lamp block itself emits nothing; the light lives in the cell opposite it, inside the room. Not a drop of it reaches the outside.

Field Value Counts as wall yes How the scanner sees it as casing, not as a kind of its own Where it may go any cell of any face: walls, floor, ceiling, edges, corners How many any number, zero included Counts against the glass cap no The scanner classifying the lamp as casing is not a shortcut in an enum but a balance decision. If the lamp counted as glass, every lamp would eat into the thirty percent reserved for windows, and the player would have to choose between seeing in and seeing inside. That is a false choice: lighting is not decoration but a precondition for working in the room at all. The same line has a second effect: without explicitly naming the lamp as shell it would read as a foreign block, so every lamp set into a wall would break the room. One rule in the scanner answers both.

The main thing about the lamp: the block itself emits nothing at all. Its is zero in every state. What glows is a cell inside the room, and the controller is what puts it there. Field Value Emission of the block itself 0, always What appears while a vanilla at level 15 in the interior cell the lamp faces What happens at that same light block is taken away again Who places and removes it the controller, in the same sweep that paints Exactly where the single neighbour of the lamp's cell that lies inside the box If that cell is not air nothing is placed — whatever the player built against the wall is left alone A lamp on an edge or corner gives no light: such a cell has no neighbour inside the room Why not simply a glowing block. The first version was exactly that: 15 while. The play session showed the obvious-in-hindsight problem — block light in Minecraft radiates in every direction, so a lamp set into a wall lights the countryside outside exactly as much as the room inside. A finished room glowed across the landscape. There is no "geometry that arranges it for free" here: the outer side of a wall is as much a neighbour as the inner one. Moving the light source inside solves it without a lighting system of our own: is the vanilla invisible, walk-through block invented for exactly "there is light here and no visible source". All of the light is born inside the room and none of it reaches the outside, and what the player sees on the lamp's face is its texture, not emission. Fifteen is the maximum, and it is not chosen "just in case": a room can be 12×12×12 inside and the lamp sits in its face, that is as far from the opposite corner as it gets. A lower level would leave dark corners in a large room, and a dark corner in Minecraft is not an aesthetic matter but mob spawns inside a sealed space you then cannot chase them out of. Tying it to also keeps the signal honest. A lamp lit in a half-built wall would say the structure works when it does not. Here light means exactly one thing: the room is done. A practical consequence for the builder: put lamps in faces, not in edges. In an edge a lamp stays a handsome wall block with not one lumen to its name, because it has nowhere to shine.

Field Value Role none Buffer (EU) 0 Max input / output (EU/tick) n/a The lamp draws no EU. That is deliberate: no power reaches the inside of a sealed room at all — the reactor inlet carries fluid from stage 3 onwards, but never EU — so a lamp that needed current simply could not work. It is bound to the room's state rather than to a grid, which is the better contract anyway: the light in a reactor hall should not go out because a cable broke somewhere.

Field Value Shape full cube 16³ (occluder) Hardness 5.0 Blast resistance 30.0 Tool pickaxe (required for drops) Sound metal Light emission 0 (the light lives in the interior cell — see above) Blockstates , — both cosmetic Shared faces culled between adjacent lamps (inherited from the shell block) The numbers match the rest of the shell: the lamp must not be the spot where the wall is easiest to open. It has three textures like every other shell block: unformed (with a bezel), a formed face (without one) and a formed edge (the bezel stays) — see "The seamless look".

Craft — ×1 at a time. The recipe reads as the lamp's construction: glowstone in the middle, glass around it, an iron body at the corners and a shielding plate at the base — a light fitting bolted to a wall of the same alloy. Exactly one plate is left in it: the lamp is a convenience, and paying palladium for it as if it were a piece of the mechanic would be wrong.

Tier: none (a passive block). Requires: shielding plates (the chain is described under casing), ordinary glass and glowstone — that is, a trip to the Nether, which the palladium demands anyway. Unlocks: nothing new — it is a convenience, not a step. A room without lamps forms exactly the same. The glowstone is no accident: it and the palladium come from the same dimension, so the lamp adds not a single new expedition to the build.

Reactor Casing — the base shell block; the room geometry and "The seamless look" are described there. Reactor Controller — the one that sets and therefore turns the light on. Reactor Glass — the other "transparent" shell block; unlike the lamp it is limited to a 30 % share. Airlock Door and the Reactor Button — how you get into a lit room and back out of it.

The Reactor Outlet is the socket a cable plugs into. It is the counterpart of the reactor inlet: water goes in there, power comes out here. The block exists not out of a wish for one more block, but because without it the reactor could not be plugged into anything. By construction the controller stands in a wall, which leaves it with four faces buried in the shell, a fifth opening into a sealed room a cable could never leave, and a sixth — the front — that the mod's machine convention reserves for the player's panel and keeps energy-inert (: a cable must never draw an arm across the interface). The result before stage 3: a reactor that ran perfectly, reported its output on the panel, filled its buffer — and had nowhere to connect. The answer is the one the water loop already uses: if something has to cross a sealed shell, it crosses through a purpose-built piece of that shell. Water through the inlet, power out of the outlet.

Property Value Buffer = 512 EU — exactly one tick of HV Tier HV Face roles source (OUT) on all six — no face is reserved EU accepted from outside 0 — a cable cannot push power in, only draw it Output up to 512 EU/t (the HV voltage ceiling) Who fills it the controller, every tick, from its own buffer Block entity yes, no tick of its own To the room scan casing — not a breach, and outside the glass limit A socket, not a battery. Its capacity is one tick of HV — the same sizing decision, and for the same reason, as the fluid inlet next door: the block has to behave as a hole in the wall that power passes through, not as a place worth hoarding in. The reactor itself is the store: 200,000 EU.

c.h: The controller pushes; the outlet never pulls
c.t: There is one direction and it is fixed: the controller pushes, the outlet receives. An outlet has no idea which room it belongs to, and teaching it to go looking would mean a search from every socket every tick. The controller already walks its own shell when it scans the room — that is where it collects its outlets. One owner, one direction, and no back-reference to keep valid when a wall is rebuilt. Sharing is even-handed rather than first-come: runs in rounds, each round hands every socket an equal share of what is left in the buffer, and the rounds stop as soon as one changes nothing. Otherwise a room with two sockets on opposite walls would starve whichever the scan happened to reach second, every time the buffer was short. A side benefit: a room whose sockets are all full costs a single pass. The top-up happens every tick and regardless of whether the reactor is running: cutting the redstone signal scrams the reaction but does not stop what is already in the buffer from being handed out. The list of outlets is rebuilt on the scan, not when a block is placed: = 40 ticks (2 s). A socket set into a wall joins the room within those two seconds rather than instantly.

One outlet gives up to 512 EU/t — exactly what the reactor makes at the HV ceiling. What you have to count is not the socket but the cable: an outlet set into a flat wall has one face exposed outward, and a single electrum cable segment carries = 192 EU/t (a cable's throughput is its segment buffer — the lesson of What you draw Cable runs Outlets in the wall up to 192 EU/t 1 1 up to 384 EU/t 2 2 the full 512 EU/t 3 3 The same principle as the water loop: five inlets in, five out, three sockets for power. The numbers differ (water is capped at 50 mB/t per line, power at 192 EU/t) but the rule is one — the station's bottleneck sits in the wall, and every line costs a cell of shell. An outlet on an edge or a corner of the shell has two or three faces exposed and can carry several cables, up to its own 512 EU/t ceiling. That is a legitimate way to make do with fewer sockets, but it ties the whole power run to one corner of the room.

The outlet is a shell block, and the scanner reads it as casing — not as a port and not as glass. Three practical consequences: it is never a breach — a socket may go into any cell of wall, floor or ceiling; it is outside the = 30 % limit — any number of sockets may be placed, and the shell loses nothing by it, neither toughness nor scanner standing; it carries / and switches to the bezel-less texture with the rest of the wall once the controller accepts the room (see "The seamless look"). Only the price limits you — that, and the fact that every socket eats a cell casing could have had.

Field Value Role source (OUT) on all six faces Buffer (EU) = 512 Max input (EU/tick) 0 — never charged from outside Max output (EU/tick) 512 — the HV voltage ceiling The only path into the buffer is, called by the controller. It returns what was actually taken, so the controller can put the remainder into another socket instead of discarding it. No face is reserved: a machine has a front to keep a cable off, an outlet has no front — the whole point of the block is that whichever face happens to stick out of the wall is the working one.

Field Value Shape full cube 16³ (occluder) Hardness 5.0 Blast resistance 30.0 Tool pickaxe (required for drops) Sound metal Blockstates , — cosmetic, as on the rest of the shell Block entity yes — a buffer and nothing else, no tick The numbers match the rest of the shell: the socket must not be the spot where the wall is easiest to open.

Craft — ×2 at a time. The copper cable in the middle is not a conductor but a statement of purpose: this is a piece of wall with a contact brought out through it. The shielding plates in the corners hold the same line as the rest of the shell, and the iron is cheap bulk that keeps the price out of palladium.

Tier: HV (the socket gives at the HV ceiling). Requires: shielding plates and a copper cable — the palladium branch and the most basic power tech. Unlocks: connecting the reactor to a grid. Without an outlet a reactor is a building closed on itself: fuel burns, the buffer fills, and nothing can take the power out.
