Reactor Controller — what fills the sockets, and why it cannot be the connection point itself. Reactor Inlet — the same idea for fluid: the one place water and steam cross the shell. Reactor Casing — the rest of the shell, the geometry, the seamless look and the crafting chain. Electrum Cable — what HV is drawn with; its 192 EU/t is what sets the number of sockets. Copper Cable — what sits in the middle of the recipe.

The Reactor Inlet solves the problem every sealed building runs into: how do you get a pipe inside without punching a hole in the wall? An ordinary pipe laid through the shell would be exactly that hole the room scanner reads any block but the permitted seven as a breach. The inlet is one of those seven: outside it a pipe connects, inside it another does, and the wall itself stays whole — the controller still counts the room as formed. Since stage 3 it is no longer a decorative cube. It now has a fluid port, and with it the one number this stage exists for: an inlet passes = 50 mB a tick and not a drop more.

Property Value Throughput = 50 mB/t Tank capacity 50 mB — exactly one tick of flow Accepts any fluid Gives up any fluid Port on faces on all six — outside and inside the room alike Direction unset: whatever the pipes pump, the inlet carries Block entity yes, no tick of its own — the pipes on both sides do the moving A crossing, not a store. Its capacity is exactly one tick of its throughput, so it behaves as a hole in the wall rather than as a reservoir: the pipe outside fills it, the pipe inside empties it, and nothing can accumulate. That is what makes the 50 mB/t figure real — a segment can never hand on more than it holds (the same mechanism that makes a cable's buffer its throughput, the lesson of.

c.h: Both directions, and one block rather than two
c.t: Water goes in and steam comes out through inlets of the same kind. There will be no separate "steam outlet": two nearly identical blocks with different holes would double the recipes and the textures and make the player remember which way round to place them — for a decision they never actually get to make. What an inlet carries is decided by what is plumbed into it. The inlet does not filter. The "water only" rule lives where it is honest — on the reactor column itself: a pipe carrying the wrong fluid should stall against the machine that cannot use it, not against a wall. Practical consequence: one inlet serves one direction at a time. Its tank holds a single fluid, so the water line and the steam line go through different inlets. A fully plumbed reactor at the HV ceiling means five inlets in and five out.

An inlet carries 50 mB/t; a fluid pipe segment carries exactly the same (= 50). So an inlet and the pipe run feeding it are one 50 mB/t line, and they can be counted together. Core layout Water, mB/t Inlets in Inlets out 1 column (4 rods) 0 0 0 2 adjacent columns 3 1 1 3 in a row 36 1 1 4 in a square 108 3 3 packed 3×3×3 room (HV ceiling) 243 5 5 That is what the block means for play: the bottleneck sits in the wall. Every extra line is another shell cell given up to an inlet, another run from the pump, and another craft costing four shielding plates. A reactor cannot be plumbed with "one pipe from the ocean".

The scanner sees an inlet as casing — it is a shell block, after all. Everything the wall around it has, it has too: the and states, the seamless art of a finished room, shared-face culling. The one thing it does not do is count as glass; it is outside the limit. So any number of inlets may be placed, and the shell loses nothing by it — neither toughness nor scanner standing. Only the price limits you.

Field Value Role none Buffer (EU) 0 Max input / output (EU/tick) n/a EU does not cross an inlet, and stage 3 did not change that. A cable run up to it from outside simply stops at the wall, exactly as at casing. Nor is it needed: the room's only producer and consumer of energy is the controller, which sits in the wall itself and pushes EU outward from five of its own faces. There is as yet nothing inside a sealed room to carry power to. The insulated copper cable in the recipe is a legacy of the original idea ("one block for pipe and cable alike") and a progression gate — not a working conductor.

Field Value Shape full cube 16³ (occluder) Hardness 5.0 Blast resistance 30.0 Tool pickaxe (required for drops) Sound metal Blockstates , — cosmetic: a face of a formed shell loses its bezel, an edge keeps it Block entity yes — a tank and nothing else, no tick NBT (how much is held), (which fluid) The numbers match the rest of the shell: the inlet must not be the spot where the shell is easiest to open. Like casing and glass, the inlet switches to a bezel-less texture once the controller accepts the room (see "The seamless look"). It matters more here than elsewhere: this is the one shell block with a distinct pattern of openings, and in a finished wall that pattern has to read as part of a panel rather than as a separate crate. A saved fluid id that no longer resolves (a mod removed, a fluid renamed) empties the buffer instead of throwing: one tick of water is not worth a world that refuses to load.

Craft — ×1 at a time. The recipe explains the block by itself: casing in the middle, pipe and cable along the edges, shielding plates in the corners. A piece of wall with both conduits already built into it.

Tier: none. Requires: shielding plates and reactor casing, a fluid pipe, an insulated copper cable. Unlocks: water into the room and steam out of it — that is, the whole of stage 3. Without an inlet a reactor is limited to what the shell sheds on its own, which caps the core at two adjacent columns.

Reactor Casing — the rest of the shell, the geometry and the crafting chain. Reactor Column — what stands on the other side of the wall and where the water goes. Steam Nozzle — where the steam goes once it is outside. Steam — the second fluid an inlet carries. Reactor Controller — what counts the inlet as wall and reports the boil rate. Fluid Pipe — what connects on both sides. Insulated Copper Cable — the other half of the recipe.

The Steam Nozzle is the reactor's exhaust. Water boiled inside the reactor columns becomes steam, the steam piles up in the columns, and it has to go somewhere. The nozzle is that somewhere: it takes steam from an ordinary fluid pipe, releases it into the block it faces, and the steam is gone. Nothing can ever be taken back out of it. Why the exhaust is a block and not a rule. If steam simply evaporated inside the column the loop would be half a loop: the player would plumb water in and never think about cooling again. Steam that has to be piped back out turns cooling into a real circuit with two ends — and it gives the room its silhouette: pipes going in low, pipes coming out high, and something hissing at the end of them.

Property Value Accepts steam only Gives up nothing — not a drop can be extracted from its tank Tank = 500 mB Vent rate = 100 mB/t Where a pipe connects any face except the one the mouth points at Particles in front of the mouth, the number of puffs scaled to the real flow (1…8) The tank is deliberately tiny — five ticks of flow. Its job is to smooth a line that briefly outran the nozzle, not to store anything: a large one would let a player park steam in it waiting for stage 5's turbine, and "steam that reaches a nozzle is gone" would stop being the truth the whole loop is balanced against. The mouth is not published to pipes on purpose. Otherwise the exhaust line could be run into the very block the nozzle vents into, and it would quietly start feeding itself.

c.h: It needs open air in front of the mouth
c.t: Steam is released into the block the nozzle faces. If that block cannot be replaced (a wall, the ground, another machine), the nozzle stalls: its tank stays full, the line behind it backs up, the columns stop boiling and the reactor's temperature climbs. There is no message about it and there will not be — a nozzle buried in a wall does nothing, exactly as a real one would. The consequence shows up where it matters instead: the coolant bar on the controller turns amber when the steam has nowhere to go, and the heat gauge rises.

One nozzle vents 100 mB/t, one pipe carries 50 mB/t , and one reactor inlet also carries 50 mB/t. A room at the HV ceiling makes 224…247 mB of steam a tick, so a reactor's full exhaust is five inlets out, five pipe runs and three nozzles. Per-layout figures are in The pipe running into a nozzle has to push into it: set that pipe face to insert mode with a wrench, as with any other fluid consumer.

Field Value Shape 10×10×10 along the mouth's direction (, one per facing) — not a full cube: the spigot sticks 10 pixels of 16 out from the wall Occlusion Hardness 4.0 Blast resistance 20.0 Tool pickaxe (required for drops) Sound metal Blockstates — all six directions Block entity yes, ticks on the server only NBT — how much steam is in the tank Orientation comes from the face the player clicked: the mouth always points away from the surface the nozzle was pressed against. It can be hung from a ceiling or set into a floor just as well — the placement decides the direction, there is no separate rotation step. The steam level is never synced to clients: the puff is spawned with on the server, which broadcasts it to everyone in range by itself. There would be nothing to show anyway — steam is invisible on the model.

A nozzle is not part of the shell. Placed inside the room it takes an interior cell (legal but pointless — the steam stays in the room); placed into a wall in place of a shell block it makes a breach and the room comes apart. Its place is outside, on the wall next to a reactor inlet, with the mouth pointing into open air.

Craft — ×2 at a time. The recipe is deliberately cheap and asks for neither palladium nor shielding alloy: a nozzle hangs outside the sealed room, so it neither holds pressure nor shields anything. The expensive part of the circuit is the inlets, not the exhaust, and three nozzles must not cost as much as another wall.

Tier: none (the block has no energy at all). Requires: a fluid pipe and a machine casing — ordinary fluid logistics, learned long before the reactor. Unlocks: a closed cooling circuit. Without an exhaust the steam tanks in the columns fill, boiling stops and there is no cooling.

Steam — the fluid itself: why it has no world form and cannot be bucketed. Reactor Column — where the steam is born and why it has to leave. Reactor Inlet — how steam gets out of a sealed room. Reactor Controller — where a stalled exhaust becomes visible. Fluid Pipe — what carries the steam to the nozzle.

The Fuel Rod is the reactor's only fuel and the end of the mod's uranium chain. It is assembled from a fuel rod cladding and one enriched uranium, goes into a reactor column by right-clicking — one at a time, up to four per rack — and gives up exactly 144,000 EU there, after which it is an empty casing again. It is the first and so far only consumer of . The mod has produced enriched uranium since, and until stage 2 of the epic not one recipe spent it: the long ore → dust → concentrate → enriched uranium chain ended in an item with nowhere to go.

c.h: Two-step fuel — and why not enriched uranium directly
c.t: The reactor could burn straight away, one step shorter. That is deliberately not A rack holds rods, not ingots. The fuel here is physical: it is visible inside the transparent rack, and "four rods" reads as an object where "four ingots in a rack" does not. The shielding plate in the recipe is the sheath. It is the same material the room is built from; the connection needs no explaining to the player. The step leaves room to grow. MOX, depleted uranium and other grades of rod fit the same shape without touching ore processing. And the same step is what makes the casing reusable. The sheath can come back; the uranium pellet cannot. Without this step, refuelling a reactor would cost exactly what the first load did (see the fuel rod cladding).

Parameter Value Config key Charge in one rod 144,000 EU = x , Durability scale 1000 points not configurable Price of one point 144 EU, rounded UP derived Contribution to output 6 EU/t before adjacency bonuses, at full depth Contribution to heat 4 scale units per tick, at full depth Life at 6 EU/t 24000 ticks = 20 minutes derived A rod is an amount of energy, not a duration. It yields 144,000 EU in every layout: the adjacency bonus buys power (the rod burns faster), the HV ceiling buys autonomy (the rod lasts longer), but what is inside it never changes. The previous edition promised "1,152,000 x adjacency multiplier" per column — that is, dense packing produced fuel out of nothing. Stage 4 closed it. Layout EU/t per rod Rod life One column (4 rods) 6 20 min Two adjacent columns 9 13.3 min Three in a row 12 10 min Four in a row 15 8 min Four in a square 18 6.7 min A 3x3 layer — 36 rods share the 512 EU/t ceiling 14.2 8.4 min A 3x3x3 room packed full — 108 rods 4.7 25.3 min The full breakdown with numbers is in Control-rod depth is a throttle, not a discount: at 50 % a rod gives half the EU per tick, half the heat and is consumed half as fast. Running gently stretches the uranium over time rather than wasting it — the total EU in a rod depends on nothing at all.

The rod has a durability bar, and it means literally what it shows: how much energy is left in it. The scale is 1000 points, each worth 144 EU. Half a bar is half a charge. A thousand points rather than 144,000, because a bar sixteen pixels wide cannot show more anyway; a round number also reads — "damage 250" is exactly a quarter spent. It is also independent of the config: a server operator can raise, the rod gets roomier, and a full bar still means "untouched". The controller spends energy in ticks of a few dozen EU while a point costs 144, so the remainder is carried: the column banks the unspent draw and takes a point off once it adds up to a whole one. Without the carry the rod would never wear at all — every tick would round to zero. The arithmetic is covered by tests and needs no game session to verify. The price of a point rounds up: with a truncating divide each point would cost slightly less than it yields, and the last few points would be free energy.

It used to not. A started rod could not be taken out, it did not drop when the rack was broken, and "just have a look at what is in there" was an expensive mistake. There was one reason: the remaining burn lived in the rack's block entity, so a returned item would come back full, which would make "pull it out and put it back" a perpetual reactor. Since stage 4 the remainder lives on the item itself, so there is nothing left to throw away: right-clicking empty-handed hands the rod back with all its durability; breaking the column (a creeper included) drops everything racked, half-burnt rods among it; a rod put back in carries on from where it stopped. A burnt-out rod does not vanish — it becomes a fuel rod cladding right where it stands. There is still no depleted rod on the output: exists in the mod and arrives by another route (mutation); wiring it to the reactor is an open question.

Craft — shapeless, x1 at a time. Two items in any cells of the grid. Refuelling happens dozens of rods at a time, and a full 3x3 layout for each one would be a punishment for scale. The item's shape is the business of the cladding's recipe — that one is a full 3x3, and it is done once.

c.h: The chain from ore to rod
c.t: Step Machine In -> out EU/operation 1 Macerator 1 raw uranium -> 2 uranium dust 300 2 Thermal Centrifuge 1 dust -> 2 uranium concentrate (x2 operations) 800 x 2 3 Compressor 2 concentrate -> 1 enriched uranium (x2 operations) 260 x 2 4 Workbench 1 enriched uranium + a cladding -> 1 rod — The result: one uranium ore = two rods, exactly, with no remainder and no rounding. Processing costs 2,420 EU per ore = 1,210 EU per rod; the first assembly adds the casing on top (~400 EU for the shielding plate, plus iron) — ~1,610 EU. On a refill the casing is already there, and the rod costs only its own 1,210 EU and half an ore. A shielding plate is a third of a palladium ingot and one tempered iron ingot, plus a hit from the forge hammer. Palladium is mined in the Nether alone, so the reactor is out of reach until that trip however many chests of uranium are on hand — but only once: casings come back.

Tier: none (the item carries no energy; the reactor it feeds is HV). Needs: (uranium + thermal centrifuge + compressor) and a fuel rod cladding — that is palladium, and therefore the Nether. Unlocks: output from the reactor room. An empty room is a diagnostic device; rods make it a generator. Growth: MOX and other grades of rod are outside this epic (see [](../../FUTURECONTENT.md), ).

Fuel Rod Cladding — the casing it is built from and turns back into. Reactor Column — where it goes and how it wears down. Reactor Controller — what burns it and what it becomes. Thermal Centrifuge and Compressor — the two machines that make enriched uranium. Macerator — the start of the chain, ore into dust.

The Mute Chip is an upgrade item that drops into a machine's upgrade slot (the first, active slot of the upgrade panel). While the chip is installed the machine is fully silent: the continuous working hum disappears, and no other sounds from the block itself play either. Pop the chip out and the sound comes back. It's pure convenience — speed, energy use and output are all unchanged. It slots into any machine or generator that has an upgrade panel (a few blocks have none — the Energy Condenser, for one), but you'll only hear the effect on blocks that make sound in the first place. In a silent machine the chip just sits in the slot doing nothing — which is expected. Mini-example: your macerator bank hums loudly next to your base. Drop a mute chip into each one's upgrade slot and the room goes quiet — grinding speed and EU cost stay exactly the same.
Uses no energy — it's an item with no energy of its own.
Not applicable (item). It only goes into a machine's active upgrade slot; hoppers and other automation don't see the upgrade slot.
Not applicable (item). Stack: 64 in a normal inventory; in the upgrade slot it's 1.

While a mute chip sits in the active upgrade slot, the machine makes no sound at all — neither its working hum nor any other sound the block would normally play. Everything else about the machine is untouched: same speed, same EU use, same output. Take the chip out and the sound returns.
Crafted at a workbench (shaped 3×3): an empty chip in the centre, ringed by any wool on all eight sides. — any wool (×8); — empty chip (×1).
An upgrade with no tier of its own. Built on the empty chip — the shared blank that future upgrade chips will also start from.
Empty Chip — the blank base this chip is built on. Upgrade system overview — how upgrade slots work.

The Overclocker is an upgrade item that goes into its own arm of a machine's upgrade panel (the top one, marked with a double-arrow hint). There are three tiers — I, II and III — and they are three separate items rather than a stack of one, so exactly one overclocker works in a machine. Each tier cuts the operation to 80 % of the previous length and doubles the EU drawn per tick. The two multipliers are deliberately asymmetric: , so every tier raises the energy spent per operation by 60 %. Speed is bought with energy, never given away. Example: an unmodified macerator grinds ore in 150 ticks for 300 EU. With tier III it finishes in 77 ticks — nearly twice as fast — but burns 1232 EU, four times as much. A copper cable can no longer feed it; you need gold.

The chip itself neither stores nor consumes energy — it changes the draw of the machine holding it. Tier Ticks (macerator) EU/tick Speed-up EU per operation — 150 2 1.00× 300 I 120 4 1.25× 480 II 96 8 1.56× 768 III 77 16 1.95× 1232
Not applicable (item). Goes into the panel's overclocker arm — one per machine. Hoppers and pipes cannot see the upgrade panel.
Not applicable (item). Stack: 64 in a normal inventory, 1 in an upgrade slot.

While the chip sits in the panel, the machine runs faster and eats more. Hover the panel's gear tab and the tooltip shows the installed tier and how far speed and draw have moved. Which tier a machine will run depends on its voltage. A machine cannot draw more than its tier allows: LV carries 32 EU/tick, MV 128. So the limit is derived, not fixed: Machines Base draw Tier Limit Draw at the limit Sawmill, electric furnace, extractor, compressor, macerator, polymerizer, distillation column, vulcanizer, galvanic bath 2 EU/t LV III 16 EU/t Alloy smelter, incubator 8 EU/t LV II 32 EU/t Assembler 12 EU/t MV III 96 EU/t A tier above the limit still sits in the slot but acts as the limit — the machine could never take in that much energy per tick. Overclocking hits the wiring before it hits the tier. A copper cable carries 12 EU/tick, so on an ordinary LV machine the first two tiers run on starter copper while the third already needs a gold cable (48 EU/tick). That is not a bug: speed is bought with a network upgrade too. What it does not do: change recipes, touch odds (including the incubator's), shorten the distillation column's warm-up, or work in generators and the condenser — output and banking are governed differently there.

An upgrade with no tier of its own. Tier I is built on the empty chip; each next tier from the previous one. The real gate is an energy clot of the matching tier, and those come only from the Energy Condenser, out of grid surplus. An overclocker cannot be bought with ore: your power plant pays for it.
Energy Condenser — the only source of clots. Empty chip — the base of tier I. Mute chip — its neighbour in the panel; the two can share it. Upgrade system overview — how the upgrade slots work.

The Statistics Chip is an upgrade item that drops into the right slot of a machine's upgrade panel. While the chip is installed the machine keeps a record of its own work, and a summary panel appears in its interface: how long the block actually ran, how much energy it received, spent or generated, how many items it processed, and how many neighbours are wired to it. Without the chip the machine measures nothing at all. That isn't an interface restriction — the instrument simply isn't there: no counters run, no data accumulates, nothing is stored in the world. Statistics are therefore a deliberate choice: you fit the chip where you actually want to understand what is going on. Mini-example: your electric furnace keeps stalling and you can't tell whether it's short on power. Fit a statistics chip and you'll see "working time" crawling while "received" sits well below "spent" — the furnace is starved, not broken.
Uses no energy — it's an item with no energy of its own. The measuring costs the machine nothing either: no EU is spent on keeping the record.
Not applicable (item). It only goes into the statistics slot of the upgrade panel (the right one); hoppers and automation cannot see upgrade slots.
Not applicable (item). Stack: 64 in a normal inventory; 1 in the upgrade slot.

While the chip sits in the slot, the machine counts: working time — ticks the block genuinely worked, not ticks it stood idle; energy — received from outside, sent to the grid, generated by itself, and spent on its work; processed — completed processing operations; now and peak — the current (averaged) EU/tick rate and the session maximum; connected — how many adjacent faces are joined to sources and consumers. Counting starts the moment the chip goes in: the instrument knows nothing of the block's past, so a machine that has been running for a week starts from zero. Pull the chip out and the totals are kept but stop growing; put it back and counting resumes from where it left off. The panel opens from a tab to the left of the machine's interface; you can drag it, and its position is remembered. Values refresh only while the window is open — close it and the machine stops sending data.

Built around a copper coil — the same sensing element that sits in the Network Analyzer — with an empty chip at the centre, two glass panes for the display window and redstone for the signal. The chip is the analyzer's built-in little brother: you carry the analyzer and question the whole grid with it, while the chip lives inside one machine and watches only that one.
An upgrade with no tier of its own. Built on the empty chip, the common blank behind every upgrade chip.
Empty Chip — the blank this chip is built from. Upgrade system overview — how the upgrade slots work. Mute Chip — the neighbouring convenience upgrade in the same panel.

Bonus Chest injection — this is not a mod block but a change to the vanilla spawn bonus chest loot. When you create a world with the Bonus Chest option enabled, the chest that spawns near you gets Ala Industrial starter items added on top of the usual vanilla loot (logs, planks, apples, stone tools). The goal is an early taste of the mod before you build your first machine. Because the items are added (not replaced), other mods that touch the same bonus chest keep working. Mini-example: create a world with Bonus Chest: ON. Alongside vanilla logs and apples, the chest may hold a couple of Enriched Uranium Torches, sometimes a wooden scythe, and — if you're lucky — a battery or a tempered-iron axe.

Not applicable — this is not a block or a machine, so no EU is involved. A few of the items in the pools are energy items (battery, battery pouch); they arrive in the chest with no charge, just like freshly crafted ones.
Not applicable. The loot is generated once, when the world and its chest are created — there is no per-tick processing.
The bonus chest itself is a plain vanilla chest with the standard 27 slots. Adding our pools does not change its size — it only widens the range of items that can appear.
No mod GUI — it uses the vanilla chest screen.
The block is not ours — it's a vanilla chest. Only the loot table is modified.

Not applicable. The items in the pools are already-registered mod items: Category What can appear Chance Starter scythe Wooden / Stone / Gold Scythe (one at random) common Torch Enriched Uranium Torch (a small stack of 8–16) common Gear Wooden or Stone Gear (one at random, 1–2) common Rare: tempered iron a Tempered Iron Pickaxe / Axe / Sword / Shovel rare Rare: battery a Battery or Battery Pouch rare The common pools land often, so most bonus chests carry at least one mod item; the rare pool is intentionally uncommon (about a one-in-ten chest) so it never devalues crafting. The exact mix depends on the world seed, so two worlds give different chests.

This is a starter feature — your first contact with the mod's tools before any real progression, much like the vanilla bonus chest handing you apples and stone tools. The rare tempered-iron tools and batteries are deliberately low-chance so they stay a lucky bonus, not a reliable resource.
Scythes — the starter tools. Tempered Iron — tools — the rare pool. Battery Pouch — a rare energy item. Uranium Torch — a starter light source. Metal Gears — a starter crafting component.

The Electrum Chest is a storage block with 81 slots (9 rows of 9) — half again as much as the Gold Chest (54). It uses no energy; it's the "civilian" top tier of the storage line. Quick example: gold chest full of ore? Upgrade it to electrum — you gain 27 slots and keep the contents. Electrum is an alloy of gold and silver, and the chest looks the part: pale gold, lighter and cooler than the gold tier. The lid is animated, and the open sound is the same metallic one the other tiers use.
Takes any items — 81 slots across 9 rows of 9. Slots Accepts Count Storage any items 81 (9 rows × 9)

The window shows six rows out of nine; the rest are reached with the scrollbar on the right — the same way the modular warehouse and the double chest work. The mouse wheel, dragging the thumb and clicking the groove all work. Shift-click puts items into the rows that are off screen too. That matters: a plain shift-click works over the window's visible slots and at this capacity would silently stop at the sixth row, reporting "full" while a third of the chest sits empty.

c.h: Why scrolling instead of one more row
c.t: The three tiers below grew by exactly one row each, because the window grew with them. That ended at gold — not by choice, but against a measured screen ceiling. Panel height . How much height the window actually gets by the GUI scale, and on the default setting the game picks it itself: the scale rises while . The guaranteed minimum is therefore exactly 240 pixels. Rows Panel height Fits 240? 6 (gold) 220 px ✓ and that is exactly the vanilla double chest — the tallest container window the game itself ships 7 238 px technically yes — with a one-pixel margin; that is not a margin 9 274 px ✗ The gold chest already sits on that ceiling. So the next tier changes the window rather than the number of rows on screen. And once the window stopped being the limit, there was no reason to charge a ring of expensive alloy for a token nine slots — hence the jump straight to 81.

Two electrum chests placed side by side, facing the same way, merge into one double chest of 162 slots (18 rows) — by the same vanilla placement rules as the other tiers: without sneaking a new chest joins a suitable neighbour by itself, sneak-clicking a side face attaches it deliberately, and sneaking elsewhere keeps it single. Different tiers never merge. The double's window is the same six-row scrolling panel; it just slides over eighteen rows instead of nine. Lid and sound are shared: both halves lift together and the sound plays once, from the seam. Automation sees a double as one container: a hopper, dropper or item pipe that fills one half continues into the other. Breaking one half returns the other to single; each half drops only its own contents. A comparator reads the fill level (for a double — the combined one, identically from either half), and the chest can be waterlogged.

A squat chest block, like every vanilla chest and the previous tiers. Properties are identical to the iron, silver and gold chests. Field Value Shape squat 14×14×14 column Hardness 3.0 Blast resistance 6.0 Tool pickaxe (any, no tier gate) Drops itself yes; contents spill when broken

A ring of eight electrum ingots around a gold chest. Contents survive the upgrade. The same ring of eight ingots gave +9 slots on the previous tiers and gives +27 here — deliberately: once the window changes mechanics anyway, a token increase for the mod's top alloy is not justified.

The chest line: vanilla copper (27) → iron (36) → silver (45) → gold (54) → electrum (81). The electrum chest does not devalue the modular warehouse: 81 slots is less than the warehouse's 108, but it is one block instead of four and needs no room to build. A double electrum chest (162) is the largest storage in the mod — and it costs sixteen electrum ingots on top of the whole upgrade chain beneath it.

Gold Chest — the previous tier. Electrum — the crafting material. Storage Module — the other warehouse answer; the source of the GUI-height measurements the scrolling decision rests on. Stock Display Frame — shows the item count without opening the chest.

The Enriched Uranium Torch is a decorative light source: light level 14 (same as a vanilla torch), but with a bright green flame and the occasional green sparkle. Place it on the floor or on a wall, just like a normal torch. It uses no energy — it's decoration, not a generator. The main perk: it doesn't go out underwater. You can place it under water and it keeps burning.

Behaves like a vanilla torch: breaks instantly by hand, has no collision, a piston will break it. What Value Light level 14 (same as a vanilla torch) Flame green, with occasional sparkles Placement on the or on a wall — one icon, both forms Underwater burns, doesn't go out Tool none — breaks by hand instantly
Wooden placement/break sound, same as a vanilla torch.

Two ways to make it, both unlocked once you have uranium dust: From scratch: uranium dust on top, coal (or charcoal) in the middle, stick at the bottom → 4 torches. Upgrade: a plain vanilla torch + uranium dust (shapeless) → 1 torch.
Tier: none (decoration). Requires: Uranium — its dust for the recipe. So this is a late-game decorative goal, once you've found and processed uranium.
Uranium — the source of uranium dust. Iron Chest — another "civilian" block with no energy.

The Gold Chest is a storage block with 54 slots (6 rows of 9) — one whole row more than the Silver Chest. It uses no energy; it's the "civilian" tier of the storage line, the step above silver. Craft it by putting a silver chest in the center of a crafting grid and surrounding it with 8 gold ingots. It looks like a proper 3D chest with an animated lid (same shape as the vanilla wooden, iron and silver chests, but gold-coloured) and the same metallic open/close sound as the iron chest. Like the lower tiers, it's a pure content block with no energy hookup — only storage inside.

The chest takes any items — 54 slots across 6 rows of 9. Your inventory shows below it as usual. Shift-click moves items between the chest and your inventory. Slots Accepts Count Storage any items 54 (6 rows × 9) Player inventory — 27 + 9 (hotbar), drawn from the texture

A normal container window — no energy or progress bars (the chest is not a machine). The window is taller than the silver chest's because of the sixth row; both labels — "Gold Chest" above the chest grid and "Inventory" below it — sit on the left. GUI atlas: (256×256, visible area 176×220 — taller than silver's 202 due to the 6th row). No energy/progress bars (the chest is not a machine). Both labels on the left: the "Gold Chest" title above the chest grid and the "Inventory" label in the gap between the chest and the player inventory.

In the world it's a volumetric 3D chest on its own texture, with a lid that smoothly opens and closes — exactly like the vanilla wooden chest and the previous mod tiers, just gold-coloured. The inventory icon is volumetric too. 3D model: reuses the vanilla chest model (lid / lock / body), baked from its own layer. Texture — (64×64, vanilla layout). Fed through the same path as the vanilla chests — correct depth, culling and mipmaps (no white outline). Lid animation: openness is smoothly interpolated by the client ticker; the easing curve matches vanilla (). Facing rotation: the chest rotates to face the player on placement (yaw around the center-top). Item icon — 3D render of the chest.

The open and close sounds reuse the iron chest samples ( / ) — the metallic sound is shared across all tiers, just like the vanilla wooden sound is shared across all wood variants. There are no separate events, so the subtitles show "Iron Chest opens/closes". Volume 0.42 (like the previous tiers — quieter than vanilla's 0.5), random pitch 0.9–1.0. Sounds: the iron chest's open and close sounds (no separate gold keys).

Two gold chests placed side by side, facing the same way, merge into one double chest of 108 slots — following the vanilla placement rules exactly: without sneaking the new chest joins a matching neighbour automatically, sneak-clicking the side of a lone neighbour attaches to it deliberately, and sneak-placing elsewhere keeps it single. Different tiers never merge. The double's window shows 6 rows; the rest are reached with the scrollbar on the right (like the storage module's warehouse window). Shift-click reaches the hidden rows too. Lid and sound are shared: both halves lift the lid together and the opening sound plays once, from the seam. Automation sees the double as one container: a hopper, dropper or item pipe that hits a full half continues into the other. Breaking one half reverts the other to a single chest; each half spills only its own contents. An open double window closes when either half is broken. A stock display frame on either half shows the combined total. Along with the doubles, every tier gained two vanilla conveniences: a comparator reads the chest's fullness (a double reads combined, the same from either half), and the chest can be waterlogged like a vanilla one.

The chest is squat — not a full cube but a 14×14×14 column (like all vanilla chests and the previous tiers). It breaks with any pickaxe, drops itself when destroyed and spills all of its contents. The block properties are identical to the iron and silver chests (same shape, same hardness). Field Value Shape squat 14×14×14 column (not a full cube, like vanilla chests); neighbors don't cull their faces against it — the render is correct, no "x-ray" Hardness 3.0 Blast resistance 6.0 Tool pickaxe (no tier gate — any) Facing horizontal, rotated to face the player on placement Render shape (a 3D chest is drawn on top of the block) Drop self via loot table; the inventory contents spill on break Sounds / (reused, see §Sound)

Crafted at a crafting table: a silver chest in the center, surrounded by 8 gold ingots — the same "previous tier + 8 ingots" pattern as the lower tiers (copper + 8 iron → iron, iron + 8 silver → silver). Type: , category. , .
Chest line: vanilla (27) → Iron Chest (36) → Silver Chest (45) → Gold Chest (54) → Electrum Chest (81).
Silver Chest — the previous tier, the template for this block. Iron Chest — the reference implementation for all chest tiers. Battery Box — the mod's other "storage" block, but for energy.

The Guide Book is Ala Industrial's in-game manual. A new player lands in a world with non-trivial mechanics (EU instead of FE, LV/MV/HV voltage tiers, cables with distance loss, machine face ports) and, with no built-in tutorial, is left to guess or read an external wiki. The book removes that entry barrier: the player receives it in their inventory automatically on first spawn (exactly once), opens it with a right-click — a full-screen view with tabs and page navigation — and works through the chapters up to a first working power grid and machine without leaving the game. The book needs no energy and does nothing mechanically — it is pure reading material. Its content is built from the same source as the mod's wiki site, so the numbers in the book never drift from the game. Mini-example: enter a new world → the "Guide Book" is in your inventory → right-click → a screen opens on the "Getting Started" tab → click the "Solar Panel" link → read how much EU it makes and how to craft it.

Auto-given on first join. The first time a player enters a world, the book is placed in their inventory exactly once. The "already given" ledger lives in per-world saved data (a holding a set of UUIDs) — it survives death/respawn/dimension changes and never double-gives on relog. Existing players get it once on a mod update too: their UUID isn't in the ledger yet, so the book is given on their first join after the update and the UUID is added. Recovery if lost — two safeguards, neither of which gates the auto-give: a craft (cheap, LV-accessible, not schematic-gated); the command (reuses the existing command; gives/opens the book). The player is never locked out of the tutorial. If the inventory is full during auto-give, the book drops at the player's feet (never lost).

Opened with a right-click — a full-screen window (not a chest: no slots, no inventory). It has: Tabs (top-level chapters) that mirror the wiki site's category grouping plus a leading Getting Started — hand-written onboarding: first generator → first cable → first machine; Energy — what EU is, LV/MV/HV tiers, cables and distance loss, face ports; Generators, 4. Machines, 5. Storage, 6. Energy Transfer, Materials, 8. Items & Tools, 9. Components, 10. Utilities. Entry list within a tab (one per block/item/mechanic), scrollable. Entry page — a spread with page navigation (next/prev) and a "back" button to the list. Clickable links inside the text — jump to another entry (and, in v1.1, to an anchor within it). Recipe widget on a page — a crafting/processing grid (draws ingredients + result; works without JEI/REI installed). Text is word-wrapped, and long lists scroll. Visually it follows the mod style — the same palette and bevel panels as the other interfaces.

The book covers every block and item already in the game: for each one, a short description, its stats (tier, EU, buffer) and its crafting recipe. The numbers in the book (EU, tiers, buffers, recipes) come from the same source as the wiki site, so they always match the game — no drift. Planned and not-yet-added blocks are left out: the book never promises what isn't in the game yet. The framing "Getting Started" and "Energy" chapters are written as an introductory tutorial for new players.

The book is an item (not a block): it can't be placed, stacks to 1, has no EU buffer. Its "shape" is an ordinary item model (→ with the icon). Right-click opens the GUI (see "Interface"); no block is placed in the world, no collision. What Value Type item, not a block Stack 1 EU buffer none Right-click opens the book screen (client-side) World placement none
The craft is a dead-simple shapeless recipe: a vanilla + (the earliest, cheapest mod component). Not schematic-gated (the book is auto-given anyway; the craft only recovers a lost one).

Tier: none (a utility, not part of the energy chain). Available immediately — it's the entry point into progression, not a rung of it. It guides the player through the mod's real progression (ore → generator → cable → machine → tiers).

v1: + — full chapter content ( is the source, as everywhere in the mod). The other 18 languages get a translated item name, while chapter content is shown in English for now; a full chapter translation comes later. All book text is via lang keys; no hardcoded strings (project rule).
The book is built from the same source as the mod's wiki site: the same content and the same numbers, but right in the player's hands.

The Industrial Workbench is a decorative full block — a steel table with a vise — and the job site of a new villager profession: the Industrialist. It works exactly like the vanilla "blast furnace → armorer" pair: place the workbench next to an unemployed adult villager and he will walk over, claim it and become an Industrialist. The Industrialist is a buyer of the mod's resources: he pays emeralds for tin, silver, nickel, uranium and dusts, and at the top level sells you the electronic circuit and copper coils — an expensive shortcut for players who would rather not craft them. One workbench = one villager, same as every vanilla profession.

The main direction is buying — you hand over resources, the villager pays emeralds; at Master level he sells components back. Levels unlock through trading, like any vanilla villager. Variety: each level has a pool of 3 trades and the villager rolls 2 at random — just like a vanilla armorer. Different Industrialists therefore offer different combinations. The Iron Chest is a storage block with 36 slots (4 rows of 9) — a whole row more than the vanilla chest. It uses no energy; it's just a bigger place to keep your stuff, one tier above the vanilla copper chest. Mini-example: Copper chest full of ore? Upgrade it: put the copper chest in the center of a crafting grid and surround it with 8 iron ingots → Iron Chest, +9 slots, contents preserved. It looks like a proper 3D chest with an animated lid (same shape as the vanilla wooden chest, only a different colour) and plays its own metallic open/close sound.
Takes any items — 36 slots in 4 rows of 9. Shift-click moves stacks between the chest and your inventory. Slots Accepts Count Storage any items 36 (4 rows × 9)
A normal container window — no energy or progress bars, just the storage grid and your inventory below it. The window is slightly taller than a vanilla chest's because of the 4th row.

Two iron chests placed side by side, facing the same way, merge into one double chest of 72 slots — following the vanilla placement rules exactly: without sneaking the new chest joins a matching neighbour automatically, sneak-clicking the side of a lone neighbour attaches to it deliberately, and sneak-placing elsewhere keeps it single. Different tiers never merge. The double's window shows 6 rows; the rest are reached with the scrollbar on the right (like the storage module's warehouse window). Shift-click reaches the hidden rows too. Lid and sound are shared: both halves lift the lid together and the opening sound plays once, from the seam. Automation sees the double as one container: a hopper, dropper or item pipe that hits a full half continues into the other. Breaking one half reverts the other to a single chest; each half spills only its own contents. An open double window closes when either half is broken. A stock display frame on either half shows the combined total. Along with the doubles, every tier gained two vanilla conveniences: a comparator reads the chest's fullness (a double reads combined, the same from either half), and the chest can be waterlogged like a vanilla one.

The Mob Repeller is a guard block: while it is wired to the grid and its field is on, hostile mobs flee the zone around it — the way a creeper runs from a cat — and cannot approach your base. Passive animals, villagers and players are untouched; neutral mobs (enderman, zombified piglin) are expelled only when already angry. This is the first tier: an 8-block radius in every direction (a cube). The block upgrades — insert a full Soul Vessel into its slot and the repeller grows into the Medium Repeller with a 16-block radius. Quick example: place a repeller by your door and run an LV cable from a Battery Box — at night creepers no longer hug the walls and skeletons stop sniping from the porch. You still need torches against spawns inside the zone: the field drives mobs out, it does not stop them from appearing.

A pure LV consumer. The field is an upkeep cost: while enabled it drains 8 EU/t whether or not any mobs are near. Run out of energy and the field goes dark — mobs can approach again. What Value Internal buffer 2,000 EU Field upkeep 8 EU/t (constant while enabled) Input up to 32 EU/t (LV) Energy is accepted through all six faces.

Twice a second the block sweeps its zone and expels actively hostile mobs: Who What happens Regular monsters (zombies, skeletons, creepers, spiders…) Turn and run past the boundary Piglins and hoglins Fear the block natively (like soul torches) — even slightly beyond the field Fliers (phantom, ghast, vex) and slimes Are pushed out Enderman (angered) Teleports away Enderman (calm), zombified piglin (calm) Left alone — until provoked Shulker Not expelled (anchored to its block) — the single exception Passive mobs, villagers, players Unaffected The zone is a 17×17×17 cube (radius 8 in every direction), matching the highlight dome.

Right-click opens the screen: energy level, the Soul Vessel slot and the dome button — it shows the zone boundary in the world to you personally (a translucent cube with a wireframe). Other players do not see your dome. The button is a toggle; the dome clears itself if the block is removed. Any Soul Vessel fits the slot, even an empty one: the line under it says how many souls are still missing. Once 80 are in, the block consumes the vessel whole on the next tick and becomes a Medium Repeller, keeping its stored energy. Souls beyond the threshold burn with the vessel — don't overcharge it. Redstone. A signal on the block (a lever, a button, a comparator) switches the field off: it goes dark and stops drawing power. Remove the signal and it runs again.

The only way is to insert a full Soul Vessel (250 souls) into a Medium Repeller. The Player Profile is a personal career screen. Vanilla statistics will tell you "42 pickaxes crafted", but it cannot see your career in the mod — how much EU your grid generated, how much ore your machines processed. The profile collects that mod activity and turns it into a career progression: a mastery-point system of 40 levels grouped into 8 themed ranks (Apprentice → Legend). Open it with the hotkey (rebindable in Controls; vanilla already uses for Social Interactions in multiplayer) or with the button in the top-right corner of your inventory. It shows your current rank and sub-level (), a mastery bar toward the next level, career EU counters (produced / usefully consumed), your "mod activity" time, and a breakdown of production by generator type. Not to be confused with vanilla advancements (one-off checkpoints) or vanilla statistics (a flat table). The profile is a set of cumulative career meters plus a rank progression.

The main source is machine work. Mastery is credited to a machine's owner at the moment it completes an operation (smelting, macerating, extracting, compressing), worth the operation's full EU cost. An operation aborted by a redstone contraption burns EU but earns no mastery — that is the anti-AFK rule. The second source is generator output, but 20x weaker. A generator runs without you, so its contribution is deliberately token: it will not let you sleep your way to Legend, yet it stops a large power farm from feeling entirely unrewarded. Only EU actually credited into the buffer counts — a generator spinning into a full buffer earns nothing at all. Charging storage blocks, teleporter jumps and pumping fluid earn no mastery whatsoever. A pump runs unattended and an oil vein holds thousands of buckets: at one point per bucket a single AFK session would skip one or two ranks, so raw extraction does not count as "useful work" — processing what you pumped does. "Earns no mastery" is not "goes uncounted". The Consumed counter answers "where did my energy go", not "what earned me points", so it is wider than the progression: it covers machine work and the price of teleport jumps. A player living on the teleporter used to see a flat zero there next to a healthy Produced figure — the station drains its buffer directly, bypassing the machine cycle, and that spending never reached the profile. A jump is booked to whoever jumped (not to the station's owner, so a hop onto someone else's public station still shows up in your own profile), once, and only on success: an aborted warmup or a refusal for lack of power books nothing. Parameter Value Config EU→mastery rate (machines) 1,000 EU of work = 1 mastery point EU→mastery rate (generators) 20,000 EU produced = 1 point Level curve exponential, x1.18 per level , Levels 40 (8 ranks x 5 sub-levels) — Sub-level Roman numerals (I...V) — Level-up notice sound only — Mastery is a derived value: it is computed from the two career EU counters rather than stored on its own, so retuning the rates in the config can never eat mastery you already earned. A rank you have reached is never taken away by a balance change — the highest level reached is remembered.
Sub-levels Rank 1–5 Apprentice 6–10 Journeyman 11–15 Technician 16–20 Operator 21–25 Engineer 26–30 Architect 31–35 Magnate 36–40 Legend

Statistics are tracked per machine owner — whoever placed it (re-assigned by placing it again). If a friend loads ore into your machine, the mastery is yours. The profile is per-player and private: on a server you only ever see your own career. Credit accrues only while the owner is online and not in creative (creative EU is free and must not convert into a career); a machine with no owner (a structure, the demo stand) credits nobody. Machines placed by other mods' automation. The "owner online" rule also covers machines placed by another mod's fake player (auto-builders, robots). No separate mechanism exists for them, and none is needed: such a player is never among the connected players, so its UUID resolves to nobody and no one gains mastery. When the automation instead acts under a real player's identity (a common approach so that permissions and land claims see the owner), the work is credited to that player — and only while they are online, exactly as for a hand-placed machine. This is deliberate behaviour, not a gap.

The profile lives in a per-player data attachment. It survives relogging and death, and is synced only to its owner. Server-side accumulation is batched in memory and folded into storage every few seconds (and on logout / server stop) — never written per tick.

The player profile is a pure screen (GUI), not a block and not an item: nothing is placed in the world, and it has no shape or collision. Its "entry point" is not a physical item but a hotkey and a widget button in the vanilla inventory (see "Entry points"). The data lives in a per-player attachment on the server; the screen is client-side. Field Value Type screen (GUI), not a block or item Placement in world none Shape / collision none Opening hotkey or the button in the top-right of the inventory (client-side) Data storage per-player data attachment (server)

hotkey (Profile) — the default, rebindable under Controls. Button in the top-right corner of the inventory (absent in the creative inventory — the hotkey works everywhere). — an operator utility command (progression debugging / QA).

A quest system, milestone buffs (when they arrive — on machines and the grid only, never on the player), a shareable server profile card, and wider statistics categories (crafting, mining by ore, a per-purpose breakdown of spending) are separate future tasks. Teleportation has since left that list: jumps count toward Consumed, they just have no row of their own on the screen.

The Stock Display Frame is a frame you hang on any container — a vanilla chest, barrel, or shulker box, or the mod's Iron Chest — and it shows the item count inside right on the frame, in real time. It uses no energy: it's a warehouse convenience, "price tags" for rows of chests, so you can read how full they are without opening a window. Mini-example: Put a diamond in the frame on your ore chest → it shows how many diamonds are in there. Swap the diamond for iron → it now counts iron ingots. Empty frame → no number at all.

An item is in the frame → the number equals how many items of that type are in the container (the item acts as a filter). The frame is empty → no number is shown (it looks like a plain frame). No container behind the frame → no number. The container is empty (with a filter in the frame) → shows . Only top-level slots are counted — it does not dig into shulkers or bundles sitting inside the chest. A double chest — vanilla or one of the mod's own doubles — counts as one container: a frame on either half shows the combined total. The frame recounts once per second.

There's no screen. The number is drawn flat on the frame's face, in its bottom strip — white with a dark outline, no backdrop. It turns with the frame (not a billboard), so it's only visible from the side the frame faces. Put a filter item in with a right-click → the number appears. Right-click again (or hit the frame) → the filter pops back to you, the number disappears. The filter item is raised and shrunk a little to make room for the digit; with no filter the frame looks like a plain one (item centred). Unlike a vanilla frame, the item does not rotate — rotation would just be noise for a filter. Filled maps can't be placed in it. Display distance — up to 24 blocks (the text hides beyond that, for performance). Formatting: the exact number below 10,000, abbreviated after that — , .

The frame is an entity, not a block (just like the vanilla item frame). It's the same size and behaves the same way: flat, on a wall, no collision. Right-click a block face to hang it, hit it to take it down; break the block behind it and the frame pops off, dropping its own item. What Value Type entity (like a vanilla item frame) Placement on a wall, floor, or ceiling face Drops itself yes (as the mod's frame item, plus the filter if any)

The Storage Module is a 27-slot block whose whole point is that it merges with its neighbours. Put two modules against each other and you have one 54-slot warehouse behind a single window. Three makes 81. Four makes 108, and that is the ceiling. Right-click any module and the window shows the whole warehouse, not just the 27 slots of the block you clicked. No energy, no redstone, any shape you like — a wall, a column, an L. The one rule: modules must touch face to face, not along an edge or a corner. Quick example: you placed a module, filled it, ran out. Butt a second one against it: open either of the two and you are looking at 54 slots as one list.
Field Value Role none Buffer (EU) 0 Max input (EU/tick) n/a Max output (EU/tick) n/a EU/tick 0 The module takes no part in the energy network: it neither carries EU nor connects to cables.

Slot Accepts Count Module storage any items 27 (3 rows of 9) Items physically sit in the module they were put into. There is no master inventory: the warehouse window is a view over every module's inventory at once, not a separate store. Everything else follows from that — what drops when you break one, and what happens when a chunk unloads.

Modules adjacent Warehouse slots Rows total Rows shown Scroll 1 27 3 3 none 2 54 6 6 none (bar drawn inactive) 3 81 9 6 3 rows 4 108 12 6 6 rows 5 or more 108 (cap) 12 6 6 rows Slots and rows are unchanged — only the window is: it shows at most six rows and the rest are reached with the scrollbar on the right. Why six is in the Balance section.

A module joins the warehouse if it touches another member face to face. Edge and corner contact does not count — so you can build two separate warehouses flush against each other. The set is worked out afresh every time the window opens, walking out from the module you clicked. Nothing is remembered, so placing or breaking a module needs no rebuilding. If a build holds more than four modules, the first four in walk order form the warehouse. Clicking a different module of the same build may give a different four — the window shows how many are connected, so this is visible.

Two window sizes: 3 rows (176x166) for a lone module and 6 rows (195x220) for anything larger. A scrollbar sits to the right of the grid, in the 19 px added to the panel width for it. The mouse wheel, dragging the thumb and clicking the track all work. A two-module warehouse has nothing to scroll to, and the bar is drawn in its inactive shade rather than disappearing: a control that comes and goes is harder to read than one visibly off. Shift-click fills the rows that are off screen too. Not a detail: vanilla's shift-click moves between menu slots, and the window only has six rows of them, so the obvious implementation would quietly stop halfway and report the warehouse full while half of it was empty. No search — 108 slots is too few to need one. What is synced. Two numbers in : how many rows the warehouse has in total, and which row the window sits on. The client needs the first to draw the bar and the second to place the thumb; the server owns both. The scroll itself travels on vanilla's, where the button id IS the requested top row; the server clamps it, so a packet asking for row 500 cannot read past the warehouse. Why a view rather than moving the slots. / are , and a menu's slot list is part of the network contract: the indices in are positions in it, so rebuilding the list under a live menu desynchronises the client. Vanilla's one scrolling display (the creative inventory) does the same thing: the slots never move, what moves is the answer the container behind them gives.
Field Value Shape full cube 16³ Hardness 3.0 Blast resistance 6.0 Tool pickaxe Drops with NBT false — contents are not kept in the item

c.h: Looks: a warehouse reads as one cabinet
c.t: The module is a steel cabinet with three drawers — one per row of nine slots it adds to the window. Top and bottom are not drawers but a body plate with an inset service panel. Adjacent modules merge visually as well. Along the face two modules share, the frame disappears: the drawer fronts run on across the joint, the tops become one continuous bench top, and the border survives only around the outside of the warehouse. A 2x2 wall reads as one six-drawer cabinet, a row of four as one long one. The merged look means exactly one thing: this is one warehouse. The moment a build grows past four modules the frames come back on all of them at once, and the build looks like separate cabinets again. That is not cosmetic but an honest signal: in a build that size the warehouse depends on which module you click (see "Merging rules"), and no seam could promise that two blocks are one store. Take the extra module away and the merged look returns. Touching at an edge or a corner merges neither the mechanics nor the picture: two warehouses can stand flush against each other and still look separate. How it is drawn. The connection is built into the block model, not laid over it. Every face is cut into non-overlapping rectangles — one band per edge, four one-pixel corners on the cap faces and the middle — and each rectangle is drawn exactly once, from either the framed texture or the open one. Nothing is offset outward and nothing overlaps, so a joint cannot pick up its own lighting or show a step. The first version instead laid patches over the cube, pushed 0.1 blocks proud, and the player saw a raised band running through the bench top and a short black line where a patch ended. A rim corner on the cap face belongs to two edges at once, so it opens only when both of its neighbours are there. Handing it to one edge punches a two-pixel hole in the east/west border at every north-south joint. The blockstate and its 21 models are generated () and are only edited through the generator. (wired into and the pre-commit hook) compares the files against the generator and separately proves the joint is seamless: every pixel of every face is drawn exactly once, no element leaves the block volume, and the wall and bench top composed from the models are pixel-identical to a reference "one big cabinet" built from the framed texture alone. Breaking a module drops its own contents and nothing else. Neighbouring modules are untouched: their items are theirs and never moved. Breaking a module in the middle of a build simply splits it — each part becomes its own warehouse. Items in the detached modules do not drop: they stay put and rejoin the shared window once the connection is restored. Breaking the assembler next to a warehouse gives the player back only what the machine itself held — the blueprint queue and the output area — and leaves the modules alone ( counts the drops exactly, so both a loss and a double drop show up). Taking the warehouse apart walks the capacity down to zero and never past it (; a count that went negative is what crashed Functional Storage). Pipes are pinned by transport, not by the presence of a port. runs sixteen ingots chest -> pipe -> warehouse and back, and separately checks that a dry run moves nothing and promises exactly what the committed move then carries — a mismatch between those two numbers is the classic duplication bug (XNet #173). Contents survive a reload. takes a module through NBT — the same path a chunk save and load takes — and checks among other things that slots do not shift: an empty slot left deliberately between two occupied ones has to come back empty.
Craft — 4 iron plates in a cross around a vanilla chest. The recipe is cheap on purpose: growing the warehouse is a consumable, not a milestone.

Tier: none — no energy required, available as soon as you have plates. Where it sits in the storage line: Iron Chest 36 → Silver 45 → Gold 54 → Electrum 81 → a module warehouse 108. The chests keep their value: they give their whole capacity in one block, the warehouse needs four. Later: the Assembler will draw its materials straight from a warehouse like this.

Gold Chest — the previous storage step Material Forms — the plates for the recipe Stock Display Frame — the reference for unloaded-chunk safety Assembler — the future consumer of the warehouse Item Pipe — fills the warehouse from outside

Ala Industrial is an industrial tech mod about energy and automation. It adds an energy system based on EU (Energy Units), generators that produce it, machines that consume it, storage and cables to move it around. This page covers the bare minimum to get going.

EU — Energy Unit — the mod's energy currency. Produced by generators, stored in buffers, consumed by machines. Tick — A game tick (1/20 of a second). EU/tick (EU/t) is the standard rate — generation, consumption and transfer are all measured in EU/t. LV / MV / HV — Voltage tiers: Low (32 EU/t), Medium (128 EU/t), High (512 EU/t). Every generator, cable and machine belongs to a tier; mixing tiers safely is the core of progression. Buffer — Internal EU storage of a block (a generator, machine or Battery Box). Sized per block. Tier — A block's voltage tier. LV machines accept ≤32 EU/t; feeding them more from a higher-tier source does nothing (they cap at their limit).

The starter progression is a loop of four blocks. Build them in this order and you have a working ore-doubling setup: Solar Panel — Produces EU during the day, with open sky above. Your first power source. Copper Cable — Cheap LV wire that carries EU from the panel to your machines. Battery Box — Stores EU for the night, so your machines can run when the panel sleeps. Macerator — Grinds ore into dust — doubles your metal output. The first real EU consumer.

Power has to come from somewhere. Start with the cheapest, simplest generator and grow from there — these are the earliest options: Generator (LV) — The simplest start: burns coal for EU on demand — and runs at night too. Solar Panel — Free EU in daylight under open sky; it sleeps at night — pair with a Battery Box. Water Mill / Wind Mill — Passive LV power from flowing water or wind — no fuel needed. Geothermal Generator — Stronger LV output from lava — a solid next step once you have a supply.

Place the Solar Panel with clear sky above it — any opaque block stops generation entirely. The Macerator doubles both ore blocks and raw ore (2 dust each). Only a ready ingot grinds back into a single dust — no doubling on that. Cables don't explode from overload; they just cap out, and the excess is simply not transferred. Mixing cable grades on one line? The whole network runs on the strongest cable present — both its throughput and its higher loss. One gold segment re-tariffs the entire run. Energy flows on 5 faces of a machine; the front face (where it points) is usually inert for EU. Store day-time EU in a Battery Box — without it, your machines go dark the moment the sun sets.
Once your first chain runs, explore the categories in the sidebar — more generators, machines, and material processing open up.
